A ten-line letter in invented signs, catalogued as Charles I to William Boswell, 1628 (TNA SP 106/5, DECODE R413). Mark Woodard recovered the simple substitution key and deciphered it on DECODE in 2021: court news of Buckingham’s return from Plymouth. His key was checked and applied here; three open signs are filled, and the sender and the date, 15 December 1627, are identified from the endorsement. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Credits · Woodard (key or decipherment used) At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter A ten-line cipher letter, endorsed “S[i]r Ra: Boswele. 24 Jan. 1627”, to William Boswell. The writer is Sir Ralph Boswell, a kinsman, not the King as the catalogue (no. 63) had it; the letter dates from 15 December 1627. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/5 ff. 20–21; DECODE R413 (login required). The cipher A simple substitution with one invented sign per letter; all 442 signs map consistently. How it was read DECODE already holds a decipherment by Mark Woodard of Furman University (9 November 2021), made with CrypTool 2. His transcription was aligned with his plaintext to give the key. What it says English court news: Buckingham has returned from Plymouth to Whitehall, is confident of the King, and does not fear his enemies in the Commons. Still open One sign stands for a whole word, probably “part”; a pair of signs in line 3 is not deciphered; two uses of one sign (p = s) are doubtful. The tally sheet’s author is unknown. Credit The decipherment is Mark Woodard’s. Lines 1–3 of the cipher, turned to the writer’s orientation: Upon Saterday being our fifteenth of the presente… Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/5 ff. 20–21, via DECODE R413.
boswell1628.html#the-document

Page one has ten numbered lines of signs, written across the sheet, with no word division. Page two carries the address, To my Especiall & most Esteemed Cosin William Boswell Esq. , a seal, and the endorsement S[i]r Ra: Boswele. 24 Jan. 1627 , that is 1627/8. Below it, in the same hand, is a list of eight topics: Hopyan, Pettyt, the Court of Wards, Yorkshire lands, Sir Anthony Aucher, Morgan, one unread, and the Earl of Dorset. The same page has a tally of every cipher sign with the numbers of the lines it occurs in. That is the working sheet of whoever took the letter apart, either Boswell or a clerk. DECODE’s own note already doubted that the King wrote it; its author and 1628 date are catalogue placeholders.
boswell1628.html#the-key

Woodard transcribed the signs as letters a – x . Aligned with his plaintext, all 442 signs map consistently: a U/V b P c O d N e S f A g T h E i R j D k Y l B m I n F o H q G r K s M t C u L v W p S (two uses, read here) w ? (two uses) x ? (one use) Letters with no sign in the text are j, q, x, z . The writer confuses P and F ( ofinion ), puts H for F ( heares = feares), and has an extra S in maskinge and L for R in loldes .
boswell1628.html#the-reading

Upon Saterday, being our fifteenth of the presente, our[s] greate Duke returned from Plimmouth to Whitehall, contrary to the opinion of very many who conceaued he [​ w x ] would not haue appeard heere before he had heard how the pulse of the Parlamente had gone. But being confident of the King’s fauour, [f]eares not the many enemies that he hath in the Lower House, especially hauing so greate a party in the Higher House by reason of the Bishops and the new Lords, which for the most [part] are(d) of his owne makinge; and to take away the ill opini[on] of such lordes … The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of line 10. Measured on the reading, the letter builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.6%, under the 95% bar. The “new Lords” are the peers Buckingham had had created, the bishops were largely of his party, and the Parliament being discussed that winter was summoned by writs of 30 January 1628.
boswell1628.html#date

In the Julian calendar the 15th fell on a Saturday in December 1627 and March 1628; 15 January 1628 was a Tuesday. With receipt endorsed on 24 January 1627/8, the Saturday is 15 December 1627. Buckingham had come back by way of Plymouth from the failed Île de Ré expedition in November 1627. The date of his arrival at Whitehall was not checked against a printed source here.
boswell1628.html#what-remains-uncertain

p = s: H in his owne ; C in our[s] greate Duke , where the sign may be a slip. Second w = “part” (C): one sign for a whole word, so a small nomenclator or an abbreviation mark. w x after “conceaued he”: not deciphered (I). Possibly a nomenclator pair or nulls. Item 7 of the topic list and the note beside the endorsement ( Bradburn? ) are not made out; whether the tally sheet is Boswell’s or a clerk’s is unknown.

The cipher Invented and Latin-like signs, several for each letter, some signs with two or three values, word signs for de, la, le, qui/que, et, pour/par, vous, car , and nulls. How it was deciphered The cipher was deciphered at the time in the margins of ff. 111v–112r, 134v and 151r. Michael Brackx transcribed every block and applied Tomokiyo's key table, which he corrected against those decipherments; the readings follow the margin where it fits the figures and the figures where they differ. What it says Camus's carrier to “le parent” can no longer help; Villeroy is to send separate ciphered packets, with code names for the carrier (“le beau frere”) and for Camus (“le seruiteur”). Still open ff. 132v, 134v block A, the f. 151r margin and foot blocks and ff. 272r–v give phrases between gaps; 57 rare signs have no value. Brackx corrected Tomokiyo's table where the margin decipherments and contact sheets of every sign required it: the sign 6 is c (and g), the plain round e is r and the looped e s, a circled G is g, ŋ is o (also l and u), φ stands for ff, f or mm, a large crossed L with a loop (Ⱡ) is the word et , ‡ is b, ɱ is l, and ʒo is the word vous . Each change rests on cribs, or on two contexts and a contact sheet. The plain 9 and ŋ still carry three values each. The label legend, with each sign's shape, is in the repository.

The images on DECODE are only 590 pixels wide, so a few digits are uncertain (538 or 558; 115). Tomokiyo’s table (Cryptiana, Cipher Used in Louis XIV’s Reign , 11B) is an image. I transcribed it into targets/desmarets1710/tomokiyo_decode.py and decoded the transcription of the 471 groups as one run, without line breaks. The result, with the words divided by hand ( reading.txt ): On a voulu tenter un evenement dans [l’esper]ance qu’il pourroit estre heureux, qu’il feroit changer la face des affaires presentes. Soit prudence soit impossibilite, on n’a rien fait, mais il y a grande apparence que ce qu’on n’a pas tente volontairement deviendra force … Peu de semaines feront connoistre ce qui en arrivera. C’est cependant la raison qui a fait differer de renvoyer vostre courier. … Le pouvoir qu’on vous envoie est assez estendu et on ne s’y tiendra pas absolument. Si vous pouvez venir a bout d’avoir des suretes et des eclaircissements sur les demandes ulterieures: on veut la paix, on la veut sure, mais on veut encores menager l’honneur du gouvernement. Enfin pourvu que les demandes ulterieures n’aillent pas a des demembrements entiers et qu’on les borne a peu de chose au dela des preliminaires, on s’y portera. … Il ne se [con]clura pas sans bien des explications et des conferences, mais voila au moins un relachement qui peut produire la paix, ce qui n’aur[oit] pas este selon toutes les apparences si l’on estoit demeure fermes dans les premieres resolutions. The first part is the text already written between the figure lines; the last 22 lines of figures decipher to the second part, which has no French over it on the sheet. Tomokiyo notes the same: the secretary deciphered on a separate sheet and wrote the clean text on the original out of step with the figures, and the letter was printed in L’intermédiaire des curieux 50 (1904), which remarked that the last lines carry no plaintext. The sense is the French position at Geertruidenberg: the King wants peace, a safe peace, but means to keep “l’honneur du gouvernement”, and will agree if the Allies’ further demands stop short of “demembrements entiers”. What is not clean. The decoded stream has local misfits that come from the table or from the transcription of it: for example “heureux” comes out with V and X for the last two letters, “presentes” as pre followed by letters that do not spell it, and “le p…n qu’on vous… envoie” has an unread word. A few cells are queried in Tomokiyo’s own table (463 “temps?”, 25 “S?”), and the 590-pixel images leave some digits doubtful. Twelve group types are not in the table at all: 94 (“ce”, three places), 539 (“l’esper”) and 565 (“oit”) are fixed by the context; 179+534 (in “differer”), 133 (“aplanir”), 65 and 147 (“renvoyer vostre courier”), 189, 229, 23 and 559 are plausible readings only, and 559 may be a null.

On 21 September I aligned each French line with the figure line under it, with four models (per-line EM, one global alignment, per-line soft EM with word-boundary bonuses, word-level EM). None converged: 111 fell under paix , seure and on , and “demandes ulterieures” sat over different figures in its two places. Those failures were real but the conclusion drawn from them was not. The French is a decipherment, but it is not written line against line with the figures, so a per-line alignment has nothing consistent to learn. Read as a single stream the groups fall out in order. The numbers are a genuine code (183 types in 471 tokens), and the repeated six-group run 119 101 402 49 197 424 is “les premieres resolutions”, which occurs in the glossed lines and again in the tail.

Seven lines of signs that Teseo Ambrogio printed in 1539 as the Devil’s written answer to a conjuration about a lost inheritance in Piacenza, no. 12 on Schmeh’s Top 25. Ambrogio’s own next page says what they meant: the conjurer was later killed by peasants “with as many iron tridents as the invoked Amon had drawn in his characters”. The commonest sign is a trident, and a homophonic solver that recovers matched Latin and Italian controls, cribs from the question, a syllabic model and Amadi’s names for the signs find no text. A pictorial omen, not a cipher. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 October 2026 Method: not a cipher Credits · David Scheers (identification, transcription, pointer to a source) · Stephen Houston (pointer to a source) · Felipe Rojas (pointer to a source) closed At a glance Not a cipher · explained by the source The document Seven lines of signs that a conjurer’s pen, “lifted into the air”, wrote by itself in answer to a question about a missing inheritance in Piacenza. Ambrogio printed them from the original sheet. Where Teseo Ambrogio degli Albonesi, Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam, Syriacam, atque Armenicam, & decem alias linguas (Pavia, 1539), f. 212v; the account runs from f. 212r to f. 213r. The question “Has Cavaliero Marchantonio, son of a rich woman from Piacenza, found all the money that Antonio Maria left, and if not, where is it?” What the signs are Ambrogio says the peasants who later killed the conjurer struck him “with as many iron tridents as the invoked Amon had drawn in his characters”. The commonest sign, a reversed E with a long bar, is a trident on its side. How it was tested Three transcriptions, a homophonic solver that recovered all 12 matched Latin and Italian controls, 17 cribs from the question, a syllabic model and Amadi’s 1580s names for the signs: no text in any of them. Credit David Scheers identified the image and sent his transcription and Amadi’s table. Stephen Houston and Felipe Rojas had printed and translated the trident passage in 2024 without drawing this conclusion. Still open Whether whoever cut the woodcut meant anything beyond the tridents cannot be shown; a code of whole words is not excluded in principle.
devil1539.html#story

Ambrogio’s appendix of alphabets ends with Arabic punctuation. He then turns to the “characters of the magicians” that Honorius of Thebes and Pietro d’Abano left and Cornelius Agrippa printed, “which need not concern us”, and adds the conjuration of Ludovico of Spoleto “to satisfy a friend and the curious”. A noble woman of holy life, often filled with a prophetic spirit, had once written in unknown letters and foretold that people would come who used such characters; some years after her death, these were written (f. 212r). The conjuration is in Italian (f. 212v): “Ve comando Amon, per li sette commandamenti, per li dicisette Mastri, per le dece potentissime parole … per Talion, Ansion, Amlion, per Giroastro terzo, per li ottanta Demone … che me debiate scrivere la verita in questa medesima … sel Cavaliero Marchantonio figliolo de riccha donna da Piacenza ha ritrovati tutti li dinari che laso Antonio Maria, & se no in qual loco sono.” No sooner had the magus put down his pen than the bystanders saw it seized and lifted into the air and write the characters below on the same sheet, though no one could see the hand that held it. A witness told Ambrogio the story when he came to Pavia, and at his request left him the original sheet (“rogatus archetypum mihi reliquit”). The woodcut copies it. f. 212v: the heading Ludovici Spoletani praeceptum sive (ut vulgo dicitur) coniuratio, cum subscripta Daemonis responsione , the conjuration, and the account of the pen. Image: Teseo Ambrogio, Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam (Pavia 1539), f. 212v; Google-digitised copy via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_yUkKq_QnrnwC).
devil1539.html#meaning

The next page (f. 213r) opens with the sentence usually quoted: “Quid vero characteres illi insinuarent, quamve responsionem ad quaesita redderent, scire omnino non curavi” (what those characters meant, or what answer they gave to the questions, I did not care at all to know). He hates the superstitions of magicians: such spirits always lay snares for those who worship them. His example is Simon Magus, and then the conjurer himself. The man had since given himself wholly to soldiering and led three or four hundred armed foot soldiers under his banner, when he fell into the hands of peasants: “Qui tot illum ferris tridentibus (quot invocatus Amon, in suis characteribus effinxerat) appetentes, percusserunt, vulneraverunt, transfixerunt. Et tricipiti apud inferos Cerbero consignandum, multis undique laetalibus cribratum vulneribus, exanime tandem corpus illius reliquerunt.” “They went at him with as many iron tridents as the invoked Amon had drawn in his characters, and struck him, wounded him and ran him through; and they left his body lifeless at last, riddled on every side with deadly wounds, to be handed over to three-headed Cerberus below.” f. 213r: “Qui tot illum ferris tridentibus (quot inuocatus Amon, in suis characteribus effinxerat) appetentes, percusserunt, vulnerauerunt, transfixerunt.” Image: Teseo Ambrogio, Introductio in Chaldaicam linguam (Pavia 1539), f. 213r; Google-digitised copy via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_yUkKq_QnrnwC). So the one meaning the source gives the characters is pictorial. The demon drew tridents, and the number of tridents was the number of pitchforks that would kill the man who had summoned him. On this account the Devil answered a question about money with an omen of the questioner’s death. Ambrogio then says he printed “this kind of writing” because the shapes of letters always interested him, and at the request of Guillaume Postel.
devil1539.html#signs

The woodcut bears this out. Its commonest sign, a reversed E whose middle bar runs on past the upright (26 of 161 signs in the transcription made here), is a trident lying on its side. The three bars are the prongs and the long bar is the shaft. Turned upright it is an unmistakable Ψ. The fork signs, a U or Ψ on a stem with or without a crossbar, are tridents and bidents standing up. Houston and Rojas (2024) called the whole set a “pitchfork script”, orientated up, down, left and right. All 21 clear examples of the commonest sign, turned upright: each is a trident, three prongs on a shaft. Image: Cut here from an image of f. 212v (Ambrogio 1539) and rotated 90 degrees clockwise. Agostino Amadi’s Venetian cipher manuscript (about 1588) has a “diabolic alphabet” of 31 signs, each named after a demon. They are the woodcut’s own signs (Acheron is the reversed E, Lybicon, Zael and Lucifer the three arch variants, Aletho and Nayn the forks, Demon the looped sign with a long tail). So a reader of the 1580s already took the woodcut for an alphabet. Read as the first letter of each demon’s name, the signs give no words, and the result scores no better than 2,000 random reassignments (z = 1.35 against Italian, 0.63 against Latin). The names are labels, not sound values.
devil1539.html#tests

Before Ambrogio’s sentence came to light here, the characters were treated as a cipher and tested hard. There are three transcriptions: David Scheers’s (153 signs, 31 symbols), one made here before the image was identified (174 signs), and a third made by cutting the image into glyphs, clustering them by shape and checking every glyph by eye (161 signs, 38 classes). The second and third agree closely. A homophonic solver was built and first run on matched controls: 153 letters of real Latin and Italian, enciphered in 31 signs with extra signs for the common letters. Test Result Latin controls (Caesar, Sallust), 6 6 of 6 recovered, 99–100% of letters; scores −1.62 to −1.86 per letter Italian controls (held-out Bible text), 6 6 of 6 recovered, 88–100%; scores −1.64 to −2.12 The Devil’s text, Latin and Italian, both reading directions, three transcriptions −2.31 to −2.50, no words; shuffled copies −2.34 to −2.52 Hebrew, Spanish, French, German, Greek, Arabic, Amharic (consonant rows); Italian and Latin with vowels dropped or merged all at the level of shuffled copies Cribs from the question (antoniomaria, marchantonio, dinari, denari, danari, piacenza, caualiero, trouati, qualloco, tesoro, figliolo; Latin pecunia, thesaurus, placentia and the names) at every position: 15,970 placements best −2.50, worse than no crib; on a control the true crib recovers the whole text Syllabic model (Ethiopic-style: one consonant per sign family, one vowel per mark) 3 of 4 syllabary controls recovered; the Devil’s text −2.51 to −2.55, the same as shuffled Amadi’s demon names as values no words; z = 1.35 (Italian), 0.63 (Latin) Both Scheers’s transcription and the one made here read a run of three identical signs in line 2. Any letter cipher of Latin or Italian would make that a tripled letter. The characters are not a letter cipher of the language of the question, nor of any language tried, under any transcription.

Whoever made the sheet (or the woodcut) could in principle have hidden a code of whole words or names among the tridents; 150 signs give too little to test that. Ambrogio does not give the number of tridents, so the count cannot be checked against the story; about 26 sideways tridents and a dozen upright forks are visible. Ambrogio’s alphabet plates elsewhere in the book were not compared sign by sign. Amadi’s Ethiopian and Armenian tables (sent privately) share only generic shapes with the woodcut.

Where Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591; DECODE R9426, entered with no author, recipient or place. The cipher Homophonic substitution on the even two-digit numbers 10 to 78, two word-end symbols and a three-digit nomenclator. Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 is the Bavarian ducal chancery’s collection of cipher keys, running from the 1530s to about 1620; DECODE has 102 key records from it (R9277–R9423), with a scatter of ciphertexts bound in among the keys. Two of those ciphertexts are dated 1619 and lie at the very end of the volume: Record Folios Pages DECODE status What it is R9425 278–280 4 Decrypted Archduke Albert’s resolution for Licentiate Morreus, 15 December 1619, with a contemporary abstract in red in the left margin; deciphered here 2 October 2026 (section 05) R9426 281–286 10 Non-decrypted the letter read here R9426’s record gives “Author: …”, no sender, no receiver, no origin city, no plaintext language, cipher type “Unknown”, symbol set “Numerical”. The images are behind a login and carry the archive’s reservation (“The image is not in the public domain. Publishing it is only possible with the permission of the Archive”), so no page of the manuscript is reproduced here. Eleven images cover ten pages: image 7 is a second photograph of the page on image 6, and pages 3 to 10 were photographed upside down. The last page is not in cipher. It closes: … und E. L. hierbei zu Bezeigung aller angenehmer freundbrüderlicher Dienste jederzeit geneigt. Geben in meiner Statt Bonn den 22. Decembris Anno 1619 . … williger Bruder und Diener — Ferdinand Bonn was the Cologne elector’s residence. Ferdinand of Bavaria (1577–1650) had been Elector-Archbishop of Cologne since 1612 and held Paderborn, Münster, Hildesheim and Liège with it; Maximilian I, head of the Catholic League, was his elder brother, which is what “herr Schwager” and “freundbrüderlich” in the clear passages, and the letter’s presence in the Munich archive, together establish. The ciphered text confirms the identification from the inside: the writer speaks of mein Thumb[capitel] , meine Landtstendt , meinem … Ertz[stift] , of calling meinen Landtag , and of Paderborn: an ecclesiastical prince with a cathedral chapter, territorial estates and a diet to summon.

Every cipher group is a number written between dots. The letters are the even two-digit numbers, in two series; the odd two-digit numbers and the three-digit numbers are the nomenclator, so the two can never be confused. a b c d e f 10 12 14 16 18 20 g h i l m n o p q r s t u x z 30 32 34 36 38 40 42 44 46 48 50 52 54 56 58 and a second series that supplies the homophones and the two letters the first series omits: a 60, 70 · e 62, 72 · i 64 · o 66, 76 · u 68 · k 74 · w 78. So each vowel has two or three equivalents and each consonant one. The values 22 to 28 never occur. Two symbols recur at every word boundary and carry no letter value; they are the word division. Single cipher letters also stand alone as initials, so that “E. L.” ( Euer Liebden , the form the brothers use for one another) is written 18 . 36. The design is conservative for 1619: an alphabet in order, with homophones only on the vowels, is a sixteenth-century habit, and it is what lets the key be recovered from 2,500 letters. The nomenclator covers what the alphabet does not: the groups stand exactly where a name, a title or an office belongs.

There was no key and no crib. The ten pages were transcribed line by line, with the clear passages bracketed and the cipher copied as written. A homophonic solver (simulated annealing) then searched for the assignment of numbers to letters that maximises the probability of the whole text under the repository’s de-1500s model, a five-gram character model built on German printed and chancery prose of 1470–1610. Six restarts over the first three pages (932 letters) were already producing German: gelegenen , Landtag ausschreiben , Quartiermeister . Ten restarts over all ten pages (2,482 letters) fixed the table, and the decryption gave continuous German. What remained were transcription errors. This clerk’s 0 and 6, 3 and 5, 1 and 4, 2 and 7 are nearly the same stroke, and a mis-transcribed digit turns one letter into another. The decoder flagged every word the language model scores poorly, a repair pass proposed single-token substitutions restricted to those confusable digit pairs, and about sixty were accepted. They are corrections of the transcription, never of the key, and a sample of them was checked again on the images at full zoom ( catolischen , einzuquartiern , wolermelt , Erwitte ). The control. The key was then applied, without changing a single value, to the neighbouring record R9425, a different letter of the same correspondence that this work had not touched. Its first cipher line is 60·36·12·48·18·14·32·52 54·42·40 30·66·52·52·18·50 30·40·10·16·18·40 → “Albrecht von Gottes Gnaden” This is Archduke Albert of Austria, sovereign of the Spanish Netherlands, whose troops are the subject of that letter. A key recovered from one text and applied unchanged to another that gives a correct opening formula and a correct name is the strongest check available here. On 2 October 2026 the whole of R9425 was transcribed and deciphered with the key, letter values unchanged; it is given in section 05.

Ferdinand has had Maximilian’s letter of the 10th “gestrigen tags”. The first half is logistics, and it is specific. On the frontier of the county of Horn and at Montfort companies are to be accommodated; the levies ( Werbungen ) are “nit sufficient”; the agent, Licentiat Morres , reports and is to negotiate. Troops are to be quartered in the villages nearest the city and at Deutz , across the Rhine from Cologne, under a particular ordinance for the quartermaster, and the march ( Fortzug ) is to follow when they are ready. Pay is fixed: … iedtwedern zwei Kopfstückh oder zwei Ort [eines] Königs-Dalers täglich zu versprechen … Then the constraint that runs through the whole letter: Ferdinand will not let his own territory be eaten. He must keep his Domkapitel and Landstände “in guetem Willen und Devotion”, he is about to call a Landtag , and his Estates must “nit alienirt werden”. Lintelo ’s company is placed near the city; Herberstorff and other recruitments are to have every possible support, and “daran nichts erwinden lassen”. For Paderborn he asks a year’s respite, where troops are already levied and a contribution and a mustering-place have been granted; he can give no firm promise about the rest. The second half is the argument for the war, and it is the passage the reveal below decrypts symbol by symbol. If the other side is reprimirt and the adversary is strengthened with so considerable a reinforcement while Catholic power is diminished, then … den Catolischen ins gemein und ohne underschied [wird] geringer Zeit übrig sein, sich [vor] des andern Theils Einfal, Gwalt und Betrangnus zu entweren. Ich vermeine, das die gemeine Zusammensetzung zu Conservation unser und in kurzer Zeit unser catolischer Religion und Seelen Seligkeit … Against that he sets the gemeine Zusammensetzung , the common union, for the preservation “of us” ( unser , the genitive) and soon of the Catholic religion and the salvation of souls, and for posterity. (Corrected 30 September 2026: the clear words before the cipher read Ich vermeine, das die on the image, not Ich hoffe , and the words between “Conservation unser” and “catolischer” are group 248 = und and the clear in kurzer Zeit followed by unser in cipher; the passage now runs without a cut.) His agent’s relation shows that a resolution cannot wait: levies are to be feared “für dem Früeling”, before the spring. The closing ciphered lines name Alexandro , the King, his lands, and “die Austilgung der ca[t]olischen Religion”. The date matters. Frederick V of the Palatinate had been crowned in Prague on 4 November 1619; Maximilian and Ferdinand II signed the Munich treaty in October and the League was mobilising through that winter. Ferdinand was one of the two brothers who were about to pay for and lead that mobilisation, and here works out in cipher where the men will sleep, what they will be paid a day, and how much of it his own bishopric can be made to carry.

R9425 (ff. 278–280) is four cipher pages (ff. 278r, 278v, 279r, 279v), a clear closing line on f. 280r, “Zur fernern nachricht und nachschreiben, den 15. 10bris Ao 1619”, and an endorsement on f. 280v: “Resolutio deß hertzogs Albrechts dem L. Morreo … ertailt”. It was transcribed from the DECODE images on 2 October 2026 and deciphered with the key recovered from R9426, every letter value unchanged. 1,524 of its 1,567 cipher tokens give sense: 97.3% ( r9425/count_r9425.py ; letters 1,471 of 1,482, nomenclator 53 of 85 tokens, of which 24 are nulls; 97.2% with the nulls left out of the count). The language check on the decrypt puts German first. It opens “Albrecht von Gottes Gnaden” and is Albert’s written answer to what Licentiate Morreus , the agent of the Duke of Bavaria as head of the Catholic League, had put to him “so woll mündlich als schriftlich”. In order: He thanks the Duke for commending to him the preservation of the Emperor and of “unsers hochlöblichen [Hauses] Angelegenheit”, and promises the same correspondence in return. He agrees that the recovery and reconquest of the kingdom [of Bohemia] and the other lands calls for every possible effort, has done “alle müglichste getrewe gute Officia” with the Emperor and the King [of Spain], and awaits their answer. Meanwhile, should the worst happen, the troops he has “anitzo auf den Beinen” are to go up to the Catholic army with orders to join it and obey its commander. A muster place, a regiment of foot and five hundred [horse] he cannot grant at present: his own levies are destined for Luxembourg , because of its situation. On the garrisoning of the fortress of Breisach he writes by this ordinary post to the King and to Oñate ; for the thousand cuirassiers the League asks to raise in the King’s name he writes to Ambrosio [Spinola], and refers the Duke to him. It is the answer to the same mission that R9426 reports on a week later, where the agent appears as “Morres”. The clear passages are transcribed as a working reading with gaps; only the cipher is counted. What it gives back to R9426. R9425 settles five nomenclator groups as nulls : 414 stands in “Kön. 414 M. und L.” beside “Kön. 165 und L.”, in “unsers 414 hochlöblichen” and in “iren L. 414 L.”; 415 in “ire L. 415 L.”; 419 in “zu gedachtem 419 End”; 416 and 417 in the same formulas. It also fixes 242 = und (a homophone of 248, in the twice-written “Kön. M. 417 242 415 L.”), 165 = Mt. and 2 = Ambrosio [Spinola], where the decipherer’s red margin has “Ambr.”. With 416 a null, R9426’s “ertz 232 416” and “zu meinem 416 232” make 232 = stift close to forced. Probable values, not counted as read: 41 = Chur- , 218 = Rath , 169 = Kriegs- , 216 = Pferd , 154 = Haus , 47 = Mt. , 31 = Vettern , 157 = Hilf . Open in R9425 (32 tokens, 2.0%): the groups 45, 149, 225 (twice each), 160, 219, 153, 15, 215, 155, 221, 136, 140 and 249, and the probable-only values above; each has one or two contexts and no key survives. 149 (“Weil 149 L. die Vestung Brisach … bedencken tragen”) is probably Archduke Leopold; “dem 140 249 Oñate” probably the Spanish ambassador. Two or three signs on f. 278v run into the binding; four single signs are illegible; five single-token slips in words whose sense is clear are counted unread.

Measured over the enciphered text ( count.py ), 2,504 of 2,614 cipher tokens give sense: 95.8% . The letters are nearly complete, 2,483 of 2,519. Two kinds of item are open. The nomenclator (31 of 32 groups, 74 tokens, 2.8% of the text). The groups that occur are 102, 122, 136, 142, 146, 154, 160, 165, 183, 200, 213, 215, 216, 221, 225, 232, 238, 239, 248, 258, 410, 412, 414, 415, 416, 417, 419 and the two-digit 33, 47, 49, 51, 57. From R9426 alone only 248 = und is established, and that from its own contexts (“Gwalt 248 Betrangnus”, “Eifer 248 Ernst”, “248 in kurzer Zeit”). The sibling R9425 (section 05) shows 414, 415, 416, 417 and 419 to be nulls: 23 of the 74 open tokens. Counting them would raise R9426 from 95.8% to 96.7% ((2,504 + 23) / 2,614); the figures on this page are not yet recounted, so they are left as measured. 410 and 412 (once each) are probably nulls of the same run but do not occur in R9425, and 232 is now close to forced as stift . No key for this cipher survives: the volume’s own key records were checked (R9419 at f. 267 is a Latin nomenclator on 1–99; R9420–R9423 are 1530s–1583 alphabets already worked through for the earlier letters in this file), and the sibling R9425’s red margin, enhanced by channel separation, is a contemporary abstract of that letter, not a group-by-group decipherment. Three names and four words. Three words decrypt as proper names whose bearers are not identified: Leicker (the Doctor Ferdinand sends to negotiate), Dernersen (named beside Herberstorff), and Marreo / Morres (the agent). Four words, 37 tokens in all, do not decrypt to German: at P1.22, P2.05, P3.05 and P4.23. Each has a single mis-transcribed digit inside a word; at this scan resolution the strokes are ambiguous, and a return to the originals would settle them. Neither 1619 letter was found in print. Briefe und Akten zur Geschichte des Dreißigjährigen Krieges , Neue Folge I/1 (ed. Georg Franz, Munich 1966), which covers January 1618 to December 1620, cites the Munich files by the old “Kasten schwarz” numbers rather than the current KAA shelfmarks, and nothing in its searchable text for November–December 1619 answers to this letter; Hurter’s Ferdinand II viii, Wolf and Breyer’s Maximilian I iv and Pastor were checked as well. “Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591” is cited nowhere in the literature that can be searched.

L." and "des Herzogen L." (the Duke of Bavaria, as head of the Catholic League), has put to him orally and in writing. He thanks the prince for commending to him the preservation of the Emperor ("our most gracious, beloved lord and cousin, his Imperial Highness") and of the interests of "our most praiseworthy House", and promises the same correspondence in return. On the substance: he agrees that the **recovery and reconquest of the kingdom [of Bohemia]** and the other lands calls for every possible effort; the Catholic princes and Estates should give help and assistance to that end, and he has already done good offices with the Emperor and the King [of Spain] and awaits further answer. Meanwhile he has resolved that, should the worst happen, the troops he has now on foot will be sent up with orders to join the Catholic army and obey its commander, and that Hungarian troops [being sent by the other side?] be countered by help for the oppressed Catholic Estates. A **muster place, a regiment of foot and five hundred [horse]** he cannot grant at present, though he would like to: his own levies are destined for **Luxembourg**, because of its situation. Since [Archduke Leopold?] hesitates to garrison the fortress of **Breisach** with the [Elector's?] troops, Albert writes by this ordinary post to the King and to **Oñate** (the Spanish ambassador in Vienna). For the **thousand cuirassiers** that the League asks to raise in the name of the King [of Spain], he writes to **Ambrogio [Spinola]** and refers the Duke to him to confer. If the Duke names qualified officers not in active command, Albert will give satisfaction. Dated 15 December 1619; endorsed as Albert's *Resolutio* given to Licentiate Morreo. The letter is the answer to the mission that R9426 (Ferdinand of Cologne, 22 December 1619) reports on: there the agent "Morres" is named and the League's quarters and levies in the Rhine–Westphalian circle are the subject. ## Nomenclator: values fixed here, and the open groups Fixed (counted as read): | group | value | evidence | |---|---|---| | 414, 415, 416, 417, 419 | nulls | "Kön. 414 M. und L." beside "Kön. 165 und L." and "Kön. L. …* **f. 280r (clear).** *Zur fernern nachricht und nachschreiben, den 15. 10bris Ao 1619.* ## Summary (modern English) Archduke Albert, sovereign of the Spanish Netherlands, answers in writing what Licentiate **Morreus**, the agent of a prince he calls "E. L." and "des Herzogen L." (the Duke of Bavaria, as head of the Catholic League), has put to him orally and in writing. He thanks the prince for commending to him the preservation of the Emperor ("our most gracious, beloved lord and cousin, his Imperial Highness") and of the interests of "our most praiseworthy House", and promises the same correspondence in return. On the substance: he agrees that the **recovery and reconquest of the kingdom [of Bohemia]** and the other lands calls for every possible effort; the Catholic princes and Estates should give help and assistance to that end, and he has already done good offices with the Emperor and the King [of Spain] and awaits further answer. Meanwhile he has resolved that, should the worst happen, the troops he has now on foot will be sent up with orders to join the Catholic army and obey its commander, and that Hungarian troops [being sent by the other side?] be countered by help for the oppressed Catholic Estates. A **muster place, a regiment of foot and five hundred [horse]** he cannot grant at present, though he would like to: his own levies are destined for **Luxembourg**, because of its situation. Since [Archduke Leopold?] hesitates to garrison the fortress of **Breisach** with the [Elector's?] troops, Albert writes by this ordinary post to the King and to **Oñate** (the Spanish ambassador in Vienna). For the **thousand cuirassiers** that the League asks to raise in the name of the King [of Spain], he writes to **Ambrogio [Spinola]** and refers the Duke to him to confer. If the Duke names qualified officers not in active command, Albert will give satisfaction. Dated 15 December 1619; endorsed as Albert's *Resolutio* given to Licentiate Morreo. A spy’s report in clear Venetian Italian from Ferdinand’s agent at Fiume during Süleyman’s campaign of 1532, with eight words in a small nomenclator: names, places, the month, the year and the signature, so that the archive lists the sender as N.N. Brice Dudout took the values from the glosses written at the time over two of Ferducci’s other letters in the same bundle, fixed them and applied them; all eight give sense, and his table of Ferducci’s 1542 letters agrees on the six groups they share. A report in clear Italian in which only names, places, the month, the year and the signature are in code. Where Austrian State Archives, Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, StAbt Türkei I 2-2-19, fols. 60–61. The online inventory lists the sender as “N.N.”, because the signature is in code. It was catalogue item 498 here, with the rest of the 1530–32 Ragusa reports. The cipher A small nomenclator: three-figure numbers for names and words, Q19 with a barred Q for Ragusa, and D with a number for the month and the year. How the key was found Two other Ferducci letters in the same bundle, of 2 June and 18 September 1532, carry the decipherment written over the groups at the time. The values were taken from them, fixed, and then applied to this letter, which has none. The two glossed letters never disagree, and a table of 1542 by the same writer agrees on all six groups they share. What it says A brigantine from Ragusa has brought “gran nove”, sent on at once to Ljubljana; and if the King wishes, Ferducci will take ten or twelve armed men to sea, pretending to go fishing, to seize the French ambassador on his way back from the Sultan. The code values are the glosses written in 1532 over two sibling letters. Still open No code group. Four words of the clear text are doubtful in the hand ( Lanbergher , a peschara , a divotione , ve se avisarà ), and the ambassador is not named.

Fols. 60–61 of the Ottoman section of the Vienna state archives hold a single letter on two leaves, addressed on the back “Invictissimo Ferdinando … et Boemie”. It opens in Latin, “Ser.me Rex atque invictissime princeps”, and continues in Venetian Italian. The writer dates it “a dì 19” and writes the month and the year in code; the archive’s dockets give “1532. 19/7” and “19. Juli 1532”. He signs in code too, which is why the inventory has no sender. The letter belongs to the reports Ferdinand received from his informants on the Adriatic during Süleyman’s campaign of 1532, when the Sultan was marching on Vienna; he was halted in August before Güns (Kőszeg). The bundles hold about fifteen such pieces from Ragusa and Fiume, by Angelo Caraffa, Michael Bucignola, the Conte da Ella, Martino Lucio and Ferducci. Nearly all carry a decipherment, interlinear or attached, made at the time or in the nineteenth century; this letter has none. The letter cannot be shown here. The Austrian State Archives charge a fee for each original reproduced in a publication, the web included (fee schedule of 9 July 2026, section 2), and their online images carry no open licence. The three views are free to consult in the archive’s online inventory . The code is a small nomenclator of the kind Ferdinand’s chancery issued to its agents: numbers in the 500s for persons, places and a few words, a letter with a number for the commonest places, and D with a number for months and years. Nothing in this letter is enciphered letter by letter. The values come from Ferducci’s own letters. Two others in the same bundle, 2-2-9 of 2 June 1532 and 2-2-24 of 18 September 1532, have the meaning written over each group by a reader of the time. Brice Dudout built the table from those two letters only and fixed it before applying it to 2-2-19. La cagion di questa sie per dinottare a vostra Maestà Serenissima come in questa hora a tardi è gionto qui el bregantino da [Ragusa] con le presente ligatte in questa; e per esere in esse gran nove, subitto subitto ho meso un mio servo ha cavallo per le poste e mandatollo a Lubiana, e scritto al signore Andrea {Lanbergher} che senza nullo ritegnio le manda a vostra Maestà Serenissima. La cosa di Chlisa è cosa certissima; similiter di monsignore gardinal Colona. Si vostra Maestà ha a piacere di aver nelle mane [l’ambasciatore] de [Francia] al suo ritorno, che verà per mare in qualche bregantino, io andarò in persona con 10 o 12 compagni harmati; si fengiremo d’andare {a peschara}, e secretto modo si sforzaremo di averllo, per aviso da vostra Maestà Serenissima. El gardinal di Medici fa gente a gran furia per la Marcha e per la Romagnia; si dici per el volgo che viene {a divotione} di vostra Maestà. … Datta [S. Vito] a dì 19 [luglio] [1532]. De vostra Maestà Serenissima humil servo [Niccolò Ferducci]. My last letter was of the 24th of last month, with the enclosed letter from your servant [Martino Lucio], under cover of Signor Andrea Lamberger. […] This evening, late, the brigantine from [Ragusa] arrived here with the letters enclosed with this one; and since they contain great news, I at once, in all haste, put one of my servants on horseback by the post and sent him to Ljubljana […]. The matter of Clissa is quite certain; likewise that of Monsignor Cardinal Colonna. If Your Majesty would like to have [the ambassador] of [France] in your hands on his return, which will be by sea on some brigantine, I will go in person with ten or twelve armed companions; we shall pretend to go fishing, and secretly we shall do our best to take him, on word from Your Most Serene Majesty. The Cardinal de’ Medici is raising troops in great haste in the Marche and in Romagna; the common people say he is coming to Your Majesty’s service. […] Given at [San Vito, that is Fiume], the 19th of [July] [1532]. Your Most Serene Majesty’s humble servant [Niccolò Ferducci]. The complete Italian text and translation are under Full texts below. Without the codes the letter is a report of unnamed people arriving from an unnamed port; with them it names its own writer, his informant at Ragusa, the date, and the man to be kidnapped.

Ferducci and his relays. Fiume was a Habsburg port on the Kvarner, and the “S. Vito” of the code is its patron saint (German Sankt Veit am Flaum ). Ferducci forwarded what came by sea from Ragusa (Dubrovnik) to Ljubljana, where Andrea “Lanbergher” sent it on to the King. The name ends in -gher in both places; he was probably of the Carniolan Lamberg family, in an office the letter does not give. Martino Lucio, “of Ragusa” in the glosses, is one of the network’s writers in the same bundle. The “gran nove”. Probably the Conte da Ella’s letters to Ferducci of 11 and 12 July, filed in the same bundle (2-2-17). The next piece, 2-2-18, is Süleyman’s letter to Ferdinand of 12 July. Clissa and Colonna. Clissa (Klis) is Petar Kružić’s fortress above Split, held against the Ottomans; the September letter’s gloss spells it the same way. What news of it was “certissima” is not said. Cardinal Pompeo Colonna, viceroy of Naples, died on 28 June 1532, and that is probably the other certain matter. The French ambassador. Not named. Francis I’s envoy to Süleyman in 1532 was Antonio Rincon. A Spanish report of April 1532 had him travelling by Sebenico and Ragusa, and on 21 June the Conte da Ella wrote from Ragusa (2-2-13) that a man said to be the King of France’s ambassador was leaving for Belgrade. Gévay has Rincon bringing a copy of Süleyman’s letter of 12 July to Venice on 20 August, so he did come back up the Adriatic, as Ferducci expected. Nothing is known of the plan being carried out. Rincon was killed near Pavia in July 1541 by men of the Marquis del Vasto. “A peschara”. The letters are certain. Dudout reads it as Venetian andar a pescar , going fishing, a natural cover for a dozen armed men in a boat. Pescara, the Abruzzo port, was Habsburg territory, so there was nothing to pretend about in going there. The Cardinal de’ Medici. Ippolito de’ Medici, appointed legate, left Rome on 8 July 1532 to join Charles V and Ferdinand against the Turks: “a divotione di vostra Maestà”, to the King’s service, fits.

No code group is open. Seven values are attested in the 1532 glosses (grade C); D7, July, is inferred from the order of the month groups and agrees with the docket (grade I). Four words of the clear text are doubtful readings of the hand, not of the code: Lanbergher (the first vowel may be a or o), a peschara (sense), a divotione (the hand has a d, three minims, o, a tall looped letter, then ione ), and ve se avisarà (an earlier reading, vostra [Maestà] sarà avisata , assumed an abbreviation that is not there). The identification of the ambassador as Rincon, and of the “cosa certissima” about Colonna as his death, are inferences from the dates. The profile records no check of a passage against the images by a person working without AI, and the text was not compared with the AIS views here. No earlier reading was found: the item was open in this catalogue, and Cryptiana and a web search on 27 October 2026 gave nothing; the letter is not printed in Gévay’s Urkunden und Actenstücke . The other Ragusa reports of 1530–32 have their decipherments of the time, and Ferducci’s letters of 1542–43 are a separate catalogue item (499).

Ser.me Rex atque invictissime princeps, domine colendissime, post servitiorum meorum humillimam commendationem. L’ultima mia fu de 24 del passato, con la inchiusa dal loro servitore [Martino Lucio], sotto littere del signore Andrea {Lanbergher}. La cagion di questa sie per dinottare a vostra Maestà Serenissima come in questa hora a tardi è gionto qui el bregantino da [Ragusa] con le presente ligatte in questa; e per esere in esse gran nove, subitto subitto ho meso un mio servo ha cavallo per le poste e mandatollo a Lubiana, e scritto al signore Andrea {Lanbergher} che senza nullo ritegnio le manda a vostra Maestà Serenissima. La cosa di Chlisa è cosa certissima; similiter di monsignore gardinal Colona. Si vostra Maestà ha a piacere di aver nelle mane [l’ambasciatore] de [Francia] al suo ritorno, che verà per mare in qualche bregantino, io andarò in persona con 10 o 12 compagni harmati; si fengiremo d’andare {a peschara}, e secretto modo si sforzaremo di averllo, per aviso da vostra Maestà Serenissima. El gardinal di Medici fa gente a gran furia per la Marcha e per la Romagnia; si dici per el volgo che viene {a divotione} di vostra Maestà. Staremo vigilanti, e facendo altro subitto {ve se avisarà}; el simille di altro che s’intenderà. Per hora no avemo altro. A vostra Maestà Serenissima humilmente mi richomando. Datta [S. Vito] a dì 19 [luglio] [1532]. De vostra Maestà Serenissima humil servo [Niccolò Ferducci]. Translation translation.md # English translation Deciphered words in [brackets]. Most serene King and most invincible prince, my most honoured lord, after the humble commendation of my services. My last letter was of the 24th of last month, with the enclosed letter from your servant [Martino Lucio], under cover of Signor Andrea Lamberger. The purpose of this one is to let Your Most Serene Majesty know that this evening, late, the brigantine from [Ragusa] arrived here with the letters enclosed with this one; and since they contain great news, I at once, in all haste, put one of my servants on horseback by the post and sent him to Ljubljana, and I wrote to Signor Andrea Lamberger to forward them to Your Most Serene Majesty without any delay. The matter of Clissa is quite certain; likewise that of Monsignor Cardinal Colonna. If Your Majesty would like to have [the ambassador] of [France] in your hands on his return, which will be by sea on some brigantine, I will go in person with ten or twelve armed companions; we shall pretend to go fishing, and secretly we shall do our best to take him, on word from Your Most Serene Majesty. The Cardinal de’ Medici is raising troops in great haste in the Marche and in Romagna; the common people say he is coming to Your Majesty’s service. We shall stay vigilant, and if anything else happens you will be told at once, and likewise of any other news we hear. For now we have nothing else. I humbly commend myself to Your Most Serene Majesty. Given at [San Vito, that is Fiume], the 19th of [July] [1532]. Your Most Serene Majesty’s humble servant [Niccolò Ferducci]. Key: decryption.txt

In January 1643 Tortona had just been retaken, the war with France weighed on the Milanese, and Madrid pressed the Italian princes bound to Spain to send troops. Eraso had forwarded the King’s letter to Ferdinand II de’ Medici. The next item in the bundle (3598,43) is the Grand Duke’s answer in Italian, Florence, 1 January 1643, which refers to the care he must take of his own states. Eraso explains in cipher what this means: the matter goes to Spain, and the delay is the Grand Duke’s gain. Of the ten cipher items of 1643–51 in entry 755, nine have their contemporary plain text in the same bundle; this is the one whose plain text is not online. The 1638 Genoa letters (target genes1638, still on an open pull request) use another table.
genes1643.html#cipher

Series of five numbers give syllables (27 fa, 32 ta, 37 as, 42 na, 47 ja, 52 al, 57 da, 62 an); disguised bigrams ( ax = la, at = sa, ha = ma) and trigrams ( sal = ra, gan = ca, tes = ve) stand for letter groups; single letters and a few code numbers complete the table. The transcription has 261 symbols.
genes1643.html#reading

Of 137 enciphered words, 115 are certain, 4 probable, 16 restored from the sense and 2 unresolved: 135 read, 98.5%. The restored words are word codes seen nowhere else ( con que , órdenes , España , respuesta , cuenta ), fixed by syntax and by chancery formulas such as “dar cuenta a V. M.”; for 166 the same sense would follow from “Madrid” or “la corte”. The full text and translation are below. To our knowledge this is the first published decipherment.

Charles V’s orders to his governor of Milan on Parma, almost solid cipher from c. 60r to c. 62r, with no decipherment in the file. Deciphered with the Imperial Cipher of 1544–1554 as Bertomeu Masiá reconstructed it and Tomokiyo pictures it, extended by hand. Gonzaga is told not to make terms with Ottavio Farnese, and when he may still seize Parma. By eye, with the sense in view; 93% of the signs are firm; several code words are open, and “the Pollo” is very probably the Pope. The main one is dated Brussels, 14 November 1549, with about 110 lines of signs. Four shorter passages come from 13 May, 30 September, 20 November and 23 December 1549. Gonzaga may act only in two named cases, and then with dissimulation. Still open Several code words; a few stretches of c. 60v and c. 61r; the last two lines of c. 64r. gonzaga1549.html#the-letters

The Estense holds 151 letters from Charles V to Ferrante Gonzaga, most in clear. Nine were flagged as partly in cipher. Five use the sign cipher treated here, and each of those carries its cipher as passages inside a clear letter, except that the 14 November letter is almost solid cipher from the middle of c. 60r to the top of c. 62r. It ends “Dat. en Bruselas a xiiij de Noviembre M.D.xlviiij”, with the signatures of Carlos and Vargas on c. 62v. The numeric letters of 15 July 1549 and 11 August 1542 and the letter of 1 July 1552 use other ciphers, so they are not part of this page. c. 60v, lines 19–21: “por otra parte ratificacion por razon de lo capitulado con el, por donde verniamos a hallarse embaraçado”. Image: Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera K, Karl V, sfasc. IV c. 60v, via the Estense Digital Library (CC BY-NC-SA).
gonzaga1549.html#reading

Ottavio Farnese had been trying to recover Parma from his grandfather the Pope, and Gonzaga had reported a chance to make terms with him. Charles answers in cipher. The whole text is under Full texts below; these are the parts that run. Ottavio is a poor foundation. He has no money, being “en desgracia del Pollo”, and nowhere to draw troops from except the lands of the Church. To carry the matter forward Gonzaga would have to declare himself, which would be “romper la guerra contra la yglesia”, since “Su Santidad” holds Parma in the Church’s name, not the Farnese house’s. The policy. “En Parma y en Plazencia nunca havemos querido emprender hasta qui ninguna cosa por via de guerra avierta.” If terms were made and the Pollo died, “se vernia luego a las manos”, and Charles would find himself “embaraçado y cargado por ambas partes”. The fear. Terms might give the Pollo an excuse “passar adelante mas desvergonçadamente en dar Parma a Horacio”, making “una frontera” against the Emperor. The order. “No deveys en ninguna manera entrar por el presente en capitulacion con el dicho Ottavio.” Two exceptions follow. If Camillo Orsini tries a stroke “en sede vacante o en vida del Pollo”, Gonzaga may do what seems best, provided it is justified and has a safe way out. If Orazio or someone else enters Parma, for instance by an agreement between the Pollo and “el rey de nerp”, Gonzaga is to find a way to make himself master of the city, “con la desteridad y dissymulacion” that Charles trusts him to use. Otherwise, while “Parma [is] en manos del Pollo”, nothing is to be undertaken against it. c. 60v, line 14: “el Pollo” in clear among the signs, in “muriendo el Pollo, se vernia luego a las manos”. Image: Biblioteca Estense Universitaria, Modena, Autografoteca Campori, Lettera K, Karl V, sfasc. IV c. 60v, via the Estense Digital Library (CC BY-NC-SA). The Pollo is very probably the Pope. The letter never says so. But c. 60v has “teniendo Su Santidad como agora tiene a Parma” where c. 62r has “estando Parma en manos del Pollo”, and c. 61v speaks of “sede vacante o en vida del Pollo”. Paul III died on 10 November 1549, and the letter of 14 November was clearly written before the news came. By 20 November the Emperor writes in clear of “este tiempo de Sede vacante”.
gonzaga1549.html#the-other-passages

20 November 1549 (cc. 64r–64v): five short passages, written after the news. “En ninguna manera se mueva ninguna cosa en Parma”, no war on the Church, and no attack on the Farnese state at such a time. The clerk’s margin notes give the same sense, and they were in view. The last two lines of c. 64r are not deciphered. 30 September 1549 (c. 50r): someone goes “con fin de tractar al prior de lombardia”, castellan of the castle, so as to throw him out and put in Mons. de Brissac. A clear margin note summarises it, and it was also in view. 13 May 1549 (c. 30r): where to find money and materials for a work, with no show of the intention. Slip c. 29 is the decipherment of the time. 23 December 1549 (c. 76r): on Nice and the Prior of Lombardy, sent to live in the castle. c. 77 is the decipherment of the time.
gonzaga1549.html#method

The slip on c. 29 gave the first values. Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana then identified the system and pictures Bertomeu Masiá’s reconstruction of the key, which shows the rule: base shape for the consonant, mark for the vowel. The key image is small and does not cover every form, so the sign table was extended from the letters themselves. The cipher was cropped into numbered panels at about seven times size, and each sign was named and given a value in a sign file, line by line. The main session did c. 60r block 1 and c. 60v. Subagents with the same brief did c. 60r block 2, c. 61r, c. 61v, c. 62r and the short passages. In all there are 3,032 signs: 2,780 with a value, 128 doubtful, 51 taken as nulls, 25 clear words and 48 unread. The text is continuous across the pages, which is one check on it: c. 60r ends “romper la guerra contra la yglesia o” and c. 60v goes on “no seria … que romper la guerra con la yglesia”; c. 60v ends “lo qual no con” and c. 61r begins “vergia”. The statistical test ( docs/_validate.py , order-4 model of Golden Age Spanish) passes. The reading scores −1.96 per letter, against −3.99 for random keys (9.5 sd) and −2.56 for keys annealed onto shuffled signs (45.5 sd), and an annealer on the real text reaches only −2.34.
gonzaga1549.html#what-remains-uncertain

Not a controlled test. Every value was chosen with the sentence in view, knowing what would make Spanish. The statistical test speaks for the key as a whole, not for any one word. Only one line of the subagents’ work (c. 61v line 15) was checked against its crop, and no person has checked any. Code words. Pollo is inferred to be the Pope. mus or mms fits “para” everywhere. inta and em stand where the Church is expected, and nerp where France is, both from the sense only. vela/bela , gien , et ud and tu are unexplained. Stretches that do not form sentences. c. 60v lines 7–8 and 23–27; c. 61r lines 4–5 and 16–18; c. 61v line 18 (“la pe gu l ro n”). Doubtful spellings left as the signs give them. “Hallarse” after “verniamos”; “arrordio” for acordio; “su rr esso” for suceso. Gamma is rr in the key but wants c here. “Plazencia” rests on an N-shaped sign taken as p from the words it occurs in. Signs with dots below. Most drop out inside a word (“car.gado”, “quisie.sse”), but some carry their plain value (c. 60r line 12), and the end of c. 64r gives no Spanish either way. People. The signs give Ursino and Horacio. Taking them as Camillo Orsini and Orazio Farnese is from general knowledge. “Dragut” for “Drigui” on c. 62r is a guess. Prior work. Bertomeu Masiá’s La guerra secreta de Carlos V contra el Papa (2009) studies this very affair and its ciphers, in Granvelle’s correspondence. It could not be read online, so these letters may already be in print there. A web search found no printed text of the 14 November letter, but the search was not exhaustive.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. 14 Nov 1549, cc.60r-62r read in part Charles V tells his governor of Milan not to make terms with Ottavio Farnese over Parma: Ottavio has no money or troops, and it would mean war with the Church, which holds Parma, and could drive the Pope to give it to Orazio Farnese. Gonzaga may act only in two cases, an Orsini stroke or Orazio's entry, and then with dissimulation. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (94% here); the holes are marked in the reading. [..] marks text not read. Passages that do not form sentences in the Spanish are given as far as they go and marked. "the Pollo" keeps the clear word of the cipher; on the evidence below it is the Pope, Paul III, but the letter does not say so. `mus` and `mms` appear to stand for "para" and are translated "to" or "for". **c.60r, first block.** And coming to the particular matter of the decision with which you stood [..] to arrange and make terms with Duke Ottavio over the enterprise of Parma, some of the considerations that occur to us about it will be touched on here, so as afterwards [..] to make known to you our intention and will. **c.60r, second block.** Having regard to how little foundation can be placed in the person of the said Duke Ottavio for an enterprise such as that of Parma, both for what is known of it and for his having no means of getting money, being in disgrace with the Pollo; and because even if he did not lack it, he has nowhere to draw the troops from, there being no neighbouring lands there from which he could get them except those of the Church of `et ud` and `tu`; and that in this way it would be necessary, to carry the matter forward, to intervene and declare yourself on our side, which [would be] to break out in war against the Church, or **c.60v.** it would be nothing (?) but breaking out in war with the Church, since His Holiness holds Parma, as he now does, in its name and not in that of the house of Farnese. [..] likewise, that though this enterprise be [done] in favour of Ottavio, [..] what would be done by making terms with him, it would seem that one wished [..] to hold [not read: about two lines, up to] "teniendo". [..] equally in Parma and Piacenza we have never wanted to undertake anything so far by way of open war. [..] the right that is claimed on our side. Besides which, if terms were made with the said Ottavio and the Pollo died, it would come to blows at once [..] without being able to avoid putting into [..] the discussion of the right claimed by the parties; and it coming in the end, [late?], to giving compensation to the Church in case it were found [..] the right to the said lands, the Duke would claim, on the other side, ratification by reason of what was agreed with him, whereby we should come to find ourselves hampered and burdened on both sides. And because finally, besides what [..] is considered of the little foundation that can be placed in the said Duke Ottavio, it is to be [gathered?] that [not read: about a line and a half] one would have to come to an agreement [..] our name [..] openly, which would not be fitting **c.61r.** for the reasons that have always been pointed out, we do not see that it is fitting to enter now into capitulation with him, both for the little fruit to be had from it and for the [occasion?] the Pollo could take from it to go on more shamelessly in giving Parma to Orazio, as if in despair, and putting him inside in the name of `em`, to make a frontier against us there, as has always been suspected and as they have sometimes said in `vela`; besides the harm that the said Duke Ottavio would do, or his fancying that in the end we would not fail our grandchildren, at least after [..] days. For all of which, having examined it well, leaving aside the agreement on the private matter between you and Ottavio, which certainly [..] can be done with [..] satisfaction, we cannot [but?] approve it. It has seemed to us that for the rest you should in no way enter at present into capitulation with the said Ottavio, and so we charge you with all force, but that you take great care to learn the outcome these differences will have, to inform us of everything, and to see whether the said Duke by any route will have a more apparent way of entering Parma than is now seen; and according to that, and to what will be learned anew from `bela`, which is expected any day, to see what can **c.61v.** and should be done according to the opportunity and the present state of affairs, public and our own. But in case Camillo Orsini should try some stroke during the vacancy of the see or in the Pollo's lifetime, as you indicate in your first letter, and it is clear to you that Parma would again be out of the hands of `inta` and of [..]obedience, we leave it to you in such a case to do what seems best to you, not doubting that you will take care to undertake nothing that is not, as you say, fully justified and that has not a very safe and easy way out, because of the harm and loss of reputation that could follow from the contrary. And likewise, in case, as is suspected, by an agreement between the Pollo and the king of `nerp` or otherwise, Orazio should enter Parma, or another person in the name of someone other than `inta` or Duke Ottavio, with whom the [..] has been made, under colour of its not having been observed and of the land being in the hands of someone unable to fulfil it, we also leave it to you to consider and look by all possible ways and means how this could be prevented, and to take care to make yourself master of the said city, with the skill and dissimulation we trust you will know how to use, according to how you see the other side proceed; so that, to settle our intention and aims, for the present, while **c.62r, lines 1-3.** Parma is in the hands of the Pollo, and by him or by the said Duke nothing new is done, nothing is to be changed or undertaken against it except in the two cases stated above. **c.62r, lines 10-13, inside the clear paragraph on the three companies of Spanish infantry.** next summer, either for the same work they have now been used in, against Dragut (?), or for anything else that might then arise. 20 Nov 1549, cc.64r-64v read in part After Paul III's death: five short cipher passages forbid any move on Parma during the vacancy of the see, or any war on the Church, and put off an attack on the Farnese. A torn letter in symbols on mourning paper, seized from Rose O’Neal Greenhow’s house on 23 August 1861 (NARA naId 1634036). Side 1 deciphers with the key found on her body when she drowned off Fort Fisher in 1864: Washington expects an attack hourly and is hunting whoever gave the alarm. About 60% of its words read as sense between paper losses; side 2 and a scrap of figures stay open. No earlier decipherment was found. 3 9 · is · ш 5 $ φ ſ ʒ · Y T ⊕ Y 3 φ Ð Y +ₓ ck is hourly expec[r]ted A ˣ+ · E Y · G 8 · I 4 · S ⊠ · U $ Washington → Confederate lines (presumed) · symbol substitution, the Jordan–Greenhow cipher · summer 1861, seized 23 August 1861 · side 1 deciphered with the 1864 key Rose Greenhow’s letter on mourning paper, Washington 1861 from Rose O'Neal Greenhow Go to the full text ↓ A torn cipher letter seized from Greenhow’s house deciphers with the key found on her body three years later: Washington expects an attack hourly and is hunting whoever gave the alarm. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: partial (60% of the cipher) Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · partial (60% of the cipher) The letter A letter in symbols on black-bordered mourning paper, about seventeen lines with a few clear words, unsigned and unaddressed. It was among the papers seized when Rose O’Neal Greenhow was arrested in Washington on 23 August 1861. Where National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O’Neal Greenhow, naId 1634036 (four images: side 1, side 2, a scrap of figures, the docket). Catalogue entry 644. The cipher One symbol per letter, with dots between words and some words left in clear. The 1864 key sheet also has signs for digraphs, numbers and common words; none of those occurs on side 1. How it was deciphered With the key sheet found on Greenhow’s body in 1864 (NARA M1091, naId 62017285, image 0484), applied unchanged except for a second form of N. 17 of 27 whole cipher words come out as English words, against at most 5 for 2,000 random keys. What it says McClellan is busy and “the panick is great”; an “attack is hourly expected”, and an effort is being made “to find out who gave the alarm”. Still open Paper losses on side 1 (two place names are conjectures), the two ink lines of side 2, and a scrap of figures that is not in this key. Credit Transcription, decipherment and controls by WAINUT (pull request #100, 27 October 2026), done with AI language-model agents. The key is the 1864 copy found on Greenhow; the Rosenbach used the same family of key on another Greenhow note in 2011.
greenhow1861.html#letter

The leaf survives in fragments laid down on a backing. NARA’s docket (image 4) reads “Written in Characters by Mrs G – on Mourning Paper. Fragments of a Letter”. It has no date, signature or address. The Library of Congress copy (World Digital Library 2706) and the Santa Clara University exhibit (item 3281) date it 23 August 1861, the day of the arrest and the seizure. The writer is presumed to be Greenhow, and the addressee her Confederate contacts at Beauregard’s headquarters, where Thomas Jordan received her reports; the letter names neither. Side 1. The heading “P 31” is not deciphered; the body is seventeen lines of symbols, with “is”, “the” and “this” in clear. Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 1634036, image 1, via the National Archives Catalog. Side 2 (image 2) has two lines of ink at the top; the rest is show-through. Image 3 is a separate scrap of figures with a few clear words.
greenhow1861.html#key

When Greenhow drowned off Fort Fisher in October 1864, trying to land from the blockade runner Condor , a cipher table was found on her. A copy of it is in the Confederate Navy subject file, NARA M1091, “DC – Codes and cryptography – Miscellaneous”, image 0484, headed “Lamb Papers CXXIX. Copied A. H. L.” (the last initial is uncertain) and docketed “This paper was found on the person of Mrs Rose O. Greenhow”. Image 0485 is a photostat of the same sheet; image 0483, a white-on-black “Confederate cipher 1864”, is a different table and does not fit. The key sheet: one symbol for each letter (left), digraph signs (th, ph, sh, st, oo, ie, ch, un, on, ei, ss), signs for words such as Thousand, Horses, Capitol, Lincoln, Washington and Richmond, the figures 1–9, and the rule “Double letter: 2d letter itself inverted”. Image: National Archives, RG 45, M1091 Subject File of the Confederate States Navy, naId 62017285, image 0484, via the National Archives Catalog. On side 1 the key works as written, with a few points checked on the signs: G (a plain 8) and U (a struck 8) are distinct, as are I (a crossed 4) and R (a looped 4). N has two forms: the hooked form of the key sheet (BEING, MORNING, FIND) and a looped l with a crossbar that is not on the sheet (LELAND, PANICK, the second N of MORNING); its value comes from context, and every word that contains it is otherwise keyed. Doubled letters are written twice (ATTACK, WILL, EFFORT, FERRY); the sheet’s inverted-second-letter rule is not used here. Controls ( decode.py ): with the key, 17 of the 27 whole cipher words are in an English word list and the mean letter-pair score is −2.49; 2,000 random substitution keys average 0.5 words (best 5) and −4.72; the key shifted by one letter gives 4 words; the true key with the signs shuffled inside each word gives at most 6. The word count understates the fit, because her spellings (BUISY, PANICK, BELEIVE) and the words cut by losses do not count.

Lines 4–10: …y. atta|ck is hourly expec|ted. they beleive this: the atta[ck] will [b]e si|multaneou[s] fr[om] [..]r[d]s ferr[y] … Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 1634036, image 1, via the National Archives Catalog. In her spelling, with words in clear on the leaf in italics; [x] marks letters supplied where the paper is lost or a sign is missing, [?x] a conjecture: Al[?l] is acti[vi]ty. McLeland (McClellan) is buisy. Myste[…] a[…] […]but the panick is gr[?ea]t. A[…] […]y. Attack is hourly expected. They beleive this : the atta[ck] will [b]e simultaneou[s] fr[om] […]r[?d]s Ferr[y], […] [?Bal]timore. […]y eff[o]rt is being made to find out who g[?a]ve the alarm. A tro[?op o]f cavalry u[…] […]nt fr[o]m here [?th]is morning. L[…] Harpe[?r’s F]erry […]ont. The letter belongs to the weeks between First Bull Run (21 July 1861) and the arrest. McClellan took command at Washington in late July; the panic in the city, the attack expected hourly, the hunt for whoever gave the alarm, cavalry leaving “this morning” and Harper’s Ferry fit that summer. A clear pencil draft in the same seized file, naId 1634043, headed “10 Aug. 1861”, says in similar words that “McClellan is very active and very discreet” and that “an attack is apprehended”. It is not a copy of this letter, but it supports the date. Three signs on the leaf are not what the key predicts: an extra R-sign inside EXPEC-R-TED, no S-sign at the end of SIMULTANEOU (the word ends in U and a dot), and no O-sign in EFF|RT, where the line ends at the ruled border. These are her slips.
greenhow1861.html#open

Side 1, paper losses: al[l], acti[vi]ty, atta[ck], [b]e, Ferr[y], eff[o]rt, tro[op o]f, [th]is, Harpe[r’s F]erry. Restorations from context, marked; the signs are lost with the paper. Side 1, clear words cut by losses ( myste… , a… , u… , l… ) and the heading “P 31”. “Edwards Ferry” and “Baltimore” are conjectures: only R, d, S, F, E, R, R and TIMORE are on the paper. Side 2: two lines give only fragments (gr…e, tim…, bo…, …ganiz…ing), 17 signs; not enough for sentences. The scrap of figures (image 3), tested against the key in review. The key writes numbers with letter-like signs (1 = a, 2 = d, 5 = m, 6 = b …; 10 = III), so these Arabic figures are not its numbers; read as the key’s digit-shaped letter signs (3 = C, 4 = I or R, 5 = O, 8 = G) they give no words, and 2 and 6 have no value at all. With “$5 dollers $25” at the top and figures from 5 to 104, the scrap looks like a money reckoning. Three key-like signs on its last line are too few to decipher. The scrap of figures filed with the letter: “$5 dollers $25 . 26 . do ll…”, then rows of numbers. Image: National Archives, RG 59, Seized Correspondence of Rose O'Neal Greenhow, naId 1634036, image 3, via the National Archives Catalog. Earlier work: applying the 1864 key to Greenhow’s 1861 material is not new; the Rosenbach did so in 2011 for another note, and the North Carolina State Archives hold a copy of the key. No decipherment of this letter was found: not on the NARA record, the Library of Congress or Santa Clara copies, nor in the Official Records , Series II, vol. 2 (the Greenhow case papers, pp. 561–577), Pinkerton’s Spy of the Rebellion (1883) or Greenhow’s My Imprisonment (1863). Fishel’s The Secret War for the Union (1996) and Blackman’s Wild Rose (2005) could only be searched through the web. A Union decipherment of the time cannot be excluded: the Official Records (II 2, p. 561) say the torn letters from her stove were “assorted and placed together so as to be read and copied”, and Jordan wrote on 29 October 1861 (pp. 564–565) that the War Department, holding one of her letters in this cipher, “ought to have worked out the key”.

Intelligence from the Greenhow ring before her arrest on 23 Aug 1861. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (60% here); the holes are marked in the reading. Heidelberg Cod. Pal. germ. 597 hides substance names in three home-made alphabets of graphic signs, and DECODE lists it with no decipherment. Wilhelm Wattenbach deciphered the alphabets in 1869 and printed passages with their plaintexts. The values of the signs were recovered here from the images by aligning them with those plaintexts. ▪ o 2 ∴ ⊡ 8 Y ˥ : ɓ 4 … = a b c d e f g h i k l … vnd ich ˥ ▪ o ⊡ ● = vnd ich hab es ϙ : ɓ 4 ▪ ● = niklas East Bavaria, near Passau · three home-made alphabets of graphic signs · 1426 Alchymey teuczsch: the ciphers of an alchemists’ notebook, 1426 Go to the full text ↓ Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 · paper, 95 leaves, Bavarian German · DECODE R2876, listed with no decipherment A circle of gold-makers wrote their recipes in German and hid the substance names in signs of their own. The compiler put the key on the first leaf and struck it through. Wilhelm Wattenbach deciphered the alphabets in 1869 and printed three passages with their plaintexts. Here the values of the signs were recovered from the images by aligning them with his plaintexts and the compiler’s own alphabet; nothing was deciphered that was not already in print. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method · key A, the compiler's 24-sign 'new abc' (f. 1r): read from existing decipherment (partial) · key B, stroke and figure signs (ff. 6v, 91v): read from existing decipherment (complete) · set C, boxes, stars and T (ff. 1r ll. 1-2, 5v-6r, 44v, 93r): key recovered based on plaintext from external sources (partial) Credits · Pamela Kalning, Matthias Miller, Karin Zimmermann (Heidelberg catalogue 2014) (key or decipherment used) · Wilhelm Wattenbach (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Read from existing decipherment · complete The document Heidelberg cpg 597, a compiler’s book with cipher passages, put forward as a candidate for the oldest cipher this project could decipher. Where A DECODE record with no decipherment, pointing to “ff. 70–71”. Those are Bernhard Bischoff’s 1954 item numbers, not folios, and the leaves are blank. The cipher Several sign sets: a crossed-out alphabet on f. 1r, a second alphabet on f. 6v and f. 91v, and a third set on f. 1r lines 1–2, ff. 5v–6r, 44v and 93r. How it was read Already deciphered in print: Wilhelm Wattenbach broke it in 1869; Gerhard Eis printed more in 1957 and 1982. Here every leaf was surveyed, and the first two alphabets were recovered and checked against the printed plaintexts. The third set was identified and partly fixed. Still open A continuous transcription of the recipe passages, the f. 6r glossary and f. 44v has never been printed; it needs the doubtful signs of two keys settled first. Credit Wattenbach 1869; Eis 1957 and 1982; Bischoff 1954.
heidelberg597.html#book

A small paper book, 22.5 by 15.5 cm, written in several Bavarian hands and dated on f. 9r: Das puch ist angehaben ym [tauro] xiiii und xxvj , begun with the sun in Taurus, 1426. Most of the recipes are headed with the name of Niklas Jankowitz. Other names are Michael von Pirpach, over a list of lucky and unlucky days, and Michel Wulfing, over a fever charm. A note on f. 94r records that on the Saturday of Easter week [14]23 “we” gave “our multiplication” to one Frydryce to work, weighed at four pounds less two lot. An address formula to Leonhard, bishop of Passau from 1424, places the circle. The book is sewn into an unexecuted 1413 charter of the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg, counts of Hals, taking the Jew Salman Teublin into their service and binding him to teach them three of his best arts. The cipher protects a working notebook. Recipes are in clear German, and the substance names, quantities and some whole sentences are in signs. A survey of all 85 images, covers included, finds cipher on f. 1r, ff. 5v–7r, 9r–15v, 20r–22r, 44v, 46r–v, 54r–61r, 79ar, 91v and 93r. The signs belong to three independent alphabets, and each has its own result below: key A and key B were deciphered by Wattenbach in 1869 and their alphabets are recovered here against his plaintexts (key A only in part, since the recipe cipher has not been transcribed); set C was not given by Wattenbach, and its values come from the 2014 catalogue’s reading of f. 93r, with f. 44v and the glossary still unread.
