Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 1r. Lines 1–2 in the third sign set; line 3 the alphabet, run together, then vnd ich in clear and the signs for hab es ; line 4 the rest of the sentence. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 1r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach deciphered the leaf in 1869: Das ist ein abc vnd das haben wir selbs neus gemacht, abcdefghiklmnopqrſstuwschch vnd ich hab es darum gar an ein ander gesetzt das man nicht sul versten das es ein alfabet sei — “This is an ABC that we made ourselves, new, and I have set it all together so that no one should understand that it is an alphabet.” The alphabet is written without a break, and the whole leaf is struck through. Wattenbach thought the strike was there because the key was too easy to guess; it is still legible. With the strike line removed from the image, the run gives twenty-four signs in the order of the alphabet the text names: a b c d e f g h i k l m ▪ o 2 ∴ ⊡ 8 Y ˥ : ɓ 4 ꝝ n o p q r ſ s t u w sch ch ϙ 88 ꝗ ꝁ × F ● ◒ • T ⊙ ♣ The signs are rendered with the nearest typographic shape. Two checks in running text: Line 3 continues after the clear vnd ich with ˥ ▪ o ⊡ ●, which is hab es , as Wattenbach printed. The recipe heading on f. 11r is ϙ : ɓ 4 ▪ ● · Y ▪ ϙ ɓ ? : 2, niklas gank?icz , with one sign unresolved. A modern reader had already pencilled “= Niklas Gankwiz” beside it. f. 11r, the name in the f. 1r alphabet, with a modern pencil gloss. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 11r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). The first eleven values, a to l, are clear on the image, and a, b, c, e, g, h, i, k, l and s are checked in running text. The last thirteen are inferred from the shape of the signs under the heaviest part of the strike, and only a few of them have been met in running text; they are grade C.

f. 6v, the opening prayer in the second alphabet. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 6v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach printed f. 6v with its plaintext: In dem namen des faters vnd des suns vnd des heiligen geistes so fach ich schuldiger man dises buch an , “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost I, a guilty man, begin this book.” Segmenting the three lines and laying them against the text gives nineteen values: : i, a hooked Y n, 3 d, a trefoil on a stem e, Ω with an inner triangle m, a stroke a, a tall stroke medial s, a blob final s, a ring with a tail f, a T with a wavy top r, a ring with a dot h, T l, a looped stem g, two loops on a stem t, a ring with a 3-tail sch, an 8 with an inner loop b, a c joined to a 2 for ch, 9 o, and a cup with a 3 for the u of vnd . Every word of the prayer decrypts with them. f. 91v, the second alphabet written out in order and struck through. Its opening signs agree with the values from f. 6v. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 91v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). The same set is written out in alphabetical order on f. 91v and crossed out, like the first. Wattenbach did not reproduce that leaf, and the catalogue notes it only as an alphabet.
heidelberg597.html#setc

f. 5v, the preface to the glossary of cover-names, clear German with runs of the third set. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 5v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach wrote that f. 1r uses “two different systems”. Lines 1–2 of that leaf are in a third set built from boxes with and without dots, stars and T-shapes, which also carries the preface and glossary on ff. 5v–6r and the notes on ff. 44v and 93r. Two printed plaintexts fix part of it: f. 1r line 1, Das ist ein abc : Das [✱ 中 ⊡̈] [⊡ ✱ T] [▪ o 2]. f. 93r, given in the 2014 catalogue as Nota wir haben versucht das [in dem caichen] der [iuncfrawn] , “we have tried it in the sign of the Virgin”: [✱ T] [∴ ⊡ ■] [2 ▪ ✱ 2 ⊏ ⊡ T]. f. 93r, the Virgo note. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 93r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Together they give ▪ a, o b, 2 c, ∴ d, ⊡ e, ⊏ h, ✱ i, T n, a filled box m, a box on a stem s and a box with two dots t. The a, b, c, d and e are the signs of the f. 1r alphabet. The i and n are not, and T, which is w in the f. 1r alphabet, is n here. The s and t rest on one word each. The glossary on f. 6r uses further dotted-box variants and has not been deciphered.
heidelberg597.html#recipes

The glossary on f. 5v was printed by Wattenbach in its resolved form: aqua fortis is called “the sharp water”, sal ammoniac “sal”, its oil “Nyczadar”, common salt “sal aller”, gold “the yellow earth”, silver “the white earth”, green oil “vitriol”. The cover-names were meant to spare the writers from enciphering every substance, and the recipes still mix them with signs. In the recipes (ff. 7r–22r, 46r–v, 54r–61r), the signs are mostly those of the f. 1r alphabet, as the name on f. 11r shows, with admixtures from the others; Bischoff noted that the sets are also used mixed. The runs are short, from one to a few words, and recur: the most frequent group appears about a dozen times on ff. 10v–15r. f. 79ar holds a struck table of sign groups, each over a pair of signs, which looks like a list of substances with their symbols.
heidelberg597.html#record

The project’s oldest deciphered cipher is from 1497, and a list of earlier candidates was drawn up to try to beat it. This book was on it at 1426 for three reasons: DECODE lists it with no decipherment, with 85 images; the Handschriftencensus entry cites Bischoff for “S. 12 (Nr. 70–71)”, which was taken to mean cipher on ff. 70–71; and the key was said to be on f. 1r. The first check on any target is for a prior decipherment. Wattenbach’s 1869 note, with its facsimiles of f. 1r, f. 5v and f. 6v and their plaintexts, settles it. The book is ruled out as a record candidate.

A letter from Rákóczi’s envoy at the Porte in a simple substitution (DECODE R496), catalogued with no decipherment and a placeholder date. A contemporary Hungarian decipherment is written between the lines; it was transcribed and checked against key values fixed from two sibling letters. About a fifth of the interlinear text stays uncertain where the hand overlaps the cipher. w i 6 x i 2 i 4 F e l s é g e d w = f · i = e · 6 = l · x = s · 2 = g · 4 = d Constantinople → Ferenc Rákóczi II · simple substitution in letters, digits and signs · 8 July 1707 Mihály Hentér to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 8 July 1707 to Francis II Rákóczi Go to the full text ↓ MNL OL G 15, Caps. D, Fasc. 80, fol. 38 (DECODE R496), listed on DECODE as non-decrypted and dated “1 January 1707”. Two other letters from Hentér in the same fascicle use the same system and carry dense interlinear plaintext: R533 (fol. 40) and R534 (fol. 46). R533’s closing formula gives a clean control. The cipher group wi6xi2i4 decrypts as Felséged , which fixes w = f, i = e, 6 = l, x = s, 2 = g and 4 = d. Other repeated formulae give n = a, 0 = o, c = h, 9 = m and 5 = k; the other graphic signs cannot be typed in plain text. These values agree with the interlinear text on R496, so the glosses are a decipherment of this cipher and not a paraphrase. Benedek Láng independently lists fols. 38, 40 and 46 as Hentér’s three 1707 letters (C.Hen.01–03) and describes their cipher as monoalphabetic.

The cipher A homophonic substitution on invented signs, Greek-looking letters and numerals, written without word division, with code signs for F.G. ( Fürstliche Gnaden , in Latin Dominationes ) and for King Ferdinand. The hands differ, so the key varies a little from letter to letter. How it was deciphered A faint gloss of the time over ten lines of R9427 gave the first key; it was improved on the sibling letter R9407 (deciphered on its own page) and re-learned on each letter by a statistical fit and a decoder that keeps whole period words; every line was then deciphered by hand. What they say King John’s diplomacy with Bavaria, the Turk, the Pressburg diet, Katzianer, Rincon at Constantinople, mining in Hungary. King John writes on 30 June 1534 that he has only a truce with his adversary: nos cum adversario nostro pacem non habere sed … inducias . Still open 695 words of the six letters, legible signs whose values the letters do not settle; no letter reaches 95%. R9409, R9427 and both letters on R9410 have holes in most sentences and are decoded, not read. Until 15 October 2026 this page covered all fourteen ciphertexts of catalogue entry 161, which are letters in at least six ciphers. The others now have their own pages: Łaski’s cipher (R9322, R9323, R9417, with R9403), the Fulda note of 1576 (R9325), a son’s letter of 1535 (R9367), R9416 (a servant’s letter and the Pressburg report), R9424 (1583, not solved) and R9319 (1583 grilles, blocked). R9291 is a key fragment, not a letter. Jörg Weinmeister’s letter of 1533 (R9407), in the same system, has its own page ; its improved key was carried back here.

R9408, R9409, R9410, R9413 and R9427 share one sign family, which is also that of Jörg Weinmeister’s letter of 1533 (R9407, written up separately ). R9427 has a faint gloss over ten lines. Aligned symbol by symbol, it showed that the commonest group w3vX is “ewr F.G.” (X, an hourglass, is a code symbol for Fürstliche Gnaden ) and gave the first homophonic key: 4 and ω e , □ and 8 n (“48” = -en ), ↓ r , ÿ t , 5 a , π b/w , the slanted ‡ g , the upright H u/v , and so on. With that key the five letters gave German in stretches, with many local errors. The key carried back from R9407 (2 October 2026). The key was then improved on R9407, a letter of the same system deciphered to 96.7% of its words. That improved key was carried back to the five letters by the shapes of the signs and re-learned on each letter: a statistical fit of the symbol values against a model of sixteenth-century German, seeded with the R9407 values, then a decoder that keeps whole period words (Deutsches Textarchiv word list) and re-estimates the key from its own output. The hands differ, so each letter keeps its own variant: E is d and ch everywhere, π b/w , 5 a and often e ; in R9408 “my” is m ; in R9413 the symbol k is the word ich ; in R9427 a lone R is und . Look-alike signs were checked at the images: in R9408 the transcribed y is two signs (dotted ÿ t , undotted γ r ) and 4 is two (closed 4 e , open ч i ); in R9409 one symbol takes da , ch and f . Separating them confirmed the values the decipherments had already given, without opening further words. Every line of the five letters was then deciphered by hand from the machine output and the values each symbol can take. The K word symbol is King Ferdinand by context (grade B): it sends Hieronymus of Zara and his son Vespasian to the Turk (R9408), the Hungarian lords “who hold with [K]” meet at Pressburg (R9413), and the Württemberg war is “against [K]” (R9413, R9427). No letter reaches the 95% bar. R9408: Jörg Weinmeister, Ofen, 8 February 1534 Signed “… Weinmaister” in cipher, like R9407. Back from his mission, he has handed over a ratschlag , put into Latin. The instruction, he says, was written without knowledge of the Turk, who pays foreign soldiers in cash and thinks himself her[r] der welt . There are sums of 100,000 and twelve times 100,000 gulden. On mining he names Friedrich Schmaltz and his brother-in-law Reinhart, miners to be sent from Schwaz and a silver purchase through Nuremberg. He reports Ferdinand’s peace with the Turk, Hieronymus [Zara] and his son Vespasian sent back to the Turk, Katzianer two months before Kaschau (Košice), and Emericus, provost of Stuhlweissenburg and bishop-elect of Neutra, who married and was imprisoned. He also reports bad half-batzen bearing the dukes’ stamp: er habe dise halbbatzen mit eur F.G. gepreck . Image P1 is a separate news page: Emperor Sigmund’s 6,000 men, Constantinople and Syria. R9409: an intelligence report of early 1534 (decoded, not read) The longest of the five, with clear phrases. The dukes and the Roman king are to agree on the confederation. A Turkish embassy has come, and the Sultan is to come to Constantinople. The royal commissioners at Pressburg and Vienna achieved nothing. Katzianer’s troops and Rascians are on the Transylvanian border, Majláth is forcing Hermannstadt ( in der Hermanstat … Meilat ), and there is dearth in Transylvania. Then the voivode’s practices, a truce in the Zips, Poland against Muscovy, seven burghers of Késmárk held for ransom, and the advice of the French and English kings to make war. Numbered articles follow on a mining concession: Antoni Slesinger, Schmaltz as mining captain, Freiberger, the gold-exchangers and silver-buyers, and the export of gold and silver refused. A postscript begins Auf den Reichstag and closes Datum ut in literis . R9410 f. 244r: “des ersten aprilis Anno 35” (decoded, not read) A treaty is in hand; the King of France has also gehandelt nit so vil als vor , done less than before. Someone will accept no treaty unless the dukes are included, kain vertrag annemen allein eur F.G. sollen … in vertrag eingeschlossen sein . The parties are to hold together bruederlich against the Turks, and the sender commends himself to the dukes als seinen lieben herren und bruedern . The writer closes in aller gehorsamen underthenigkait , dated the first of April [15]35. R9413: an agent to the dukes, June and July 1534 Three letters (July, 7 June, and “8 Julij”), addressed to the dukes’ secretary Waisenfelder. The dukes’ letters were received with joy; there is no reliable news of the Turk. Cornelius was delayed because der kunigs von franckreich orator antonius rincon had come to Constantinople. Then Katzianer’s riders and Transylvania, the bishop of Wardein before Margrave Georg’s castle of Hunyad, the Württemberg war and the Landgrave. An ore sample found near Ofen assays at 2½ marks of silver. The Turk is at sea with about 200 galleys, and the Hungarian lords meet at Pressburg. Herr Caspar is to be dispatched, and Antoni kept at the dukes’ cost. R9427: a newsletter of April 1534 (decoded, not read) Dated 15, 21 and 24 April [15]34, with a postscript of 25 April. It opens durchleuchtig hochgeborn fursten gnedig … , as the contemporary gloss over the first lines has it. Its subject is the Württemberg affair (the Bund, that is the Swabian League, the dukes of Württemberg, the Landgrave, “kain vertrag”), with Ferdinand, Christendom and Hungary. A provost and priest alhie has taken a wife and been imprisoned. The dukes’ letter came durch Stehan on 23 April.

The record R9410 holds a second letter on ff. 246–247 (images P3, P4 and P6; P5 repeats P4). It was transcribed by hand on 2 October 2026, 65 lines and 2,342 signs. A contemporary gloss over its first line ( accepimus literas vestras ) and the clear phrases show that it is in Latin. The German key of f. 244r, re-learned against a Latin model, gave Latin at once. Here the sign that is und in German is et (and in before q ), and the hourglass follows Vestre and Vestrarum as F.G. does in German: it is the code for Dominationes . The letter is decoded, not read: about 18% of its words are unread and most sentences have a hole (23 October 2026). The passage below holds; it is given line by line as in r9410/reading_p3p6.txt , with clear words in square brackets, [X] the hourglass code and {?} an unread word: [In quantu] [autem] vestre [X] certiores fieri cupiunt de st atu rerum nostrarum sciant nos cum adversario nostro pacem non habere sed {?} inducias quas cum nos sancte et invio[l]abiliter servaremus et servare parati essemus parte ex alia tam ip se quam ad eum pertinentes non cess[a]runt ne que cessant inducias huiusmodi multis mo dis infringere (“As for Your Lordships’ wish to know the state of our affairs, know that we have no peace with our adversary but … a truce, which, though we kept it holy and inviolate and were ready to keep it, he and those who belong to him did not cease and do not cease to break in many ways.”) The letter thanks the dukes for their letters and for passing on news of the Landgrave and of the Duke of Württemberg, and says the king had written that he would send his own envoy. It thanks God for preclaram victoriam , a famous victory which it believes good for all Christendom. It speaks of the adversary’s people writing to the dukes tam impudenter pro libito , and of a man back at Constantinople, from whom letters dated at Constantinople came that very day. It closes by offering omnem amiciciam et fraternitatem nostram : Datum Bude ultima Iunii , Anno (15)34. The royal “we”, the “adversary” with whom there is only a truce, and Buda as the place make it a letter of King John Zápolya to the Dukes of Bavaria. The letter does not say which victory it means. 375 of its 422 words have a sense (88.9%).

R9408, 123 words (parts of the news page P1, the greeting, the clauses of the ratschlag , the signature’s forename); R9409, 304 (the salutation and date, about half of P7, names); R9410 f. 244r, 42 (lines 3–5, a two-sign group, the place in the date line); the Latin letter, 47 (the opening, two clauses, two name groups at P4.12 and P4.20); R9413, 94 (the opening of P1, the description of the ore, a sign group on P5, the address); R9427, 85 (line ends, names on P2, the signature). The signs are legible; their values are not settled by the letters. All are open code or value questions (grade I or open), not missing material. The K word sign is no longer open: King Ferdinand by context (grade B), though no key in the volume gives it. Grades: the System A′ passages quoted above are C (key and context agree); the identification of the Latin letter’s sender as King John is inferred from its content ( I ), as is “Hieronymus [Zara]” in R9408.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. R9408, ff. 236-239, Ofen 8 Feb 1534 read in part Jörg Weinmeister (signed in cipher) to the Dukes of Bavaria from Ofen, 8 Feb 1534, with Latin clear passages: his mission, the Turk's power and money, mining (Schmaltz, Reinhart), Katzianer before Kaschau, the priest-bishop Emericus and bad coin with the dukes' stamp; a separate news page on Emperor Sigmund, Constantinople and Syria. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (90% here); the holes are marked in the reading. Where DECODE notes that the Stadtholder’s cabinet deciphered none of them. Kauderbach wrote the figures without separation, so the office could not tell where a group ended. The cipher The digits 5 and 8 never occur inside a group and are nulls; the rest falls into about sixty two-figure groups, one key for all four years. How it was read A homophonic solver found nothing. Kauderbach’s own 1761 cipher (DECODE R936) uses two-figure numbers for letters and syllables; its numbers do not fit, but its vocabulary does. An annealing search for a one-to-one assignment converged twice to the same key, and hand correction fixed the rest. What it says The Dutch argument over the thirteen-thousand-man augmentation in 1755, Colonel Yorke and the Saxon subsidy treaty, and the Treaty of Versailles of May 1756 (“une consternation extraordinaire ici”). Still open The names stay in clear capitals ( S./. , Q./. , P./. ); their 1754 meanings are known only from context. Kauderbach (1707–1785) served the Saxon legation at The Hague from 1739 for almost thirty years; his despatches went to Count Brühl in Dresden (“Votre Excellence”). The Dutch post office copied them for the Stadtholder’s cabinet, and the copies are in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, Prins Willem V inv. 201, beside the d’Affry intercepts of inv. 192. Most are wholly in clear. DECODE catalogued the ten with figures, from photographs, and transcribed three. The Hague cabinet’s note on DECODE gives the reason for their failure: “the codegroups are not separated, by blanks or dots as is usually the case.” A first count showed no preferred period of two or three figures from the start of a passage, and the copyists’ spacing is not systematic. Two figures behave differently from the rest. 5 and 8 are rare (135 and 78 in the first 6,096 digits), never follow 5 or 8, and typically stand next to the clear sigla ( …254 M./. , J./. C./. 8095… ). Deleting them as single figures restores a clean two-figure phase (index of coincidence 0.027 against 0.021 for the shifted reading; for four-figure windows 0.155 and 0.161 at offsets 0 and 2, 0.103 at 1 and 3). A short Viterbi pass over the pair frequencies then repairs the places where a copyist dropped or doubled a figure. What is left is a table of about sixty two-figure groups: first figure 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, second 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, never 0, 5 or 8. Every letter shows the same frequency profile, so one key served from 1754 to 1756 at least. A homophonic solver failed on that table. A hill-climbing solver that decrypts synthetic French in the same form (sixty codes, two per cent noise, nulls, realignment) at 98% produced nothing on the real stream, in French, German, Dutch or Italian, with nulls or merged look-alike figures. The statistics of the stream still looked like language (entropy, vowel alternation 0.63, long exact repeats such as 19 29 14 44 nineteen times), so the units were not single letters.

Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden 10024 Loc. 08236/11 Bl. 5, the cipher for “Kauderbach in Den Haag”, 1761 (DECODE R936): pour chiffrer and pour déchiffrer , one number for each letter or syllable, the capitals A–Z for persons and states (S la Hollande , T l’Angleterre , U France ), and 6. est faux chiffre . DECODE’s transcription has “30 ni?” for 30 m . Image: Sächsisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, 10024 Geheimer Rat, Loc. 08236/11 Bl. 5, via DECODE R936. DECODE also holds the Dresden chancery’s cipher register, and one of its leaves is the key made for Kauderbach in 1761. It explains the 1754 system at once: a null figure, capitals in clear for the names, and a single number for each of about seventy letters and syllables. It is not the same key (its numbers use 5 and 8), but a successor of the same design. So the problem became an assignment: each 1754 code to a different item of the 1761 vocabulary. A simulated-annealing search over such assignments, scored by a four-letter French model built from contemporary diplomatic letters, reached the same key from two independent starts (seeds 22 and 24, −3.85 per letter, against −3.95 for true French on the same model), and the result was French. Reading the decryption then settled what the 1761 vocabulary lacked or the search had misplaced: 27 in (principales, provinces, interet), 91 ou , 33 qu , 79 st , 17 par , 22 pas , 46 qui , 66 pour , 23 fai , 76 ke (Yorke, Kniphausen), 77 z (treize, declarez), and the exchange of 01 oi and 12 ai , found independently by both readers (avoit, etoit, croire; raisons, mais, Pais Bas). 01 oi · 02 de · 03 re · 04 au · 06 ie · 07 le · 09 ne · 10 z? · 11 p · 12 ai · 13 y (re) · 14 i · 16 e · 17 par · 19 a · 20 fe? · 21 ce · 22 pas · 23 fai · 24 s · 26 et · 27 in · 29 t · 30 an · 31 b · 32 n · 33 qu · 34 du · 36 si · 37 en · 39 pr · 40 em? · 41 la · 42 ra · 43 c · 44 on · 46 qui · 47 f · 49 sa · 60 ent · 61 h · 62 que · 63 u/v · 64 d · 66 pour · 67 se · 69 l · 71 te · 72 g · 73 o · 74 ci · 76 ke · 77 z · 79 st · 90 k? · 91 ou · 92 r · 93 il · 94 m · 96 co · 97 x · 5, 8 nulls

[Clear: the Estates of Holland will separate on Saturday until a new convocation.] Il n’y a pas eu depuis longtems une assemblée des etats de Holl. dont les objets de deliberations aient eté plus importans et en meme tems plus embarassans pour cet etat. D’un coté l’ouverture faite par le comte d’Affry presente mille epines, et quant au fond et quant a la forme des conferences a entamer …; de l’autre coté le colonel Yorke, qui ne s’endort pas dans ces circonstances, demande dans un memoire … des explications sur ce a quoi l’on peut se tenir relativement aux engagemens … The overture is to go through commissioners, conferences auxquelles le marquis de Bonnac agira et parlera comme chef de l’ambassade ; the opponents of England font assez connaitre que le principal but est de negocier un [traité] de neutralité . Yorke himself, dans des momens d’impatience, se sentoit incliné pour le sisteme des anticontinentistes ; Kauderbach thinks Hanover the right place pendant qu’on y est encore dans l’incertitude des evenemens en Amerique . On a aujourd’hui des avis certains et positifs que le [traité] dont on parle depuis si longtems a eté signé a Versailles le deux de ce mois, et selon ce qu’on m’a [fait] conter confidemment, il a pour objet primo la neutralité des Pais Bas, secundo il doit y etre stipulé qu’aucune puissance ne donnera aucun secours a l’ennemi de l’autre … et tertio … de ne pas lui etre contraire relativement a l’election d’un Roi des Romains. The sigla. The capitals with ./. (S, Q, P, U, J, C, M, E, Y, Z, W, B, G) are names written in clear, as in the 1761 key, but their 1754 meanings differ from it. S is almost certainly Holland (the Estates, the provinces), Y a subsidy treaty, Z troops; the rest are identified from context only and marked as sigla in the decryptions. Rare codes. 10, 20, 40 and 90 occur twelve times in all and are guesses; 13 stands for y and apparently also re (membres, reflexion); 66 may stand for er inside some words. R1954 (four pages in a letter-like hand): decoded, not read. After the look-alike digits were resolved on 23 October 2026, garbled runs remain on f. 2 lines 6, 8 and 13 and f. 4 lines 6–10 and 17–25; the digits there are legible but do not decode with the key, slips of the Dutch copyist. Only the original despatch (Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, Geheimes Kabinett, not online) could settle them. Transcription slips. The DECODE transcriptions and the new ones both drop or double figures; the decryption files list those found. The clear passages were transcribed quickly and are summarised, not edited. The percentages are the readers’ estimates of the share of the ciphertext that gives sense; 99.9% of the groups carry a key value.

In the autumn of 1520 the Revolt of the Comunidades held much of Castile. The Junta of the rebel cities sat at Tordesillas, where Queen Joanna lived, and wanted her to reign in place of her absent son. On 5 December the governors’ army, under the Count of Haro, took the town back; it was sacked and several of the Junta’s procurators were captured. Charles V was in Germany, at Worms for his first Diet. Lope Hurtado de Mendoza, a gentleman of Charles’s household, had been sent to the governors as the Emperor’s confidant. On 10 December he wrote twice from Tordesillas. One letter, in clear (PTR,LEG,2,36,6), tells of the sack and lists the prisoners; Antonio Danvila printed it in the 1890s in his documentary history of the Comunidades. The other, 36,8, is entirely in cipher, and says what could not be written openly about the governors and the grandees. Its dorse reads “Carta de Lope Hurtado de x de dez.”. It fills both sides of one leaf, 44 lines on the recto and 42 on the verso; the two pages can be seen on PARES . Hurtado’s later letters from Rome, of 1522 to 1524, use a different cipher, a code of three-letter groups with an alphabet of cursive signs, and have their own pages: Rome, 1522 and Rome, 1523–24 .

A substitution of single letters by about 37 signs: Latin letters, figures and invented shapes, among them a barred o for t , a cross for s , a 9 for a , a long ſ for g and a ⊤ for z . The words are kept apart, as in the clear hand. Vowels and a few consonants have more than one sign; the encipherer used them unevenly. Some signs stand for two or three letters: one gives a , l or h , one i , j or y , another e , h or p , so the reading of those signs is settled by the word. Persons are written as dotted sigla, ·fre· , ·lis· , ·los· , ·lus· , ·ym· , short groups between points whose meaning is not in the letter. The last lines of the verso mix cipher with words in ordinary letters (“fynes”, “lo primero”, “vra altza”, “el bien del rreyno”, “creo q no”), and cipher and clear read on as one text. The transcription names each sign by a single character of a working notation ( targets/lopehurtado1520/key_K4.tsv ); the names are labels for shapes, not values. In that notation the key is: letter signs (labels) letter signs (labels) a g, F* n n, φ, ∂* b / v q* o w, H, W c 7 p B*, b*, X* d Z, E, ∂*, Y* q c e s, V, B*, b*, X* r r, A f Q, f s t g S t O h F*, b* u N, U i / j / y 8, d*, Y* x x, X* l P, l, F* z T m o * a sign with more than one value. Two rare signs, △ and ■, have no value; the second also marks a blot. The commonest sign, labelled s , is e (575 of about 3,700 signs), then g = a (433) and w = o (295). The frequencies are those of Spanish.

The key that was supposed to fit. A slip by the archivist J. Paz in the bundle says the key is to be found in Hurtado’s letter of 23 September 1520 (PTR,LEG,2,36,2), which Danvila printed deciphered. Its values are incompatible with this letter, so the key had to be recovered from the ciphertext. Breaking in. The signs were transcribed from the PARES images in the working notation. The repeated groups that had to be vuestra magestad opened a homophonic letter substitution. A first key, K1, was built from lines 1–16 of the recto only and frozen, with a SHA-256 hash recorded. Held-out lines. Two stretches of the verso were kept out of the work. Lines 1–11, transcribed after K1 was frozen, gave 0.747 of their words in a Spanish lexicon under K1, against 0.326 at the 99th percentile of 200 control keys with the values permuted. Lines 11–17 were transcribed and frozen before any decoding and used to fix no value; the later keys K2 and K4 both read 0.827 of their words, against a median of 0.288, a 99th percentile of 0.519 and a maximum of 0.596 for the controls. The full reading. The rest was deciphered word by word, deciding between near-identical signs against a Spanish lexicon (the Quijote and Danvila’s documents). K3 became K4 when one value, ſ as s , was withdrawn after Dudout’s own look at twelve doubtful signs on a sheet of sign shapes, made without any reading offered; that look also settled holgado , cardenal , necesidad and oficio . The statistical check here. The project’s validator ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the reading of 3,432 signs (35 sign types) with a four-gram model of Golden Age Spanish, as mean log-probability per letter: the reading gives −2.139, random keys of the same shape −5.439 on average, and a key annealed onto the shuffled ciphertext at best −3.118. Verdict: pass.

The ·fre· negotiates with the Junta and hesitates to accept “la governación”. Dudout takes him to be the Admiral of Castile, Fadrique Enríquez, named co-governor in September 1520 and known to favour a settlement with the Comuneros; fre would abbreviate his first name. That is a hypothesis: nothing in the letter proves it. The other sigla (·lis·, ·los·, ·lus·, ·ym·, ·y·) are not identified. ·lus· and ·los· seem to refer to the Queen and her household at Tordesillas. The Queen “por cuerda”. Whether Joanna was of sound mind was the political stake of the Junta, which wanted her to reign. That the ·fre· called her sane was, for Hurtado, a sign that he might give way on the agreements. The Marquis of Denia , Bernardo de Sandoval y Rojas, governor of the Queen’s household, had been expelled by the Comuneros in September and came back after the town was taken. “Having sent away the women” probably refers to the Queen’s attendants. The Naples precedent. Ferdinand the Catholic, in Naples in 1506–07, left sees, commanderies and keeperships unfilled until his return; Hurtado recommends the same to keep hopes of favour alive. The lords named in the clear : the Count of Benavente, the Marquis of Astorga, the Count of Miranda, the comendador mayor , don Pedro Girón (the Comuneros’ captain) and the Count of Haro, “who holds the office of captain”. The Cardinal and the Constable of the later proposals are presumably the two other governors, Adrian of Utrecht and Íñigo Fernández de Velasco, whose seat was Burgos.

Lope Hurtado de Mendoza to Charles V, Tordesillas, 10 December 1520 (AGS PTR,LEG,2,36,8) Five days after Tordesillas was retaken from the Comuneros, Lope Hurtado de Mendoza, Charles V’s confidant with the governors of Castile, wrote two letters on the same day. One, in plain text, tells of the sack of the town and the capture of the Junta’s procurators; Danvila printed it in the late nineteenth century. The other, entirely in cipher, says what could not be written openly: the Admiral hesitates to govern, the Marquis of Denia is hated, the army is “very badly commanded”, and the see of Jaén and every vacancy should be held back to keep loyalties. An archivist’s slip in the bundle said the key was to be found in a letter of 23 September; it was not. We rebuilt it from the letter itself. El ·fre· está ganoso de asiento con los de la Junta como quiera que fuese ; dize que lo haze por el mal aparejo que {ay} de sostener la gente que aquí está. Hizo a la reina que, delante del ·y· de muchos cavalleros, dixiese que mandava que toda la gente de la Junta se derramase, e mandólo tomar por testimonio para enviar a requerir con él a don Pedro Girón ·y· a las ciudades. El conde de Benavente, marqués de Astorga, conde de Miranda, comendador mayor no se hallaron allí ; sabido, entendió luego ·ym· en remediarlo. E así fueron al ·fre· y el testimonio se rasgó ‹…›, no por voto suyo : antes estava en medio. E aun estando así, dixo que a la reina tenía por cuerda, e no y ase cada día mill vezes, de que {temo} que algún día haga cosa sobre los conciertos que sea muy dañosa. Escrívale ·lis·, encomendándogelo todo a él ·y·, rogándole que, pues ya lo ha, pues esto [está] en tan buen estado, que trabaje que se conserve sin que se asiente cosa contra las preeminencias reales. Escriva vuestra alteza de su mano algunos renglones, que todo es menester, por a él [y] al conde de Benavente, encomendándole mucho que mire que en esto no se haga cosa de{s}ordenada por la necesidad ‹…›, porque si él quiere nada se puede hazer que sea malo, porque todos los otros que aquí están har[í]anlo que de partes de vuestra alteza se les dixiere ; y {certifico} que les ‹…› vuestra alteza su venida. Y que si lo que acá ay no bastare para sostener el e{x}ército, que vuestra alteza {mandará} prove{e}r de allá ; porque de ‹…› dezía que no ay con que se {sostener[á]}, he miedo que hiziesen algo ; e aun si se pudiese enviar algún crédito, lo tendría por mejor. E sobre este artículo mande vuestra majestad despachar luego posta, porque conviene. El marqués de Denia viene aquí con más pasión de la que era menester, {segund él} tiene ; está muy mal quisto a muchos : les ha pesado tanto de su venida como de averlo saqueado. Vuestra alteza le deve mandar que se temple mucho, trabaje con amor de contentar los criados de ·los· y de servir a la señora ·lus· y la ‹·tar·›, que es ‹…› mejor que lo solían hazer, porque dizen que la tenían mal contenta, que agora le ha pesado de su venida ; y aunque ·los· no ha holgado con él. Y pues está contenta ·hs· de aver echado las mugeres, que no cure de hazer mudança hasta la venida de vuestra alteza, sino sostener en el estado que está, {para} que dizen que trae determinación de revolver todo ; y según la ‹…›ción que tienen y la mala [vo]luntad con que les reciben, creo que no sería bueno lo que hiziese. El obispado de Jaén e otra qualquier vacante que oviere deve vuestra alteza detener, de no ‹…› proveerla, porque acá an muchos que esperan que vuestra magestad les hará merced, y esta esperança los obliga a servir ; quando se dé a uno, se estragará la voluntad de los otros. El Rey Católico, quando estuvo en Nápoles, tuvo muchos obispados y encomiendas y tenencias sin proveer hasta su venida. Pues pero está agora todo, que estava entonces : más necesidad tiene vuestra magestad de hazer lo al‹o› que {p}ueda a los que desean servir [a] vuestra alteza. El ·fre· está agora en aceptar la governación, con que dize que la tendrá {entre tanto} que se haze correo a vuestra majestad {para} que le envíe los poderes como los pide ; ·ni· quería que la aceptase ·ni· que vuestra majestad le enviase los poderes, porque no tiene sosiego para tal cargo, que cada día muda el pensamiento en mill cosas, ·y· todavía tiene fin a hazer por el reino. Si la aceptare, vuestra majestad mandará proveer lo que conviene. El conde de Haro haze el oficio de capitán, como las otras cosas. Como ay aquí muchos señores, son mal de concertar para lo que es menester, especial ·fre· e el conde de Benavente, que {e} tiene unas ‹…›, por {donde} ay muy mala orden ; e deste e{x}ército y la gente muy mal mandada, como es de muchos, que es el mayor temor que tenemos. {E} cada ora se tiene por mayor ventura tomar este ‹…›, porque, según la manera que ay, creo que todo se {perderá} si esto no se acertara. Por‹…› a unos parece que {e} sería bien que el cardenal y algunos del Consejo y contadores viniesen aquí, y que de aquí se usase de justicia e de hazienda ; y que el condestable [e]stuviese [en] lo de Burgos con aquellas montañas, e a otros que este lugar ‹…› proveído, y con la gente que era menester para guardarle ; y que los governadores y Consejo e contadores se junten en Burgos. Para esto ay un gran inconveniente : estar el marqués de Denia, tan mal quisto aquí de los criados de ·lis· y de todo el {pueblo} ; e si {se da a otro}, agraviar sería. Vuestra alteza lo mande mirar todo e mandar proveerlo, que es más a su ‹…› servicio. Estos grandes, si a r‹…›, tienen tres fynes: lo primero, lo q[ue] les cumple ; y después, poder [con] vra altza ; luego, el bien del rreyno, si ellos quedasen sin necesidad. Translation translation.md # English translation The ·fre· wants a settlement with the men of the Junta at any price; he says he does so because of the poor means {there are} of maintaining the troops here. He had the Queen say, before the ·y· and many knights, that she ordered all the Junta’s troops to disperse, and had this recorded as testimony to summon don Pedro Girón ·y· the cities with it. The Count of Benavente, the Marquis of Astorga, the Count of Miranda and the Grand Commander were not there; on learning it, ·ym· at once set about remedying it. So they went to the ·fre·, and the testimony was torn up ‹…›, not by his vote: he stood in between. And even so, he said that he held the Queen to be of sound mind, and ‹…› a thousand times a day, so that {I fear} he may one day do something about the agreements that would be very harmful. Let Your Highness write to ·lis·, commending everything to him ·y·, begging him, since it is now in such good state, to work to preserve it without anything being settled against the royal prerogatives. Let Your Highness write a few lines in your own hand – everything is needed – to him [and] to the Count of Benavente, urging him to see that nothing disorderly is done here out of necessity ‹…›; for if he is willing, nothing bad can be done, since all the others here would do whatever they were told on Your Highness’s behalf; and {I certify} that ‹…› Your Highness’s coming. And if what there is here should not suffice to maintain the army, let Your Highness {order} provision from there; for from ‹…› it was said that there is nothing to maintain it with, and I fear they may do something; and if some credit could be sent, I would think it best. On this point let Your Majesty send the post at once, for it is needed. The Marquis of Denia comes here with more passion than was needed, {as he} has; he is much disliked by many: his coming has grieved them as much as having sacked the town. Your Highness should order him to restrain himself greatly, to work with good will to satisfy the servants of ·los· and to serve the lady ·lus· and the ‹…›, better than was done before, for they say she was kept discontented, and that now his coming has grieved her; and yet ·los· has not been pleased with him. And since she is content ·hs· to have sent away the women, let him not think of making changes before Your Highness comes, but keep things as they are; for they say he comes resolved to overturn everything, and given the ‹…› they have and the ill will with which they are received, I believe what he would do would not be good. The see of Jaén, and any other vacancy that may occur, Your Highness should hold back and not fill, for there are many here who hope Your Majesty will grant them favour, and this hope binds them to serve; when it is given to one, the goodwill of the others will be spoiled. The Catholic King, when he was in Naples, kept many sees, commanderies and keeperships unfilled until his return. But as everything stands now, as it stood then, Your Majesty has even more need to do ‹…› what you {can} for those who wish to serve Your Highness. The ·fre· is now about to accept the government, on condition, he says, of holding it {until} a courier is sent to Your Majesty for you to send him the powers he asks for; I would wish ·ni· that he accepted it ·ni· that Your Majesty sent him the powers, for he lacks the steadiness for such a charge: every day he changes his mind about a thousand things, ·y· yet he means to do well by the kingdom. If he accepts, let Your Majesty provide as is fitting. The Count of Haro holds the office of captain, as in everything else. Since there are many lords here, they agree badly on what must be done, especially ·fre· and the Count of Benavente, who have ‹…›, whence very great disorder; and in this army the troops are very badly commanded, as any force with many heads: that is the greatest of our fears. And at every hour it is thought great luck to take this ‹…›; for, the way things go, I believe everything will be {lost} if this is not got right. ‹…› Some think it would be good for the Cardinal and some members of the Council and the contadores to come here, and justice and finance be administered from here; and for the Constable to see to Burgos and those mountains, and others to this place, ‹…› provided and with the troops needed to hold it; and for the governors, Council and contadores to meet at Burgos. There is a great difficulty in this: the presence of the Marquis of Denia, so disliked here by the servants of ·lis· and by all the {people}; and if [it] is given to another, it would be an affront to him. Let Your Highness have all this examined and order provision for it, as is most to your ‹…› service. These grandees, if they ‹…›, have three aims: first, what suits them; then, standing with Your Highness; and then the good of the realm, provided they are not left in need. I do not think they would mind Your Majesty keeping them [in your service]. Key: key_K4.tsv

A 231-figure Italian cipher paragraph in a friar’s letter to the Emperor (DECODE R2159), a substitution with two figures for each vowel. The key was recovered using the opening words Tomokiyo had published as a crib, and every figure was decrypted; checked against the manuscript, the apparent polyphony turned out to be ten misread 4s and three encipherment slips. Tomokiyo transcribed the cipher paragraph in his article on variable-length figure codes in the Austrian archives (DECODE R2159, R1408, R2179 and a Starhemberg letter of 1758). His note on this one: from Fra Giovanni di Lucca to the Emperor, 30 May 1644, in Italian; “the number groups may consist of one or two digits, but there is no difficulty in identifying individual groups because the groups are delimited by dots.” DECODE’s public record says Non-decrypted (no decipherment on file), cipher type Unknown , symbol set numerical, two pages, partly encrypted, with a placeholder date range of 1686–1877. The images need a DECODE login. Unconstrained annealing fails. A homophonic annealer with a 5-gram Italian model (Villari’s Machiavelli e i suoi tempi , I promessi sposi , La Mandragola ; 4.1 million letters, v written u ) was run from sixteen seeds. All sixteen converged on the same optimum, estreesitenetrentiuenieseist… , which is not Italian. The solver recovers a matched 231-letter Italian control in one seed of three, so this is a flat landscape, not a proof. As transcribed, the crib is inconsistent with a substitution. Al principe di = 3 11 | 26 21 17 17 6 15 26 1 | 8 17 . From di , and from il = 17 11 later in the text, 17 is i ; in principe the second 17 must be n . Eight letters survive without contradiction: 3 a, 11 l, 8 d, 17 i, 26 p, 21 r, 1 e, 19 t. Crib-fixed annealing. With those eight fixed and the other sixteen figures free, six seeds converge on one decryption at −2.50 nats per 5-gram: alpriicipeditrantiuanialoimpediroconoinmodocheilturcononlidiaaiutoefaroriuoltase… : lo impedirò … che il Turco non li dia aiuto e farò rivoltare… Word after word is Italian, to the last group. On the uncorrected transcription two figures seemed to carry two letters (see the note after the key). Holding the rest, 17 decrypts as n in principe (twice), manderò , con una , non , vinto , and i in di , il , impedirò , li , lui , dumilia , finché ; 19 as t in Transilvania , rivoltare , sua , humiliato , vinto , and s in Transilvania , se sarà bisogno , Cosachi . No third value is needed for either. A Viterbi decode over the two alternatives with the same model makes each choice mechanically and agrees with the hand decryption except at two places noted below. Control. The crib-fixed procedure on five shufflings of the same ciphertext (same figures, same counts, same eight letters fixed) reaches −3.40 to −3.68 per 5-gram against −2.50 for the letter, about 200 nats over 227 5-grams. The unconstrained false optimum in step 1 scored the same as the true decryption, so the model does not pick the solution by itself. The eight crib letters do, and the shuffles show that eight fixed letters on this text do not manufacture Italian on their own.

The writer’s 4 is a crossed stroke that looks like a barred 7; his 7 is plain. Tomokiyo’s transcription reads the crossed 4 as 14 in most places but as 17 in ten: principe twice ( 26 21 17 14 6 15 26 1 ), manderò ( 12 3 14 8 ), con una ( 6 13 14 23 14 3 ), non twice ( 14 18 14 ) and vinto ( 23 15 14 22 18 ). Three times it stands where t is wanted ( Transiuania , rivoltare , humiliato ); since the page has the same figure in both places of Transiuania , these are more likely the writer’s encipherment slips for 22 than transcription errors. Whether the two uses of 19 differ in shape has not been checked. The cipher has no polyphonic figure. The key above is the corrected one: 19 is s ; the three places where t is wanted are the writer’s slips.

Al principe di Transil[u]ania lo impedirò con ogn[i] modo che il Turco non li dia aiuto, e farò rivoltare contra di lui, se sarà bisogno, il principe di Bog[o]dania, et li darò dumilia Cosachi, et manderò a voi con una sua lettera all’Imperatore che non faccia pace fin che non l’habbi humiliato o vinto. As to the Prince of Transylvania: I shall by every means prevent the Turk from giving him help, and if need be I shall make the Prince of Moldavia rise against him and give him two thousand Cossacks, and I shall send [him] to you with a letter of his to the Emperor, that he make no peace until I have humbled or defeated him. Transiuania ( 19 21 9 14 19 15 25 3 14 15 3 ) has no l , and ogn modo lacks the i of ogni . The page shows no dropped group in either place, so these are the writer’s spellings. Bogodania ( 4 18 2 13 8 3 14 17 9 ): Bogdania is the ordinary Italian and Turkish name of Moldavia (Boğdan). The extra 13 is on the page, so it is the writer’s. lucca.html#context

In February 1644 György Rákóczi I, Prince of Transylvania, invaded Habsburg Hungary in alliance with Sweden and France and with the Porte’s leave. Through the spring Ferdinand III’s diplomacy worked to have the Ottoman support withdrawn and to find pressure on Rákóczi’s eastern flank. The paragraph is a first-person offer, carried by the friar, from someone who claims to be able to work on the Porte, to set the Prince of Moldavia (Vasile Lupu) against Rákóczi, and to dispose of two thousand Cossacks. Who is speaking is not in the cipher, but the clear text around it says who. The friar, sent on from Vilnius by the King, came to il suo Generalissimo il Sig. re Stanislao Conespolschi , the Grand Hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski. He told him it was the moment to help the Emperor, and Koniecpolski “answered angelically” that he would, from affection for the House of Austria and from zeal for religion and reason of state. Then comes the cipher. After it, the friar reports that the offer has not yet taken effect, because Rákóczi has sent a great sum of money to Constantinople to have the Prince of Moldavia deposed ( fatto mazul ). The letter is dated from Brody, Koniecpolski’s residence. Koniecpolski kept his own relations with Moldavia and the Tatars, and had beaten the Tatars at Ochmatów that January. (The clear frame is summarised here, not transcribed letter by letter.) Fra Giovanni di Lucca (Giovanni Giuliani da Lucca), Dominican, is known from his Relatione and Itinerario as a missionary of the 1620s and 1630s to the Tatars, Circassians, Abkhazians, Mingrelians and Georgians, and from later work in Moldavia (Cristian Luca, 2004, not consulted here). A Dominican who moved between Moldavia, the Cossack lands and Vienna is the sort of courier such an offer would use.

Ten letters of January to March 1637 from Hesse-Kassel’s general war commissary in Westphalia, catalogued on HCPortal as unsolved. No fitting key was found among the Hesse-Kassel key sheets inspected; the homophonic two-digit table was recovered from the ciphertext alone, with digraph signs and a small code. 95.9% of 9,736 cipher groups decipher: unpaid garrisons, Ehrenbreitstein, the refused safe-conducts for the Cologne peace talks, the Dutch alliance. Otto von der Malsburg served Landgrave Wilhelm V as general war commissary for the Hessian army in Westphalia. In 1637 Hesse-Kassel was under imperial ban, Upper Hesse was occupied, and the landgrave had moved his army into East Frisia, where he died in September. File 4 h Nr. 1411 at Marburg keeps Malsburg’s reports from January to March of that year. Each is a clear letter with long cipher runs, and several are nearly all cipher. folio HCPortal date cipher groups read 3 496 5/15 Jan 1637, signed 455 96.5% 12 497 Wesel, 7/17 Jan 1637 712 96.9% 14 502 Jan 1637 695 92.8% 15–16 503 Jan 1637 (“Triplicat” and a letter) 1,086 95.0% 18 504 14/24 Feb 1637 639 96.9% 23–24 505 7/17 Feb 1637, signed 2,015 97.6% 25 506 5 Mar / 23 Feb 1637, signed 592 97.5% 28–29 507 28 Mar 1637 (old style), signed 3,165 96.0% 30–31 508 “Duplicat” of ff. 28–29 (3,241) used as a check copy 32–33 509 French letter signed “232”, 3 Apr 1637; news extracts of March 377 88.1% The cipher is a homophonic substitution into German. The table has 89 two-digit groups: e has seven (16, 33, 48, 49, 61, 79, 84), u seven, a and o six, n, i and t five, and the rarer letters two or three. The order of the table is irregular. Common letter pairs have capital signs: N and D for ch , Y and G for ei , Z and O for st , W and P for ss , L and A for tt , R, C, E and M for mm , X, j and J for sch , H for ll , S and F for au , T and B for ff , Q for ai . Single figures are ordinary numerals (“5 [tausend] Reichsthaler”). About forty-five three-digit groups between 115 and 273 are codes for places, persons and military words. The writer leaves no word spaces and the groups are separated by dots. The same layout, a two-digit table with digraph signs and codes from 111, appears in the key that Wilhelm Burchard Sixtinus took to Hildesheim, Bremen and Hamburg in December 1635 (HCPortal key 5). Some code numbers even coincide (193, 201, 210, 212). But Sixtinus’s table does not decipher Malsburg’s letters: the chancery issued each correspondent his own table in a common pattern.

He does not know where the garrisons’ keep is to come from now that the contributions from the open country have ended, both here and in <239>. The rations are now reckoned monthly in Kassel Viertel of grain, because the non-commissioned officers draw double bread. It is still time to press the King of Hungary (Ferdinand III) for the peace talks and for safe-conducts for the Hessian envoys to Cologne. Wesel, 7/17 January 1637 (f. 12) … dan durch Friesslant mitt Wagen ⟨und⟩ Pferden zu gehen ist unmoglich. … Es ist von guter Hant avisiret, dass man zu Regenspurg geschlossen, <H#> Gesanten nach {Cöln} keinen salvum conductum zu erteilen. [?Hiergegen] berichtet mich der Statthalter Nesselrot, dass der Bischoff von Wirzburg an ihn im Augustto geschriben … Mitt der [140] wurde man durch [137] apart zu {Hamburg} oder Lubeck tracti[r]en lassen. Word has come from a good source that Regensburg (the electoral diet that made Ferdinand III King of the Romans) has resolved to give the Hessian envoys no safe-conduct to Cologne. Statthalter Nesselrode reports a letter from the Bishop of Würzburg; the alternative is separate talks at Hamburg or Lübeck. January 1637 (ff. 14–16; decoded, not read) The provisioning of Hermannstein (Ehrenbreitstein) and its garrison; Obrist Hoffman’s troops and routes by Marburg, Corbach and Brilon; Jan de Werth in person at Cologne (in clear). On ff. 15–16: no audience yet; notice that the truce (“Stilstant”) is ended; companies of foot and of dragoons, recruiting patents already issued; the ambassador of the States General; “er redet aber nirgent von fried machen, sagt er wolte einen finger aus der faust drumb geben”. 14/24 February 1637 (f. 18; decoded, not read) Re-read on 23 October 2026, the sentences build German, but open three-digit codes fall in most of them. A passage that holds: es seint aber die [212] ein Teils so erfroren, das auch etliche zu Kroppeln worden, ⟨und⟩ etliche Glidder haben mussen ablosen lassen; so seint auch viel ⟨ffreundt?⟩ hernach gestorben The winter march: men frozen and crippled, limbs amputated, many dead since. 7/17 February 1637 (ff. 23–24; decoded, not read) Re-read on 23 October 2026; as in f. 18, open codes break most sentences. A passage that holds: welche er aber nunmer aus dem Fundament, das Hermanstein nit effectivement proviandiret sei, disputiret ⟨und⟩ nichts [?gestehen] wil. … Stecken also [?in der] Bruhe, wissen nit, womit wir ihn zwingen wollen, ⟨und⟩ befinden nun in [d]er That, das wir mit einem Frantzosen gehan[d]elt haben. A dispute over whether Hermannstein had been “effectively provisioned”, and over payments and gifts to the commanders; “we find in fact that we have been dealing with a Frenchman” (Ehrenbreitstein was then held by a French garrison). Reichsthaler owed on account, ransom for prisoners, the peace talks said to be moving to Picardy, Margrave Sigismund of Brandenburg’s commission, a separate peace with the imperial commissioners, and garrisons so run down that men must leave. 5 March / 23 February 1637 (f. 25) <120> has resolved to content the cavalry; payment for ransoms and other costs; bills of exchange still not received at Cologne. 28 March 1637, old style (ff. 28–29) The longest letter: his journey held up for days on the Watten; twelve-pound guns, constables and ammunition; Jan de Werth between the Ruhr and <268>; whether the States General will take Hesse into their alliance and give a muster place in the Cleves country; the planned junction at Cloppenburg, Quakenbrück, Minden, Vechta, Wildeshausen and Diepholz, and the colonels Uffeln and Carpf. Large paired capitals (AA, GG, OO, XX, CC, KK) stand for names.

The catalogue entry asked first whether Malsburg’s key was among the Hesse-Kassel key sheets of 1635–52. HCPortal describes 176 key records from the Marburg key volumes, each with the people who used it; all were fetched. None names Malsburg as a user (one list of name codes gives “Otto v. der Malßburg – 523”), and the tables of the likeliest sheets (Sixtinus 1635, a sheet of “1637 or before”, and two others) do not decipher f. 3. The eighteen scans were transcribed group by group. Annealing a homophonic key on f. 3 alone (455 groups, about 80 symbols) gave only letter noise. Three letters together (1,575 groups) gave the same key from every start and German text. The capital signs were then valued where the text demanded them: no[N] = noch, la[W]en = lassen, ge[X]lo[W]en = geschlossen, Ste[A]in = Stettin. The digit table was re-annealed over all the letters with the signs fixed. The reading was measured by splitting each deciphered run into words of 17th-century German (the Deutsches Textarchiv prints of 1470–1670, plus names and spellings checked in context). A group counts as read when all its letters fall inside words. The ten letters give 9,338 of 9,736 groups (95.9%); the 193 open code groups account for half the rest, and 97.9% of the non-code text reads. The same measure on shuffled keys gives 50–58%. It counts groups inside words, not sentences: read as sentences (reading audit, 22 October 2026), ff. 3, 14, 15–17, 28–29 (and the duplicate 30–31) and 32–33 had open codes, stray letters or noise in most sentences. On 22–23 October every letter was built into sentences on the scans, letter by letter with the decode: ff. 3 and 28–29 now hold, while ff. 18 and 23–24 turned out to have open codes in most sentences, and ff. 14, 15–17, 30–31 and 32–33 stay decoded, not read (in the German extracts of f. 33 about thirty words of a fast second hand are also unread). The letters that read, with the alphabetic block, hold about 53% of the cipher (estimated); each of them builds coherent sentences but reads at 89–93% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs, so even these are partial. Every group that did not read was checked again on the scans: 24 misreadings and 2 doubled groups were corrected, and 210 were confirmed as the writer wrote them.

Historical constraint, not recovered identity Peter Melander is a documentary lead, not an identification of 43. Geyso, Beiträge , part III (1926), p. 99 n. 2, says that Melander sought “absolute Gewalt” through Malsburg, citing a letter from Malsburg at Wesel on 16 November 1636 , old reference Kr. A. 1636, III . The phrase is in Geyso’s paraphrase; the original has not been inspected. It concerns authority to reward and punish officers and does not itself establish the disputed command relationship with Swedish generals. Geyso pp. 115-117 and Hofmann pp. 68-69 also describe January retention offers to Melander. They weigh against an accomplished dismissal, although they can coexist with the conditional reading above. No inspected source connects a named man to both the distinctive command clause and code 43. The numerals 43 and 45 in other key alphabets are not name equations, and the later February and March letters have unresolved antecedents of their own. The smallest useful next comparisons are the original letter of 16 November; the cipher sheets catalogued as LHA Koblenz 47/4400 (1635-1641, not inspected); and a possible Hoff report of 17/27 March 1637 in HStAM 4 f Staaten F, Frankreich 1297 . The last could help trace the other LL-like occurrence, but neither the report’s presence nor common code values has been established. The January paragraph may copy another speaker’s intelligence; Malsburg’s authorship of the surrounding letter does not settle that question.

Partial reading: the document stays "decoded, not read". ## Translation ⟨I arrived back safely yesterday evening … and found Your Princely Grace's gracious letter … there,⟩ I would indeed like to set out from here with <H#> train as soon as possible ⟨and⟩ by land, since Dunkirkers were lying on the Watten a few days ago, and arrive by [235] at the appointed place with God's help. But since I am to bring [193] [212] guns ⟨and⟩ [197] <V>, and the enemy (who, between [149] ⟨and⟩ the Ruhr, has about 6 {companies} [193] <e> <n> {companies} [200] ⟨and⟩ 1 {company} of dragoons [?lying], and besides <K> {regiment} [212] from Lorraine, about <4#> [?horse] strong, coming to join) now gathers ⟨and⟩ wants to take the field, it is not advisable to go overland; by water, though, it is slow ⟨and⟩ cannot be put in hand so quickly, for it takes a great deal of time before ships that go to sea ⟨and⟩ are not to be had here are ordered; ⟨and⟩ […] {companies} [200] have to be taken away from here so necessarily, twelve {companies} [213] cannons, with proper [208] ⟨and⟩ [XX] train loaded on them ⟨and⟩ provided with the necessary [194] ⟨and⟩ fodder, would have to be, to say nothing of the great cost. ⟨And⟩ a contrary wind can come, so that in <f> ⟨or⟩ <K> weeks one cannot move a step backward or forward. Moreover, the [168] would have to be asked for a free passage, for no garrison would let such a number of ships pass without express orders. Thirdly, the enemy would easily guess [129]'s intention from it ⟨and⟩ forestall it. Fourthly, besides this, no [193] can be taken from these quarters (because the old {companies} are weak ⟨and⟩ the new ones are not coming up), nor guns either, since the commanders daily demand more of both. There are indeed the <0> new twelve-pounder guns from [220] here, but not yet mounted on carriages; nor does one have any shot ⟨or⟩ [197] wagons, gunners ⟨and⟩ equipment. ⟨And⟩ Wartenberg [has been] discharged, and will now take service again with the [?French]. Therefore it is not possible to take him or his {regiment} ⟨…⟩ and the colonels Uffel ⟨and⟩ Karpf from their posts (because the enemy has brought fire-mortars ⟨and⟩ guns m[181] to Warendorf, but one does not yet [?know] his intention). Uffel also asks, since his [260] now looks so bad, not to be wrangled with; and he will not willingly [?want] to stand under […] in [215]. ⟨But all this must be demanded, and especially⟩ about the withdrawal of the troops ⟨and⟩ the re-appointment of commanders, if Uffel ⟨and⟩ Karpf were [?both to go along], everything must first be considered ⟨and⟩ agreed with the <V>, ⟨which, according to his letter, will be here in a few days, to learn⟩ and the resolution of the conclusum, what [126] ⟨and⟩ [153] will do this summer ⟨and⟩ how soon they will take the field; 2, whether they will take {the States} into their alliance; 3, whether they will allow a muster place in the Cleves country, <4#> [XX] give passage ⟨and⟩ repassage at Lehrort over [174] ⟨and⟩ lend a bridge for it, [?will] bring along. […] yet, without any presumption (if it can only be done on account of the enemy above), not to rush, but first to wait for the return of [122] from m[214], who, as soon as he has arrived here again, wants to take the [200] ⟨and⟩ go to {the States}, ⟨and⟩ to see first where the enemy, who is together, will turn ⟨since⟩ Jan de Werth is also getting ready to march between the Ruhr ⟨and⟩ [268]. For the conjunction ⟨…⟩ could happen nowhere sooner ⟨and⟩ more conveniently than at Cloppenburg or Vechta, since they could be sooner from Minden to Quakenbrück than to Verden or elsewhere, ⟨and⟩ they have Osnabrück on the other side; nor can the enemy do them any harm, since Cloppenburg, Vechta, Wildeshausen and Diepholz are poorly garrisoned. Fürstenau, however, is occupied with [oo] <s> […] [193] ⟨and⟩ <o> {companies} [212]; but the Hase lies between, so that they can go safely [?…] [216] from the enemy who is in garrison there, ⟨and⟩ that the Reiderland can be taken first, as the Mansfelder did. For the Frisians are now recruiting 1 {company} [193] from <o>tkopffen, and are throwing up a sconce between Stickhausen ⟨and⟩ Bossem at the pass where one can cross. […] the roads are also said to be […] so bad that one cannot yet get through them with wagons ⟨and⟩ horses. ⟨I have … answer for this,⟩ that, because of the enemy's gathering ⟨and⟩ the absence of [160], I cannot take any [193] [212] ⟨or⟩ guns out of the garrisons, nor change the command quickly. ⟨…⟩ But as soon as [122] comes, {the States} shall be answered on all points humbly ⟨and⟩ in detail, ⟨and⟩ the <V> urged to set out quickly by one ⟨or⟩ the other road to [129]. Whether I [?nevertheless] ⟨and⟩ <+> should go to [147] alone with {the States}' train even before the return of [122], on that I await orders, ⟨and⟩ will keep myself ready for that case at all times. ⟨… stands with him,⟩ Colonel Hohendorf came ⟨to me on the way⟩ and reports that he had sent the rest of his [191], some <4H> men, back to the Vegesack, who intended now to take the Land of Hadeln, which belongs to Saxe-Lauenburg, with his troops ⟨and⟩ to seek quarters there; he has also gone to m[123] at [?Rantzau]. ## Notes - Lehrort: the Rhine crossing below Wesel. The passages were transcribed into R731_signs.txt : about 330 signs, 15 sign types plus dot clusters. The transcription is tentative. The low swash stroke may be a pen link rather than a sign, and the dots above and below the bars (÷, ∴, ::) were collapsed into one token, although they may be vowel marks. solve731.py is a swap-annealing substitution solver with a 4-gram model trained on Pápai’s deciphered letters. On a control, Pápai’s own text cut to the same line lengths and enciphered at random, it recovers the text exactly (−8.96 per 4-gram, against −8.87 for real text). On R731 it reaches only about −10.1 under every reading tried. So R731 is not a simple Hungarian substitution on this transcription. A recurring group has the letter pattern of Pasa read backwards, but it did not lead to a key. Kálmán Benda’s edition of Pápai’s Turkish diaries (1963) is not online; whether it prints these passages is not known.

In August 1578 Don John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II and governor of the Netherlands, was in the field against the States General and asking Madrid for money. Antonio Pérez answered him in his own hand after the arrival of Don John’s envoy, Don Alonso de Sotomayor. The letter is plain Spanish with four cipher passages, which say that the Council of Finance has “not a single real”, that providing what is needed is “impossible”, and that the asiento just made will not be followed by another. Don John died six weeks later, on 1 October. Pérez was arrested in July 1579 for the murder of Escobedo, Don John’s secretary. The letter is in the Fernández San Román collection of the Real Academia de la Historia, whose digital library publishes the images under a Public Domain Mark. Image 2. The second cipher passage, 2? 10 7:e 16:e 6:+ 6:e 4 23:ev? and the lines that follow, between the clear quando no huviesse otras causas and the clear y advierto a V. Al. The writer’s clear hand and the numbers alternate within a line. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, 2/Ms Caja 8 no. 4, image 2, via the RAH Biblioteca Digital.
perez1578.html#cipher

It is neither Pérez’s cipher with Vargas Mexía (1578–1579) nor the “general cipher” of Don John and Escobedo (1576–1577). It is the numerical syllabary found in 1577 in the despatches of the Spanish embassy at Genoa (Simancas, Estado, leg. 1410), with departures peculiar to Pérez. A number is a consonant (6 d, 7 c, 15 l, 16 m, 17 n, 20 p, 22 r, 23 s, 24 t); a mark after it is the vowel (+ a, a dot e, 6 i, a hook o, an i-stroke u); single numbers are vowels (10 a, 4 e, 18 o, 1 u); superscripts are a final n (^), s (a bar), r and l. A draft of 4 February 1577 (Estado 1410,196) announces to the ministers in Italy the change of the “cifra general” but does not contain the table. In Pérez’s hand 8 is g (b in the Genoa table) and an 8 with a small 2 is ble . The key is targets/perez1578/key.tsv (K_P2).
perez1578.html#method

A sibling key. The 1577 Genoa table was rebuilt on cipher and descifrada pairs of AGS Estado 1410 and validated on 1410,78–79 (87.3% of words, 95.5% of characters). Four values were learnt on Pérez’s own lines (9 = g, 8 = g, X = r, the i-stroke = u) and 27 = x after the first test below. Three tests, one decisive. A lexical-coverage test on held-out lines did not separate the key from its controls, because a syllabary yields words even when shuffled; it was declared inconclusive. On the pair 1410,69–70 (4 August 1577), with the cipher frozen before the decipherment was opened, the key reached 72.4% of words and 88.5% of characters against at most 25.3% and 55.7% for 200 controls: significant, but under the 75% word threshold, so not validated. On a fresh pair, 1410,65–66 (Genoa, 19 July 1577; PARES 3576652), the key K_P2 was frozen (SHA-256 4d5eb01d…), twelve cipher lines were transcribed in two passes and frozen before the descifrada was opened, and words containing 8 were excluded by a rule written in advance. Result: 81.3% of words and 87.9% of characters, against at most 16.5% and 47.8% for 200 controls (100 permuted consonant values and 100 shuffled unit orders). The criterion, 0.75 of words and 0.85 of characters and above every control, was met.

Ningún otro is expected, but gan contradicts the u; the word is left unresolved. {ir}: the first sign of the second passage is blotted; the 2 (= i) and the superscript for r can be seen (probable). {estrecho}, {dicho}: a barred 7 followed by a hook stands for cho both times, as the words require; the sign is not attested elsewhere (probable). {imposible}: sign 14. “por 14 16 po si 8²”: 16 = m, 8² = ble , so 14 is i here (in the Genoa table 14 = gu). One occurrence (probable). {cunplira}: the 7 with an i-stroke carries an oblique superscript stroke, read as ^ (= n); “no se cunplira” is required by “con protesto de que” (probable). {estragar}: the letters s-t-ra-ga-r are certain (8 = g in Pérez’s hand); the exact sense of the verb in the sentence is uncertain. Prior work: no edition found in Mignet (1845), in the CODOIN, in Cryptiana or in recent work on the San Román collection (Ávila Seoane, 2024, on Don John’s autographs). Not checked: Gregorio Marañón, Antonio Pérez (1947), whose appendices print many of Pérez’s letters; if the letter is edited there, the present reading becomes an independent check of it.

Two letters in a cipher whose vowels are odd digits, never read: a student thesis of 2017 deciphered their neighbour and printed the key. WAINUT applied it unchanged to the other two, from photographs of a microfilm-reader screen: about 65% of the words decode verbatim, but most sentences have holes, so neither letter counts as read. Gr1n c7nS7l1zS7n43 d14hl1 dS l3S l3t3Gr1 … Gran conSolazSone dahla dS leS leteGra … unknown → Ottavio Piccolomini · consonants plain, vowels as odd digits · c. 1646 · decoded with a published key, not read Two cipher letters to Ottavio Piccolomini, c. 1646 Go to the full text ↓ A student’s thesis deciphered one letter of a Piccolomini cipher run and printed the key; applied to the two letters it left aside, the key gives Italian, but from poor photographs not yet sentences. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 6 November 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: none (key obtained, text not read) Contributed by WAINUT (solution, transcription, verification) · Also credited · V. Vlnas (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · none (key obtained, text not read) The letters Inv. 24874 and 24876, two Italian letters to Ottavio Piccolomini, undated on the frames and probably of 1646, by writers not identified. 24874 begins in mid-letter; 24876 has two cipher blocks among clear lines (news from Vienna, Linz and Ratisbona). Where State Regional Archives Zlámrsk (SOA Zámrsk), Rodinný archiv Piccolominů. The images are photographs of a microfilm-reader screen in the appendix of V. Vlnas’s 2017 thesis (appendix B21, B22); letters are 15–20 pixels high. Not on DECODE. The cipher Consonants written plain, vowels a e i o u as the odd digits 1 3 5 7 9, even digits and plain vowel letters as nulls. In this cursive hand the digit 5 and the short s look alike, and so do 9, g and q, so many words depend on a choice by sense. How it was deciphered With the key V. Vlnas printed in 2017 for the neighbouring inv. 24873 (ch. 4.2, table 3), applied unchanged; the additions are 0 as a null, long s, and class signs for the lookalikes. Two passes of transcription per letter, reconciled on the image, and one independent blind check. What it says In 24874: letters received, “gran consolazione dalla di lei lettera”, a request for a just and exact report, and “l’arciduca mio signore”; the clear tail announces Don Miguel de Salamanca. In 24876: that the Duke of Bavaria wants peace by all means. Only part of this builds sentences. Still open Most sentences have holes, about 15 signs are unresolved, and a clean scan from SOA Zamrsk has not been ordered. The writers and dates are not known. Credit The key is V. Vlnas’s (2017). WAINUT transcribed the two letters, decoded them and checked them, working with AI agents; no human palaeographer has checked the text.
piccolomini1646.html#the-letters

Inv. 24873 to 24876 sit in a run of Piccolomini cipher frames that Vlnas dates, where dated, to 1646; 24873_2 is dated in clear “li 13 [?9bre] 1646”. In 1646 Piccolomini served Spain in the Low Countries, and Archduke Leopold Wilhelm was named governor of the Spanish Netherlands at the end of that year, which fits 24874’s “governo” and “l’arciduca mio signore”, though nothing in the text names him. 24876’s Bavarian passages fit Bavaria’s move toward a separate truce in late 1646; this is context, not a statement of the letter. V. Vlnas deciphered 24873 in his thesis Počítačová analýza šifrované korespondence rodu Piccolomini (Hradec Králové 2017) and did not decipher 24874 and 24876. That decipherment is prior art; what is new here is the first transcription and decoding of these two.
piccolomini1646.html#the-key

The even digits (2, 4, 6, 8 and 0) carry no value where the word around them reads as Italian: 24874 has 65 of them in 645 signs. A six is close to b and to t in this hand, so at two places a six stands where the sense needs another letter; both are marked as repairs. The writer often writes a doubled consonant once, as in 24873. The key was frozen before the bare frames were transcribed and then applied to part of the cipher postscript of 24873_2, which Vlnas did not print. The 14 groups copied there all decode to Italian unchanged ( desidera Sua Altezza , ragguaglio , sono , come ancora lei , che venendo , se ne possa governare ). That is weak evidence: the key is a published table that could not have been tuned, the solver chose and scored the groups, and there is no external decipherment to grade against. The stronger support is that the key turns both letters, in two hands, into running Italian on the solver’s signs and on the blind check’s copy alike.
piccolomini1646.html#the-reading

Of 116 words in the cipher part of 24874, 76 decode verbatim from the signs (65.5%), and of 50 in 24876, 32 (64.0%). These are word counts of the decode, not a read share: the words do not yet build sentences (2 of 6 cipher sentences in 24874, 1 of 3 in 24876). Counted strictly, with no s/i or g/q/u/v choice, the figures are 33 of 116 (28.4%) and 14 of 50 (28.0%). Marked repairs, 6 and 4 words, are counted apart, and so are 7 and 2 words known only from context. Both letters are therefore decoded, not read. 24874 gives, in part: “Ecelenza havrà recevuto la mia delli [tredeci] … gran consolazione dalla di lei [lettera] … desidera dunque una giusta et per[…] relatione … asicurandola che … havrà consolatione”. Lines 1 to 3, the faintest on the photograph, are mostly holes. The decoded text with every hole, and a draft English translation, are under Full texts; the clear passages there are draft readings from the photograph and are not counted.
piccolomini1646.html#uncertain

Neither letter builds sentences; the holes are mostly in 24874 lines 1–3 and 14–20 and in 24876 block A. A clean scan from SOA Zamrsk, not ordered, should raise both letters much further. About 15 signs stay unresolved after the blind check at three to four times magnification. Most read words depend on a class choice by sense for the lookalike shapes; the class-free figures are 28%. The clear passages are draft readings from the photograph only. The writers are not identified, the signature of 24873_2 is not legible, and 24874 and 24876 are undated. The held-out test is 14 groups chosen and scored by the solver. No human palaeographer has checked any sign.

A Venetian despatch from the Escorial in a numerical cipher, catalogued on DECODE (R1875) with sender and recipient unknown. The chancery wrote a complete contemporary decipherment on the despatch and barred the cipher; the text was transcribed from it, and the key was not rebuilt. It reports Madrid’s view of the broken-off Anglo-French peace talks and the talk of a union with another court: the Family Compact with France, signed in secret that August. … 45239 . 36 . 39 . 11552314 39 … (p. 2, under the bar) Le sciolte negoziazioni fra le Corti di Londra e di Versaglies… Escorial → Doge and Senate of Venice · numerical cipher, Italian · 13 October 1761 Sebastiano Foscarini to the Doge, Escorial 1761 Go to the full text ↓ Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 (Serie) Busta 30 f. 178; DECODE R1875. Catalogued as a ciphered letter from “…” in Spain to an unknown recipient, 13 October 1761. It is despatch no. 178 of Sebastiano Foscarini, Venetian ambassador at the court of Charles III, written at the Escorial. The Venetian chancery deciphered it on the despatch itself and struck the cipher through. The text here is transcribed from that contemporary decipherment, which covers the whole letter.
