From the chancery decipherment, with abbreviations as written: Com’ebbi l’onore di rassegnare a VV. EE. mercordì S. M.a e tutta la Reale famiglia si sono trasferiti in questo soggiorno. La poca distanza di ove io pure mi sono condotto, animato dal mio rispettosissimo desiderio di manifestare a V.a Ser.tà in ogni miglior guisa il vero impegno della mia buona volontà, e mosso dalla torbida configurazione de’ tempi presenti, i quali esigono tutta la maggior vigilanza, come avrebbero bisogno di una mente illuminata ed attiva per agevolarsi il camino al conoscim.to di quei maneggi, i quali per tutti i riguardi possono interessare la sapienza dell’Ecc.mo Senato. Le sciolte negoziazioni fra le Corti di Londra e di Versaglies sono la fonte da cui scaturiscono infinite congietture e sistemi politici. Li soggetti più sensati e meglio conoscitori delle massime de’ Principi e del vero interesse di questa Corona sono nella ferma persuasione che ella non potrà più oltre riguardare con indifferenza nell’intiera sconfitta del Christianissimo nell’America negli immensi acquisti che avevano fatti, e che vie più possono aggiungersi all’Inghilterra nelle sue poderose forze del mare. Questi raggionam.ti trovano molti seguaci ma non sono atti ad estinguere il peso di quelli i quali esaminando diligentem.te lo stato militare e maritimo e la forza dell’erario di questo Monarca, le pacifiche disposizioni del suo animo e il genio de’ suoi Ministri, credono difficile il caso che possa uscire dalla massima sin ad ora professata. Quindi questi due ultimi obbietti vengono distrutti con la risoluzione che non sempre i Principi e i Ministri loro possono servire al proprio piacere, ma che la necessità impone bene spesso la legge e abbatte tutti li più opposti dissegni, e passando con ciò a dimostrare l’urgenza e la copia dei mali giungono perfino a riflettere sulla costituzione di alcuna altra Corte, e credono agevole il caso di una congiunzione atta a sostenere li vicendevoli interessi. [clear:] Sono per ogni conto rispettabili li autori di questi pensamenti, ma io non posso produrli all’Ecc.mo Sen.to che spogli di qualunque autorità, quanto mi sembrano degni di tutta quell’attenzione ch’io prometto a VV. EE. anche in questo grave proposito. Grazie. Dall’Escoriale 13. Ottobre 1761. Sebastian Foscarini Amb.r In English: the King and the royal family moved to the Escorial on Wednesday, and Foscarini has followed them, the better to follow events in troubled times. The broken-off negotiations between London and Versailles give rise to endless conjecture. The most judicious observers think Spain can no longer look on with indifference at France’s complete defeat in America, at the vast conquests England has made there, and at the further gains its sea power may bring. Others, weighing the King’s army, navy and treasury, his peaceable nature and the temper of his ministers, doubt that he will depart from the policy he has followed so far. The first group answers that necessity often overrides the wishes of princes and ministers, and after setting out the urgency of the danger they go so far as to consider the position of another court, expecting a union to defend common interests. Foscarini passes these views on “stripped of any authority”, but worth the Senate’s attention. Grades: the decipherment is contemporary (H). Two words struck out by the clerk on page 3 and replaced between the lines by “nel” and “negli” are his corrections, not text.
r1875.html#the-cipher

The cipher is written as runs of digits, with groups separated by points and many of them ending in 6, 7 or 9. It has nothing in common with the 1628 syllabic cipher of R1874 in the same busta. According to crittologia.eu, eighteenth-century Venetian ciphers had dropped the old code dictionary and kept only an alphabet and an orderly syllabary. About 37 barred lines carry 1,565 letters of plaintext. The bars cover much of each digit, so a group-exact transcription, and with it the key, was not attempted; the text does not depend on it.

The key. Rebuilding it would need a group-exact transcription through the ink bars, aligned with the decipherment. Foscarini’s other ciphered despatches in the Dispacci Spagna are not on DECODE.

No. 178. Sole copy. As I had the honour of reporting to Your Excellencies, on Wednesday His Majesty and the whole Royal family moved to this residence. The short distance to where I too have come, prompted by my most respectful desire to show Your Serenity in every best way the true commitment of my good will, and moved by the troubled configuration of the present times, which demand the greatest vigilance, as they would need an enlightened and active mind to ease the way to knowledge of those dealings which, in every respect, may concern the wisdom of the Most Excellent Senate. The broken-off negotiations between the Courts of London and Versailles are the source from which spring endless conjectures and political systems. The most sensible persons, and those who best know the maxims of Princes and the true interest of this Crown, are firmly persuaded that it can no longer look on with indifference at the entire defeat of the Most Christian King in America, at the immense acquisitions that they had made, and that may be added ever more to England in her powerful forces at sea. These arguments find many followers, but they are not able to outweigh those who, carefully examining the military and maritime state and the strength of the treasury of this Monarch, the peaceable dispositions of his mind and the bent of his Ministers, think it unlikely that he could depart from the maxim professed until now. Then these last two objections are overturned by the resolution that Princes and their Ministers cannot always serve their own pleasure, but that necessity very often lays down the law and overthrows all the most contrary designs; and going on from this to show the urgency and abundance of the evils, they come even to reflect on the constitution of some other Court, and think easy the case of a union fit to sustain their mutual interests. The authors of these thoughts are respectable on every account, but I cannot put them before the Most Excellent Senate except stripped of any authority, though they seem to me worthy of all the attention that I promise Your Excellencies in this grave matter too. Thanks. From the Escorial, 13 October 1761. Sebastian Foscarini, Ambassador. Address: To the Most Serene Prince of Venice etc. etc. No. 178, sole copy. Docket: 1761, 13 October, received 2 November, Escorial, Ambassador, no. 178, sole copy.

BnF fr. 20974 is titled Clefs de la correspondance chiffrée de François, duc de Guise, avec quelques lettres de lui (1556) (Gallica btv1b9062131g ). Tomokiyo’s catalogue of the volume numbers the letter no. 1 (pp. 1–4) and lists no contemporary decipherment for it. Pages 1–3 are forty, forty and thirteen lines of signs with no clear text at all. Page 3 is bound upside down and its lower half is blank. Page 4 is the letter’s blank verso. The lower half has a key sheet pasted onto it, dated 1556 and headed for the general d’Albany (Tomokiyo’s no. 2): an alphabet, nulls, and code signs for the Pope, the Emperor, Ferrara, Venice and Parma. That key is the source of the catalogue’s year. Its signs are not the letter’s. Page 1, lines 1–7: apres a este leu en la presence de ceulx qui est[oient] … pour luy remonstrer la necessite que la uile a pour … feit residence et preschat … plustost que ung estranger . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 20974 p. 1, via DECODE R2276.
r2276.html#cipher

Tomokiyo reconstructed the Nevers–Piles alphabet from Jean de Piles’s letters of 1586 to the Duke of Nevers in BnF fr. 3612, which is not digitised. His table gives one or more signs for each letter from a to z , three nulls, and a few codes: de, et, que, qui, quil, luy, les, des, Mr . Decrypted with the table, this letter at first gave mostly nonsense. The cause was the transcription: closed and open boxes, plain and hooked v , the cross × and the lying loop ∞ are easy to confuse, and each pair has different values. After two transcription passes and six rounds of checking against the images, the key used here has one value per glyph, as in Tomokiyo’s table. It adds code signs attested by their contexts: Sign Value Evidence ʒ followed by Ձ cardinal “cardinal de lorraine”, “cardinal de peleue”, “cardinal alanus” ʒ alone le, du, d “lung le grand”, “le doien”, “le duc de parme”, “du dix neufiesme” ce ligature pour (and o) “pour empescher”, “pour cela”, “pour la presenter” b b leur “leur sainte intention”, “leurs peines”, “leur uolonte” ꝺ with raised o faire “la faire tenir a Rome”, “a uous faire seruice” (also in fr. 4715) large hooked b ie “ie luy nommai”, “ie uous suplie” (6 of 6 in fr. 4715) dotted × vous (or null) “uous asseurer”, “depuis uous scaues” (always vous in fr. 4715) dotted cursive M lettre “le contenu de la lettre”, “la lettre signe”, “une semblable lettre pour fortifier” boxed cross ⊞ parle twice in fr. 4715 under “parle”; here once plausibly (“ouy parler”), once not The sibling is BnF fr. 4715 f. 2 : the Cardinal de Guise to Nevers, Soissons, 6 October 1586, in the same cipher, with its decipherment written above every line. All 29 of its lines were aligned here, about 1,050 sign–value pairs. It confirms Tomokiyo’s values, and in that hand the sigma-like ꝺ is mostly t , not a . The letter at fr. 3413 no. 62 , from Cardinal Pellevé’s household in Rome to Jean de Piles in August 1589, uses the same alphabet.

Il proposa deux choses, | une le moien de la faire tenir a Rome ? et fut prie le capitaine Tr|on de l’enuoier a son frere pour la presenter, de quoi ils s’excusent, | disant que cela ? trop de soupcon a leur maison et a son nom, | et mesme que pour les choses passees … qu’il failloit moien | d’obtenir du chapitre une semblable lettre pour fortifier … The rest of page 1 loses its right edge from line 16 to line 31. The page closes: “il semble au langage de ? Bardin que son maistre n’ait pas … du contentement qu’il esperoit … il ne fault pas faire demonstration … tost response, et ne se ueult ioindre” . Bardin is the Duke of Lorraine’s agent in Paris, the one quoted in the orbais letter. r2276.html#date

Date. The letter gives only “de Reims du dix neufiesme de iuin”. The year follows from its content. The see of Reims fell vacant with the murder of Cardinal Louis de Guise at Blois on 24 December 1588, and the duc d’Elbeuf, whose ransom is being agreed, was taken at Blois on the same day and held at Loches from March 1589. The dean Frison is “maintenant a Rome” with the act of postulation. In the orbais letter, written in Rome on 23 August 1589 by Cardinal Pellevé’s secretary to Jean de Piles, Rome “depeschera … dedans deux jours le doien” . So the letter is of 19 June 1589 . Pellevé himself was named to Reims only on 10 May 1591. Writer. The writer had been in Rome shortly before (“pendant que i’estoie encores a Rome”). He writes from Reims, lodges with the vidame Robilard, and uses the cipher of Jean de Piles, abbé d’Orbais, who was the League’s envoy in Rome earlier in 1589 and whose abbey lies near Reims. Piles is the likely writer, but the letter is not signed. Addressee. The addressee is not named. He had approved the postulation (“uous l’aues eu agreable a condition qu’il se contenteroit du reuenu de l’archeuesche”) and is distinct from Mayenne and from the Cardinal de Pellevé, both named in the third person. He is probably in Rome.
r2276.html#method

The three pages were fetched from DECODE and transcribed sign by sign into ASCII labels, 93 lines. Page 1 was done by hand at twice the scan size. Pages 2 and 3 were done by two agents at 1.5–3×, and page 3 was transcribed turned upright. A free homophonic annealing under a French 5-gram model failed: the text collapsed into e and s . A decoder that allowed each sign a small set of values, then a word-level decoder with a 30,000-word lexicon of sixteenth-century letters that re-estimated those sets, brought out the content: chapitre, chanoines, archidiacre Brulart, postulation, lansquenetz, Parme, Elbeuf . The decryption itself was done line by line against the images in six rounds. Each word was checked against the signs by an aligner, which measures the fraction of signs that agree with the key ( measure.py ). Two decoding figures are reported; neither is a reading figure (see the Extent above). Sense counts every sign inside a real word or a declared null: 3,600 of 3,920, 91.8%. Strict counts only signs that agree with the key: 3,484, 88.9%. The difference is the writer’s slips and doubtful glyphs, accepted from context.
r2276.html#residuals

Re-measured 5 October 2026. 3,600 of 3,920 signs give sense (91.8%) with key version 8, which applies the boxed cross ⊞ = parle at page 1 line 21 ( ouy parler ). The Gallica microfilm (btv1b9062131g) was fetched at full resolution and every unread line re-cut at native size: its rare-sign strokes are no clearer than DECODE’s, and none of the candidate corrections on t1.16, t1.39 and t2.2 turns an unread word into French. The remaining open words of two or more signs (about 80) need the manuscript itself. Lost paper (illegible): the right edge of page 1 from line 1 to 4 and 16 to 31, and the left margin of page 2 on lines 1–2, 15–28 and 39–40 (about a fifth of the line). These signs are not counted in the 3,920. An ink blot on page 3, line 2, hides one word, perhaps armees . Single signs (too short): about 25 isolated signs in running text that the sentence does not need, for example page 1 line 18 (ʒ), line 35, line 38, and page 3 line 4 (the barred Z). Codes: the boxed cross ⊞ before Bardin (p. 1 l. 36), probably a title. A barred Z and an 8 with a raised t on page 3 have no attested value. Open words: about 80 words of two or more signs, with no candidate that fits both the signs and the sentence. The worst passages are page 1 lines 16 and 22–26 (Madame de Sainct Pierre’s reply, next to the tear), page 2 lines 2–3, 13–16 and 39, and page 3 lines 1, 5 and 9. Doubtful readings (grade C): capitaine Tron (p. 1 l. 11–12, a name decrypted from the key alone); en uerite (p. 2 l. 2); sont (l. 28); commodite (l. 35); depesches (p. 3 l. 10); de Lique (p. 2 l. 34); the year 1589, inferred as above. The transcription, the key files, the decrypted text and the alignment tools are in the repository folder. So is the aligned sibling fr4715_aligned.txt , which also serves the orbais letter.

Letter from Reims, 19 June [1589], BnF fr. 20974 pp. 1-3 (DECODE R2276): the lines that read (p. 1 ll. 1-15, 27-37; p. 2 ll. 4-12, 22-35; p. 3) read in part Written from Reims, probably by Jean de Piles, abbé d'Orbais: while he was still in Rome the chapter of Reims made an election or postulation for the archbishopric, of the grand archdeacon Brulart (who consented in tears) and of the dean Frison, now in Rome with the act of postulation. Things have stayed so until the present. Monsieur did not think that he still had in mind the first practices, though I can, since I am here; he wants that, if this is not done, […] […] […], but I did not see much likelihood of putting this forward again, and therefore I thought that those who went to me […] all think […] out of envy or jealousy to believe that the thing could succeed. From Reims, the nineteenth of June; and I beg you to be assured of my fidelity in doing you service. He agrees to the Duke of Elbeuf's ransom at fifty thousand écus, which […] […] to raise on the towns; there are messieurs dispatched for that. Louis XIII’s letter of 1631 to his resident at Genoa and the cipher passages of Melchior de Sabran’s letter-books of 1633 and 1635 (BnF Baluze 155, fr. 4134, fr. 4135) share one cipher. George Lasry recovered its key with CTTS in 2022 and in 2026 deciphered 18 letters from 43 images: the Prince of Monaco, a plot to seize Savona for Savoy, Genoa in the war of 1635. One code and seven listed leaves are open. 58 e2 y2 11 r q 8 m n h1 a+ e1 55 c2 8 e3 9- y1 7 r b 10 … que touche ledit prince de Monacho … 7 a k = A · 8 n = E · 55 = prince · 35 = Genes · 2 = doubled letter Dijon and Genoa → Paris · homophonic letters with a word nomenclator · 1631–1635 · key recovered by George Lasry The Louis XIII–Sabran cipher, 1631–1635 from Louis XIII → to Claude Bouthillier Go to the full text ↓ One cipher served the King’s letters to his resident at Genoa and the resident’s reports home. George Lasry recovered its key from the cipher alone and deciphered 18 letters, from Monaco to a plot to seize Savona. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 21 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (96% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by George Lasry (solution) and Harumi-Matsuba (verification) · Also credited · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (96% of the cipher) The letters Louis XIII to Melchior de Sabran, French resident at Genoa, Dijon, 28 March 1631; and 17 letters of Sabran to Bouthillier, secretary of state, copied in his letter-books of 1633 and 1635. All in French. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France: Baluze 155 f. 79 (DECODE R2748); Français 4134 ff. 46v–73v; Français 4135 ff. 132–252. All on Gallica. The cipher 22 letters with up to four signs each (letters, digits and invented shapes), 41 two-digit codes for common words, ten signs for names, and signs that double the letter before them. How it was solved George Lasry recovered the key in 2022 with the built-in cryptanalysis of CTTS (CrypTool Transcriber and Solver), from the King’s letter. In October 2026 he transcribed all 43 images and completed the code list with Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI Codex. Re-checked here mechanically, statistically and against an earlier independent reading. What it says The King keeps the Prince of Monaco in play without a treaty (1631); a sergeant-major offers Sabran the castles of Savona, a plot Savoy is running, and it is discovered (1633); Genoa helps the Spanish fleet while France fights for Valenza (1635). Credit Key, transcription, edition and translation by George Lasry (pull request 84). An earlier AI reading of nine 1633 leaves by Harumi-Matsuba (issue 56) agrees with his on 88% of the letters. Still open One code (46); 212 name signs read from context only; a few runs that do not read; a 1636 copy in another key, too short to break alone. With the context-only name signs and these runs counted as holes, the written-out reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 92.9% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. The other seven leaves listed beside the 43 images carry no further cipher, except a short margin note on f. 218r, read here. This page joins two earlier entries: Louis XIII’s letter of 1631, which had its own page, and a partial reading of the 1633 letter-book sent in as issue 56. They are one cipher, so they are one entry.
sabran1633.html#letters

Melchior de Sabran was the King’s resident at Genoa from the end of 1629 to about 1638. Français 4134 and 4135 are his own letter-books: copies of his despatches to “Monsieur Bouthillier”, with the secret passages copied in cipher. Claude Bouthillier countersigned the King’s letter of 1631; his son Léon, comte de Chavigny, held the office from March 1632, and which of the two received each later letter is not settled. Most photographs show only part of a letter. sabran1633.html#key

George Lasry’s key sheet, with the signs as the fr. 4134 clerk wrote them. Codes in brackets with a question mark are identified from context. Image: George Lasry, key sheet drawn in CTTS from BnF Français 4134 (Gallica), 22 Oct 2026. Letters. 22 letters, each with one to four signs: lower-case letters used for other letters, digits (7 = A, 8 = E, 9 = I, 10 = O, 11 = V) and invented shapes. There are 51 letter signs in all; S has four. Word codes. 41 two-digit numbers for common words and syllables, numbered in the order of their first letter: 17 bon , 24 ce , 26 de , 35 Genes , 47 monsieur , 55 prince , 59 que , 66 tion , 68 vous . Names. Ten signs for names, identified from their context: France, Spain, the Republic (of Genoa), Savoy, the Senate, Parma, Mantua, Piacenza, an agent, and Garbarino. Doubling. Three signs repeat the letter before them. The clerks’ hands differ from leaf to leaf, so the same sign can look different. The clerk of ff. 57 and 242v–245v, for example, writes H with a straight stem and F as a script L, where the others use a “6” and a straight b.

Baluze 155 f. 79r: the first cipher passage, on the Prince of Monaco and Sabran’s stay at Genoa, and the start of the second. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Baluze 155 f. 79r, via DECODE R2748. The King thanks Sabran for his despatches and answers two points. The cipher carries the first, the Prince of Monaco, who had offered through his agent Orazio Rossi to come over to France. In George Lasry’s reading the King declines the conditions, and keeps the door open: je n’ai pas ivge a propos d’y entendre pour plvsievrs bonnes raisons, n’y de faire venir ici le sievr Rossy … sans entrer pour le present en avcvn avtre traicte avec luy, ny avssi faire avcvne rvptvre de la negociation Richelieu broke off the Monaco talks after the peace of Cherasco so as not to offend Savoy; Monaco came under French protection only in 1641.
sabran1633.html#savona

Français 4134 f. 50v, the page with the most cipher (276 signs), with George Lasry’s decipherment in red: sergent maior des chasteavx ve savine nomme garbarin (“ve savine” for de Savone ). Image: BnF Français 4134 f. 50v (Gallica); decipherment overlay by George Lasry in CTTS. In June 1633 Garbarino, sergeant-major of the castles of Savona, offered to hand them to France or to Savoy. Sabran passed the offer in cipher to the French agent in Savoy and kept out of sight, suspecting a trap. In the summer Garbarino came back dressed as a peasant and set out Savoy’s plan; Sabran sent him away without an answer. In September the plot was discovered and the munitioner of Savona and two others were brought to Genoa. Genoese histories record Giambattista Garbarino of Sassello, executed for treating with Victor Amadeus of Savoy; Sabran’s letters show the affair from the French side. From the letter on f. 57 (summer 1633), with the enciphered words in bold: qu’il luy faisoit scavoir le lieu ou seroit les echeles , celluy ou debvoit arriver mile homm[e]s seullement par mer , nomme le fornace , vn mile sur savone a deux mousquettades de l’endroict dv chateav “He let him know the place where the ladders would be, and the one where a thousand men were to land, by sea only, named Le Fornace, a mile from Savona, two musket shots from the castle.” Français 4134 f. 66r, 23 September 1633: the plot discovered. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 4134 f. 66r, via Gallica (BnF IIIF).
sabran1633.html#campaign

The nine letters of 1635 (Français 4135) follow the first year of the open war with Spain. France, Savoy, Parma and Mantua besieged Valenza from September to the end of October and failed; on 13 September a Spanish fleet took the Lérins islands off Provence, and Genoa, formally neutral, let it use its ports. Sabran’s ciphered passages propose to reopen the Monaco talks or to surprise Monaco with troops from Pinerolo (“fewer than thirty Spaniards” there), to take Tortona and Serravalle and prefer Novi to Gavi so as not to alarm Genoa, and record that Genoa’s state inquisitors paid his own servants 25 écus a month. The last letter, of 18 December, reports 4,000 Spaniards landed at Vado. The French text and English translation of all 18 letters, with notes, are in George Lasry’s READING.md .

S. Tomokiyo lists eight more places in the same cipher: Français 4134 f. 51; Français 4135 ff. 217, 226v, 227v, 231v, 239v, 243; and Baluze 156 f. 157. Each was examined on the Gallica image on 22 October 2026. In Français 4135 his folio numbers name two-page openings, so both pages of each opening were examined. No further cipher. f. 51 is all clear: it is the start of the letter of 2 July 1633 whose cipher is on f. 52, already deciphered. Ff. 217r, 226v, 228r, 231v, 239v, 240r and 243r are clear. The faint cipher under the letter on f. 227v is ink showing through from f. 227r; in mirror image it matches that page line for line. The other pages of these openings are among George Lasry’s images. One image renumbered. Lasry’s image “215v” is f. 216v. Letter 11 runs from f. 216r to f. 216v and ends there, so the passage printed first in his edition is its close. A margin note. Beside a “+” on f. 218r are two cipher lines (17 signs) that his transcription lacks. With his key they read [c]a d’avoir / [s]antimant : the cipher of the clear words at that place, “a d’avoir … [res]sentiment”. Baluze 156 f. 157 is another cipher. It is a copy of 9 February 1636, written at Genoa after Sabran had left for court. It reports that Duke Doria, at the Lérins islands, was gathering the Spanish galleys of Naples and Sicily for a design on Marseille. Its 136 symbols (15 runs) are lower-case letters, digits and doubled strokes. Neither Lasry’s table nor Tomokiyo’s Servien–Sabran key of 1632 gives French. Two cribs fit: “munitions en galeres de genes ”, if code 36 is galeres as in Lasry’s list, and “faire donner audit”. Together they give ten symbol values. An annealing solver run inside the clear context gives no French, with or without them: about five signs per letter type is too little.

Word cover. 84% of the deciphered text falls in French words of three letters or more. The same measure gives 92% on the King’s letter, which George Lasry deciphered in full in 2022, so that is its ceiling; shuffled keys give 37%. Against an independent reading. Bartolomeo Tantucci to messer Antonio del Vescovo, 25 August 1528 (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 17, DECODE R4805), endorsed “questa cifara è quella di Balìa”. George Lasry recovered the 41-sign homophonic key from the ciphertext alone with CTTS and Claude; about 85% of the 282 signs read: bishoprics for the nephews, the Cardinal of Naples and Pitigliano. Bartolomeo Tantucci → Antonio del Vescovo, Siena · homophonic substitution · August 1528 · key recovered from the ciphertext alone Siena no. 17: Tantucci in the cipher of the Balía, 1528 Go to the full text ↓ A Sienese letter of August 1528 with three secret points of government set in cipher between clear connecting words; George Lasry recovered its key from the ciphertext alone and about 85% of it now reads. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered from ciphertext-only · Extent: partial (85% of the cipher) Contributed by George Lasry (solution) ciphertext-only At a glance Ciphertext-only break · partial (85% of the cipher) The letter Bartolomeo Tantucci to messer Antonio del Vescovo, rector of the cathedral and member of the Balìa, from Sarteano(?), 25 (or 20) August 1528. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2 “Lettere in cifra”, no. 17; DECODE R4805, catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher Homophonic substitution, 41 signs, no word division: up to five signs for each vowel, every double letter written with two different signs, and the ordinary “che” abbreviation used as a sign. How it was deciphered George Lasry transcribed the cipher in CTTS; Claude recovered the key by frequency and contact analysis, isomorphs and cribs (15–17 October 2026). What it says Rumoured bishoprics for “the nephews”, the Cardinal of Naples and the affairs of Pitigliano, and a plan to cut off victuals; “parlo breve et in substantia perché la cifra vuol così”. Still open The opening words of two points and one phrase; “el Mustetto”, the Countess and the “Otto”. With them, Lasry’s reading builds coherent sentences and reads at 94.3% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. Credit George Lasry, with CTTS and Claude: transcription, key and reading, sent by email to Daniel Bourdeau on 17 October 2026. This page reports his result. This letter belongs to the Sienese bundle of cipher letters, in which each letter has its own key. The two other sixteenth-century Sienese pieces in George Lasry’s report, no. 15 (Bandini, 1547) and R4794 (the unnumbered artillery slip) , are different ciphers, each with its own page; the bundle is described on its own page .

George Lasry’s reading, unchanged (cipher and clear text together; abbreviations expanded in brackets; (?) and [?] as in his edition): 1528. Molto mag[nifi]co et generoso Cavaliere etc. poi che V.S. è absente al mag[istra]to di Balìa, li comunicamo alcune cose importanti del governo, acciò possa intender cose che occorranno, haver lo intrinsico. In prima qua per molti et quasi publico, non che el Mustetto(?) l’à(?) a certe promessioni di non so che vescovadi per li nipoti; non so se è vero. Secundo [?]o a date(?) vi dà lo Cardinale di Napoli circa le cose di Pitig[l]iano, perché v’à parentado; et anco è stato cosa de la contessa quando erano giovani; pare che aon [con?] essa n’abbi facto lo amore. Terzo Otto(?) volendo lo avere, lco[??]stren[?]niare, non vi vada vittuaria né siano lassate praticare lo nestro [nostro] contado. Parlo breve et in substantia perché la cifra vuol così. M[esser] Bart[olo]meo Lamilucci(?) [Landucci?], quale era segretario da la Pratica, et la potrà leggere agevolmente. Di Sart[ean]o(?) a dì 25(?) di agosto 1528. … Deditissimo Bart[olome]o Tantucci questa Cifara [è] quella di Balìa His translation: “Since Your Lordship is absent from the magistracy of the Balìa, we communicate to you some important matters of the government … First: here, among many and almost publicly, [it is said] that the Mustetto(?) has(?) certain promises of I know not what bishoprics for the nephews; I do not know whether it is true. Second: the Cardinal of Naples has(?) given and gives [his hand] in the affairs of Pitigliano, because he has kinship there; and it has also been a matter of the Countess, when they were young … Third: the Otto(?), wishing to have it, [in order to] constrain(?) [it] …, let no victuals go there, nor let [anyone] be allowed to deal with our contado. I speak briefly and in substance because the cipher wants it so.” Address: “Al mag[nifi]co et generoso cavaliero M[esser] Ant[oni]o del Vescovo rectore Dig[nissi]mo de la eccl[esi]a cattedrale. Cifara.” In August 1528 Siena was governed by the Balìa of the popular regime that had expelled the Noveschi in 1524–25; Pitigliano was an Orsini county under Sienese suzerainty, and the “Cardinal of Naples” should be Vincenzo Carafa, created cardinal in November 1527 (George Lasry’s identifications, which he marks as not verified).

Most magnificent and generous Knight etc. Since Your Lordship is absent from the magistracy of the Balìa, we communicate to you some important matters of the government, so that you may understand the things that will occur and have the inside knowledge. First: here, among many and almost publicly, [it is said] that the Mustetto(?) has(?) certain promises of I know not what bishoprics for the nephews; I do not know whether it is true. Second: the Cardinal of Naples has(?) given and gives [his hand] in the affairs of Pitigliano, because he has kinship there; and it has also been a matter of the Countess, when they were young: it seems that he made love with her. Third: the Otto(?), wishing to have it, [in order to] constrain(?) [it] ..., let no victuals go there, nor let [anyone] be allowed to deal with our contado. I speak briefly and in substance because the cipher wants it so. Messer Bartolomeo Lamilucci(?) [Landucci?], who was secretary of the Pratica, [is there] and will be able to read it easily. From Sarteano(?), on the 25th(?) of August 1528. Most devoted Bartolomeo Tantucci. [Endorsement:] This cipher is that of the Balìa. Address To the magnificent and generous knight messer Antonio del Vescovo, most worthy rector of the cathedral church. Cipher. Contents From: Bartolomeo Tantucci To: messer Antonio del Vescovo, rector of the cathedral, member of the Balìa Place: Sarteano(?) Date: 25 (or 20) August 1528 — dated in the clear text Tantucci writes to messer Antonio del Vescovo, rector of the cathedral, who is away from the Balìa, to give him 'the inside knowledge' of three matters of government, each put into cipher between clear connecting words. First, it is said here by many and almost publicly that the 'Mustetto'(?) has(?) certain promises of I know not what bishoprics for 'the nephews'; he does not know whether it is true. Second, the Cardinal of Naples has intervened and intervenes in the affairs of Pitigliano, because he has kinship there, and also because of the Countess, with whom, when they were young, he seems to have had a love affair. Third, the 'Otto'(?), wanting to have Pitigliano, mean to constrain(?) it: no victuals are to go there, and no one is to be allowed to deal with 'our contado'. He speaks briefly and in substance 'because the cipher wants it so', and names messer Bartolomeo Lamilucci(?) [Landucci?], formerly secretary of the Pratica, as the man who will be able to read it easily. The letter is dated from Sarteano(?) on 25(?) August 1528, signed 'Deditissimo Bartolomeo Tantucci', and endorsed 'questa cifara è quella di Balìa'. Historical context and dating In August 1528 Siena was governed by the Balìa of the popular (Libertini) regime that had expelled the Noveschi in 1524–25 and repulsed the papal–Florentine attack at Porta Camollia on 25 July 1526; the city [report page 27] leaned on the Emperor, while the restored Florentine republic (1527–30) was at war with Charles V and the Pope [Hook, Siena: A City and its History, 1979; Roth, The Last Florentine Republic, 1925; Malavolti, Dell'historia di Siena, 1599]. Sarteano, in the Val di Chiana on the Florentine border, was a Sienese subject town. Pitigliano was an Orsini county (Count Ludovico, son of the condottiere Niccolò, then Gian Francesco) under Sienese suzerainty, a standing object of Florentine and Roman interest [Bruscalupi, Monografia storica della contea di Pitigliano, 1906]. The 'Cardinal of Naples' of 1528 should be Vincenzo Carafa, archbishop of Naples from 1505, created cardinal on 21 November 1527 [Eubel, Hierarchia Catholica, III]; this identification, his kinship with the Orsini and the affair with 'the Countess' are not verified here. The 'Otto' are unidentified: Florence's Otto di Pratica had given way to the Dieci di Libertà e Pace in 1527, so a Sienese body is possible. The 'Pratica' of the former secretary is likewise unidentified. Open points. Unidentified: “el Mustetto”, the Cardinal of Naples (Vincenzo Carafa?), the Countess (of Pitigliano?) and the “Otto”. A cipher slip on the league of the Duke of Milan and the Marquis of Ferrara against Venice and the offer of Bianca Maria Visconti to Leonello d’Este (Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 8, DECODE R4797). The clear memorandum on the same sheet is its contemporary decipherment: aligned sign by sign, it gives a simple substitution key that reads all 166 cipher signs. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 18 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The document A slip of six lines, clear cursive mixed with cipher, under a clear memorandum on the same sheet. Unsigned and undated; c. 1440–41 from its contents. Where Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308, fasc. 2 “Lettere in cifra”, no. 8; DECODE R4797 ( Concistoro_2308_51 ), catalogued “1500–1599” with no status. The cipher A simple substitution in letter-like signs: two signs for a , one for s and ss , one for u , v and b , and two name signs, for the Duke of Milan and the Venetians. How it was deciphered The memorandum’s last three paragraphs open with the slip’s clear words. Aligned letter for letter with them, the four cipher runs give one consistent key, which reads every sign. What it says The articles of a league between the Duke of Milan and the Marquis of Ferrara to make war on Venice; the Duke “aveva dato madonna Biancha a missere Leonello”, the Marquis’s son. Still open The memorandum’s first four paragraphs decipher a covering letter that is not on the sheet. Writer and date are not given. Credit The contemporary decipherer of the memorandum. George Lasry’s report of 17 October 2026 listed no. 8 as not yet deciphered and called a link with the memorandum “possible but speculative”. This page puts the alignment to him. The other pieces of the Sienese cipher file are listed by key on the Concistoro 2308 index . Nos. 7 , 19 and 21 are different ciphers, with their own pages; none fits this key.
siena8.html#sheet

The upper two thirds of the sheet are a clear memorandum in seven paragraphs. Each paragraph opens with an underlined catchword, and the words after it run on as plain prose: the layout of a decipherment, where the clear words of the ciphered letter are copied and the cipher after them is written out. The first four paragraphs (the Marquis of Ferrara “rimesso nel duca di Milano a fare guerra e pace”, “di papa Felice”, Niccolò Piccinino, Lucca) belong to a letter that is not on this sheet. The fifth opens “Nel polizolo dicto segue”, “in the said slip there follows”, and the last two catchwords, Anchora disse and antiveduto questo , are clear words on the slip below. The slip. Clear cursive at the start of line 1, “Anchora disse” in line 3, “e stato antiveduto questo” in line 5; everything else is cipher. Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 8, via DECODE R4797. The project’s inventory of 24 September 2026 took no. 8 as deciphered at the time, from the memorandum’s contents alone. George Lasry’s report of 17 October 2026 lists it as not yet deciphered, “c. 400 symbols”, with no interlinear plaintext, a relation to the memorandum “possible but speculative”. On 18 October the slip was transcribed sign by sign and aligned with the memorandum, and the alignment settles the question.

The memorandum’s last three paragraphs, transcribed here (catchwords in italics): Nel polizolo dicto segue : [ modo? ] leggiere e capitagli e legha fral duca di Milano el marchese di Ferrara a fare guerra a Viniziani e sua legha. Anchora disse el duca di Milano aveva dato la donna Biancha a misser Leonello figlolo del marchese. Antiveduto questo e no puo manchare che questo udrete grandissimi facti. The decipherment above the slip: “Nel polizolo dicto segue”, then the three paragraphs that match its cipher runs. Image: Archivio di Stato di Siena, Concistoro 2308 fasc. 2 no. 8, via DECODE R4797. The slip’s four cipher runs, deciphered with the key rebuilt from that text (in the cipher’s own spelling; names in brackets are single signs): le|giere e chapitoli e legha fra [duca di Milano] el marchese di ferrara a fa|re [ guerra , faint, in clear] [Viniziani] e sua legha [duca di Milano] aveva dato madonna Biancha a missere Leonello filgliuolo de marchese e non puo manchare che questo udirete grandissimi fatti “… to read the articles of the league between the Duke of Milan and the Marquis of Ferrara, to make war on the Venetians and their league. He also said that the Duke of Milan had given Madonna Bianca to messer Leonello, the Marquis’s son. This being foreseen, it cannot fail that you will hear of very great deeds.” The pattern words leave no room for chance: 5 9 T 9 5 is aveva (the shape ABCBA), F T W W 2 W 2 is ferrara , L T Z PHI T L L Z is leonello ; the sign 7 is d in dato , madonna , di , de and udirete , and the two a signs never stand for anything else. The cipher and the memorandum differ only in spelling ( chapitoli / capitagli , madonna / la donna , fatti / facti ).

Twenty-one letter signs and two name signs, rebuilt from the alignment (sign names as in the transcription, targets/siena8/transcripts/no08.txt ): Letter Sign Letter Sign a z-shaped 2; hooked long s m I-beam c cross n stroke through a ring (φ) d 7 o 2 with a crossed foot e b with a crossed ascender (once a small raised 2) p hooked long stroke f o with a tail q hooked q (once) g η-like n r double ring h c s, ss long s joined to a crossed h i double long stroke t square l two rings joined u, v, b 9 duca di Milano: double cross with four dots Viniziani: box-like H The key is not among the filed keys compared by eye in September; the two keys of about 1440 that name the same persons, R4748 (“Cifra cum fratre Bernardino”) and R4749, have not yet been compared with it sign by sign.
siena8.html#date

The Marquis whose son is Leonello is Niccolò III d’Este, who died on 26 December 1441; “papa Felice” in the memorandum is the antipope Felix V, elected in November 1439; and Bianca Maria Visconti married Francesco Sforza in October 1441, so the report that her father had given her to Leonello belongs before that. The slip therefore dates from between November 1439 and October 1441 (most likely 1440–41). The writer, perhaps a Sienese envoy at Milan, is not named. This dating is proposed here, not written on the sheet.

The covering letter whose cipher passages the memorandum’s first four paragraphs decipher: not on this sheet and not among the DECODE photographs of the busta. Doubtful signs: a faint group in line 3, read as the clear word guerra ; the end of the s sign in sua ; the missing l of de(l) ; the p of puo ; the q and u of questo , which occur only once. None changes the reading, which the memorandum gives. George Lasry’s confirmation of the alignment, and whether he counts c. 400 symbols for the whole slip with its clear words (the cipher signs alone are 166).

Five despatches from Genoa, June to August 1523 (DECODE R9488–R9498), in two ciphers; no earlier decipherment was found. The key of the earlier cipher was recovered from the ciphertext alone with a solver scored on 1520s Castilian; the key of the later one was rebuilt from a Soria letter of December 1523 filed with the court’s decipherment. The June and July letters are deciphered nearly throughout, the later ones in part: the Venetian league, Siena, money for the Swiss and Andrea Doria’s offer of his galleys. pT937pcq · Og9cba qoPPaeq · sig lod saq · leh rap Otaviano · Campofregoso · Rey de Francia · en Italia Genoa → Charles V and Gattinara · two ciphers: graphic letter signs with a small code, then a homophonic alphabet with a large code · June–August 1523 Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 to Charles V Go to the full text ↓ Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro A-28 (9/28) ff. 248–584 · DECODE R9488–R9498, eleven records, all marked Non-decrypted (no decipherment known) · five letters and their duplicates Key B rebuilt from DECODE R9844, a Soria letter of December 1523 with the court’s decipherment · key A recovered from the ciphertext alone with a solver (simulated annealing) · a split entry: the key-A letters count as a ciphertext-only break, the key-B letters as a key recovered from external plaintext Daniel Bourdeau · posted 19 September 2026 · updated 6 November 2026 Method · key A (June and July letters): key recovered from ciphertext-only (complete) · key B (from late July): key recovered based on plaintext from external sources (partial) · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) ciphertext-only At a glance Key recovered · key A from the ciphertext alone (complete); key B from external plaintext (partial) The letters Eleven ciphered letters of Lope de Soria to Charles V, 1523–24: five despatches from Genoa, June to 13 August 1523, most in two or three copies, one to the chancellor Gattinara. DECODE lists them as not deciphered. Where Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid (DECODE R9488–R9498 and related); Bergenroth calendared only the letter of 13 August, from its clear parts. The cipher Two ciphers; Soria switched in late July. Key A has about twenty-five graphic signs and a few code words; key B is a homophonic alphabet with a large code of three-letter groups ( sub que, xab Francia). How it was read Key B was rebuilt by aligning a Soria letter of December 1523 (R9844) with the court’s decipherment beside it. Key A had no crib: a simulated-annealing solver scored on Castilian state papers found the alphabet from about a thousand transcribed signs. What it says The league with Venice being closed, the French king’s expected descent on Italy, a proposal to open war on the Venetians, and Andrea Doria offering his galleys to the Emperor. Still open The June and July letters are deciphered nearly throughout; key-B passages are deciphered in main content. Code groups rip, pur, qed and mul in key A and a dozen in key B are open.

No key for either cipher survives among the keys DECODE has from the same collection (BRAH 9/15, R9815–R9832), which were checked one by one. soria1523.html#keys

Key B (from late July 1523) is a homophonic alphabet of Latin-looking letters and signs, with two to four signs for the commoner letters, and a large code of three-letter lower-case groups: sub que, zog de, yed en, xab Francia, soc rey, zic principe, pic tab su Magestad, pup tab V. Magestad. The same cipher is in DECODE R9844 (BRAH 9/30 ff. 34–37), Soria to Gattinara, 30 December 1523. Its decipherment is on ff. 36r–36v, and aligning the two gave the first thirty groups and most of the letters. The Genoa letters then added the rest. Key A (June–July 1523) has about twenty-five graphic signs (ʒ, crossed ʒ, ⊖, α, ε, φ, π, ꜑, the tt ligature, the figures 2 3 7 9) and a handful of lower-case code words. The writer kept the word divisions. Its values: plain signs plain signs a 9, ꜑ n c o α, ꝓ (alone = que ) s ε, π e ʒ, crossed ʒ t ꜩ d c+ꜩ ligature l 2 u/v 3 i (b) 7 c ⊖ g (a) ꜑ with double bar r small o, L, Y m ∂ p б y φ f ♀, long-stemmed hook x m-sign Code words: cap que, lod de, leh en, luc duque, lih Milan, cip Venecia, mos infanteria, lim mil, sig lod saq Rey de Francia, rap Italia. The copies of the June letter spell out uenecia , infanteria and mil where another copy uses the code word, and that fixes three of them.
soria1523.html#method

The key-A block of the July letter (f. 444r–445v, 32 lines) was transcribed into ASCII names for the signs, with the code words set apart. The counts pointed to a near-monoalphabetic cipher. There were few signs; one sign stood alone ten times, which had to be y ; and one pair, c before the tt ligature, never separated, so it was a single sign. A simulated-annealing search over sign-to-letter maps was scored with a character 4-gram model of Danvila’s edition of Castilian state papers of 1520–21. It returned la liga general , cinco mil infantes , exercito and con la esperança from random starts in a few seconds. The remaining values, the homophones for a , o and e , and the code words were then fixed by hand. They were checked against the two other copies of the June letter and the duplicate of the July letter, which use different homophones in the same places. The work took one session; the model was given the images and nothing else for this cipher.

… escriven de Milan como tenian nueva que era arrivado en Venecia un secretario del duque de Milan, el qual avia traido el mandado del Infante para concluir la liga con los venecianos, y que por esto el duque de Milan avia prometido al dicho Infante diez y ocho mil ducados, y que con esto tenian por cierto que se concluiria la dicha liga, y por esto se partia con diligencia el protonotario Caracciolo para ir a Venecia. Y ansi mismo escriven de Milan como aviendose [comen]çado de amotinar la infanteria … les avian enviado una paga … an escrito el duque de Milan y el señor Prospero al duque [de Genova] que quiera esforçarse de ayudar con alguna suma de dineros, y el respondio que no puede dar dineros, pero que tomara quinientos infantes de los del exercito para que esten aqui y los pagara por un mes … de manera que nadie atiende sino a su propio interese. The league of Venice with the Emperor was signed on 29 July and published on 15 August 1523. Here it is still being bought, with Milanese money on the Archduke Ferdinand’s mandate.
soria1523.html#july

[…] de Leon escriven a los veinte y tres del mes pasado como lo esperavan, que vendria muy presto el Rey de Francia para pasar en Italia; pero hasta agora no se juntava gente de guerra para que puedan pasar tan presto con exercito. Podria ser que pensasen de pasar con solo la gente d’armas, con esperança que calaran los [qed], y con la esperança de los venecianos, y pensando valerse de los cinco mil infantes que tiene en Provença … Y creo que los dichos [rip] usaran con [pur] los tratos que uso Otaviano Campofregoso quando se fizo la liga general y pasava este Rey de Francia en Italia, que una vez nos deçia que querria entrar en la liga y otras veçes dava palabras por dilatar, fasta que paso el dicho Rey, y a la ora el se declaro nuestro enemigo … fuera bueno començarles luego la guerra. Desto se seguirian dos buenos efetos: lo uno, que se desgravaria el estado de Milan del aposiento del exercito y estaria mejor alojado en el Bergamasco y Bresano; y lo otro, que luego seria tomado Bergamo, de donde podrian sacar dineros para alguna paga a la infanteria. Y no seria milagro que se tomase presto Bresa o Verona. The [rip] can only be the Venetians or their government, still undecided a fortnight before they joined the league. Soria recalls how Ottaviano Fregoso, Doge of Genoa in 1515, strung the league along and then declared for France once Francis I had crossed the Alps. The closing and the post data of this letter are in key B. They report that Monsieur de Beaurain has arrived; Adrien de Croÿ, sieur de Beaurain, was the Emperor’s envoy to the Duke of Bourbon that summer.
soria1523.html#gattinara

A long paragraph on Siena. The Sienese “comunidades” might be freed from their “tiranos” and governed as a republic. Soria argues that things voted by many are hard to carry through where opinions are divided, and that the Emperor would be better served by one man governing “de mano de su Magestad”. Y al cabo creo que avra de venir a esto, porque los seneses, de la condicion que son, que cada qual querra ser señor, y los otros no piensan sino solo en su propio interese. The first seven lines keep several open groups. A short passage names Beaurain again, at Turin.
soria1523.html#july26

Beaurain carries this letter. Three days earlier a Piedmontese courier left by land for the Abbot of Nájera. Soria asks that the Emperor provide twenty-eight thousand escudos to a doctor at Constance to pay certain Swiss who have agreed to descend on France, and twelve thousand to a treasurer. The names of the doctor and the treasurer are not deciphered.
soria1523.html#august

Andrea Doria y el principe de Salerno estan muy descontentos del rey, porque les avia quitado la enpresa de esta ciudad y la avia dado al bastardo de Saboya; y a me [hablado] uno que se dize Jeronimo Doria, que es uno de los principales de esta ciudad, de parte del dicho Andrea Doria, y dizen que si V. Mag. [quiere] aceptar en su servicio al dicho Andrea Doria con sus quatro galeras, que el lo servira de muy buena voluntad … Andrea Doria and the Prince of Salerno are discontented with the King of France. He had taken the enterprise of Genoa from them and given it to the Bastard of Savoy. Jeronimo Doria, one of the leading men of the city, spoke to Soria on Andrea Doria’s behalf: if the Emperor would take him into his service with his four galleys, he would serve “de muy buena voluntad”; and “lo mismo me a dicho de parte del principe de Salerno”, he has told me the same on behalf of the Prince of Salerno. The passage was collated with the duplicate R9498, which spells in code some words R9497 spells in letters ( pep un, tun parte, xap le) and so fixed quitado , uno and quatro . [hablado] ( xuf yic ) is graded I and [quiere] ( sob e; seb sob∞ is qualquiera in R9491) M. A second passage: Soria has pressed Antoniotto Adorno to make the republic pay what it owes under the capitulation [made in the time of Pope Leo]. Adorno has asked Martin Centurion to take it up with the Emperor. On 6 November 2026 this second passage and its last lines on f. 579r were also collated sign by sign with R9498. Every spelled word agrees. The duplicate writes pac for sobre . Its tec ∞ in the Salerno sentence showed that R9497’s z7∞ is spelled in letters, me a (z = m, as in acometido ), not a code group for hará . The 13 August letter measures 404/408 units read (99.0%). Andrea Doria came over to Charles V only in 1528, so this is an early approach.

Key A code words not fixed: rip (3x, the Venetians, graded C), pur (3x, the Emperor’s side, M), qed (2x, the Swiss, M), mul , dus , cop , and the opener TZ . Key B groups still open or guessed: yac , fob , taf , tu , pel , pug , zib , sib , xif , sab , 7 pes , per ; guessed: paf tiempo, tin papa, sud respuesta, xa hasta (M). Decipherments of R9491 lines 1–7 and the personal names in R9494 are graded M. The written-out reading of R9491 builds coherent sentences but reads at 88.1% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. The rest of the key-B passages are C, and the June and July key-A texts H/C. Not collated sign by sign: R9490 (spot checks only), R9493 (checked at the doubtful words), R9496. R9498 is collated in full (block 1 on 30 September, block 2 on 6 November 2026); paf , sud and xuf yic are the same groups in both copies and stay context-only.

Decryption read_r9488.md # R9488 / R9489 / R9490 (9/28 ff. 248-253), Soria to Charles V, Genoa, June 1523 — key A, reading One letter in three copies. Cipher block f. 248r-248v (R9488), 28 lines, transcribed and collated with R9489 (full) and R9490 (spot checks) in keyA_june.txt. Decoded with the key-A alphabet (keyA.md) plus R = f, Y = r. Code words fixed here: cap = que, lod = de, luc = duque, lih = Milan, cip = Venecia (R9489 writes cip where R9488 spells 'uenecia'), mos = infanteria (same), lim = mil (same). Open: dus (2x), cop (1x), nra (L17). ## Reading (normalised spelling kept close to the letter; [ ] = tentative) [... y ansi mismo] escriven de Milan como tenian nueva que era arrivado en Venecia un secretario del duque de Milan, el qual avia traido el mandado del Infante para concluir la liga con los venecianos, y que por esto el duque de Milan avia prometido al dicho Infante diez y ocho mil ducados, y que con esto tenian por cierto que se concluiria la dicha liga, y por esto se partia con diligencia el protonotario Caracciolo para ir a Venecia. Y ansi mismo escriven de Milan como aviendose [comen]çado de amotinar la infanteria de [dus], les avian enviado una paga, y que con esto pensavan de sosegarla por agora; y para esto, y acabar de pagarles lo que se les deve, an escrito el duque de Milan y el señor Prospero al duque de [Genova] que quiera esforçarse de ayudar con alguna suma de dineros, y el respondio que no puede dar dineros, pero que tomara quinientos infantes de los del exercito para que esten aqui y los pagara por un mes; y pareceles que con esto descarga de gasto al exercito y guarda mejor esta ciudad, y quita el uso a los que tienen cargo por [dus] de pedirle dineros, y a el de darlos; de manera que nadie atiende sino a su propio interese. ## English They write from Milan that news had come that a secretary of the Duke of Milan had arrived in Venice with the Infante's mandate to conclude the league with the Venetians; for this the Duke of Milan had promised the Infante 18,000 ducats, and so they took the league as certain, and the protonotary Caracciolo was leaving in haste for Venice. They also write that the infantry having begun to mutiny, a pay had been sent them, with which they hoped to quiet it for now; and to finish paying what is owed, the Duke of Milan and Signor Prospero [Colonna] have written to the Doge [of Genoa] to make an effort to help with some sum of money. He answered that he cannot give money, but will take five hundred infantry of the army to be here and pay them for a month; they think this relieves the army of cost, guards this city better, and ends the habit of those in charge of [..] asking him for money and his of giving it: so that no one looks to anything but his own interest. Context: the Venetian league with the Emperor was concluded on 29 July 1523 and published 15 August (CSP Spain vol. 2 no. 587); Marino Caracciolo was the imperial protonotary sent to Venice. And so I think the [rip] will do: they will delay the agreement with [pur] until they see what the King of France will do; and if they see that he has the means to come or to send an army into Italy, they will be his friends and will make no agreement with [pur]. sp106r725.html#dating

DECODE dates the records “1558–1625”, the span of the volume. The words the codebreaker recovered date them closely, because they belong to one year: Marques Inichiosa : the Marqués de la Inojosa, Spain’s ambassador extraordinary in England from the spring of 1623 until he was recalled in the summer of 1624. C. Barberino : Francesco Barberini was made cardinal in October 1623, the nephew of the Pope elected that August. Il Principe and Re d’Inghilterra : Prince Charles and James I, with the Prince distinguished from his father, as he was in every despatch of the Spanish Match. Palatinato , liga , Papa , Nuncio , Imbassiatore di Venetia , Stato , Governo , Cattholico . That is the London of 1623–24: the Prince back from Madrid, the Spanish embassy under suspicion, the Palatinate unrecovered, the papal dispensation and the Venetian ambassador at the centre of the traffic. The DECODE note on R657 wondered whether the hand was Thomas Phelippes’s; Phelippes died in 1625 and had long been out of favour, and on this evidence the file is his successors’ work.

The sender and recipient are therefore given with a query: Turculeț by the key, Sieniawski by the collection.

Translation R7481_en.md # R7481, Polish news from Bender for Hetman Sieniawski, [summer 1709]: English translation Translated from `R7481_reading.txt` (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026): the whole letter is cipher (key B), checked against the interlinear gloss and the contemporary fair-copy decipherment on p. 3, which agree. Nothing is unread. The writer's Latin phrases are translated; "WMM Pan" (Waszmość Miłościwy Pan) is rendered "Your Gracious Lordship". ## Translation From here this comes to hand: seven hundred unarmed Swedes with Colonel Gyllenkrook ("Gilenkruk") have gone over to Suceava (Soczawa) and are still staying there. After them some eight hundred Cossacks also went over, but many of them have run away; barely four hundred are left. The Turks are gathering at Bender, but in very small numbers, and the time for their designs has already passed. The King of Sweden, with Mazepa, is then to go to Suceava, and from there to Rákóczi. Whatever occurs to me in future I shall not fail to report. The letter to Your Gracious Lordship written on the business of the frontier is only a pretext for communicating things worth knowing. In confidence, however, I earnestly beg that it should not be made public that Your Gracious Lordship will have news from me as well. Bien des gens pretendent que la defunte Czarine n’a jamais eu la moindre intention de faire un pareil testament. Que c’est une piece supposée et fabriquée entre le Prince Menzicoff? et le Baron Osterman et le Sr Macarif, secretaire du cabinet de la Czarine, dont ce dernier imitoit parfaitement la signature, et qui par ordre de cette princesse avoit souvent signé des actes d’importance. Ces mesmes gens donnent pour raison de leur doute à cet egard qu’il faut que si la piece est veritable la Czarine n’ait changé de sentiment par rapport à sa succession que trois heures avant sa mort. Car quelques jours avant son decès on voulut luy insinuer de declarer le Grand Duc pour son successeur. Elle repondit qu’elle entendoit que la princesse Elizabeth sa fille luy succederoit. Ils ajoutent que les princesses et M. le duc d’Holstein n’oseroient s’inscrire en faux contre cette piece pour deux raisons, dont la première est que leurs partisans trois ou quatre jours avant la mort de la Czarine ayant esté mis en prison et deposés de leurs charges elles se trouvent aujourd’huy sans le moindre appuy en Russie. p79 Necessaires pour que ce mariage se fasse le plustost qu’il se sera possible, et ils n’auront pas grande peine à y reussir car il n’y a plus personne icy qui ose s’opposer aux volontez et au pouvoir du Prince Menzicoff?. C’est peut estre la seule clause de ce testament dont M. le duc d’Holstein obtiendra l’execution, car s’il ne prend pas de luy mesme le party de sortir de Russie il s’y trouvera forcé par les desagremens qu’on luy donnera. On pourra neantmoins avoir encore quelques menagemens pour luy pendant quelques mois. Il n’y a pas 4 mois que la Czarine a reconnu ces parents qui consistent en un frère, une sœur, 3 neveux et 3 nièces. Les biens consistent en plusieurs maisons et terres que le defunt Czar avoit confisquées sur des seigneurs rebelles et dont il avoit fait une donation à la Czarine. Elles peuvent rapporter 30000 roubles de rente. La question est de sçavoir si on mettra ces pauvres parents en possession de ces biens. Ce seroit pe[u] connoitre la Russie que de croire que l’on payera? à ce duc non seulement le million de roubles que la defunte Czarine laisse à la duchesse aussy bien que la pension de 100000 roubles qu’elle luy a assignée. Je ne sçais mesme si on luy laissera partager les pierre[r]ies et meubles que cette princesse a laissez. p81 On pretend avec justice que M. de Rabutin? a eu beaucoup de part à la confection de ce testament. Ainsy il ne faut pas douter que l’Empereur n’en garentisse l’execution, parceque cette garantie luy donne de s’immiscer dans les plus importantes affaires de Russie. p123 Dans d’autres carosses à six chevaux estoient les dames d’honneur tant de la Czarine que de ses deux princesses. Mr le duc et Mme la duchesse vinrent recevoir Sa Majesté à la portiere de son carosse, et on fit trois decharges de plusieurs petits canons d’une livre de balle qui estoient sur le quay en face de l’hostel d’Holstein. Ce jour la mesme on distribua au peuple et aux soldats quatre bœufs rotis et 40 barriques de vin. Hier tout le monde a repris le deuil excepté la maison de Mr le duc d’Holstein qui ne le reprendra que dans huit jours. Voilà, Monseigneur, ce qui s’est passé de plus remarquable de ce mariage. Si on en juge par l’exterieur les nouv[e]aux mariez paroissent forts contents l’un de l’autre. Peut estre M. le duc avoit il fait ses essais de mariage avec des femmes difficiles à contenter et qui luy avoient donné le mauvais renom qu’il avoit parmi le beau sexe. Je tiens d’une de ces femmes ce que j’ay eu l’honneur de vous marquer à son sujet dans ma precedente, non dans la p124 Veue d’egayer ma lettre, mais parce que je sçais qu’il est important qu’un ministre sache si un prince qui aspire à une couronne est en estat d’avoir des successeurs . Mr Des Campredon m’a communiqué l’ordre que Vostre Grandeur luy a envoyé pour faire partir le Père Cailleau que nous n’avons jamais pû determiner par de bonnes raisons à prendre le parti de sortir de Russie de son propre gré et se rendre à Riga pour profiter de l’occasion d’un vaisseau françois qui doit bientost partir pour France. Pour ne le point espouvanter, nous ne luy avons rien fait entendre des ordres du Roy à son sujet mais seulement fait envisager que les moines ayant eu depuis peu un sort fatal en Russie il estoit à craindre qu’il ne luy arrivast aussi quelque fâcheuse catastrophe. Comme il n’y a point de bastimens françois à Petersbourg et que le Roy n’a pas jugé à propos de fournir de l’argent pour le voyage de ce religieux et de l’officier russe qui l’escortera jusqu’à Riga, Mr Des Campredon et moy avons jugé à propos de faire faire une queste parmy les François p125 Qui sont icy pour subvenir aux frais de ce voyage. What it says The old duke courts the condottiere he had fought a year before: Cremona under Venetian attack, Asti promised to the Dauphin for French help, Cosimo de' Medici, the new pope, and again and again a plea to come. Credit Sixteen of the nineteen slips were deciphered before: the Duke's own chancery or Sforza's filed a decipherment or a later copy next to every slip in italien 1584, and a nineteenth-century copyist deciphered two of the 1446 slips into italien 1597. Three slips of December and November 1446 have no clear text that could be reached and are deciphered here. What is new is the key's identification. Still open Parts of 12 December and the cramped verso of 1 November, from low-resolution images of an undigitised volume; scattered words elsewhere; one slip (f. 145) and one translation (f. 131) not reached. One more slip of the Duke's, of 23 January 1447, is in his second key and has its own page . The cipher letters his envoys Marcolino Barbavara and Pietro da Pusterla sent Sforza in the same months, in another key, are on their page .

f. 8, Abbiategrasso, 11 January 1447. The first line reads “Come altre volte ve habiamo avisato ne pare”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1584 f. 8, via Gallica (IIIF canvas 11). In the winter of 1446–47 Filippo Maria Visconti, last of his line, was losing his war with Venice. Cremona, the dowry town of his daughter Bianca Maria, was threatened, and the man who could save it was her husband Francesco Sforza, whom the Duke had fought the year before. The Duke wrote to him, often several times a week, on small parchment slips wholly in cipher. Sforza kept them, and his archive came to Paris with Louis XII's conquest of Milan. Mazzatinti's inventory of 1883 marks twenty-one of them “In cifre: membran.”. The key, in an eighteenth-century copy headed “Filippo Maria Duca di Milano”: the alphabet with its homophones and the start of the syllable table. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Carteggio Visconteo-Sforzesco cart. 1597 no. 23, via DECODE R5323. The Visconti chancery's cipher books are lost. Copies of fifteenth-century keys made in the Milan archive are kept in Carteggio Sforzesco cart. 1597 and are on DECODE as anonymous key records dated “1450–1555”. Two are headed with the Duke's name. No. 23 fits the slips at once: on f. 8 the first nine signs give come al t r e v ol t e , the opening of the translation filed beneath it. Letters have two to six homophones (e is ÷, ·‖·, ⊢ or a blot); every vowel-and-consonant pair has its own sign (ab, ac … uz); che, per, come, quando, non, perché and six other words have signs; and names have looped signs: the Duke of Milan, the Pope, the Venetians, the Duke of Ferrara, the King of Aragon (Re de Ragona), Rome, the men-at-arms, the Conte d'Urbino. Use on the slips identified three of the copy's blank labels: Á is Cosimo de' Medici, a looped sign with two crosses is the Marquis of Mantua, and a looped sign the copy gives for the Duke stands for “Dux Mediolani” in his title. Two traps: the syllable sign written par is os and per is or, while the word per has a sign of its own. The full table, with what was added from the slips, is in targets/visconti1446/key.md and the workers' notes in texts/key_additions_*.md .

Eight of the eleven letters in italien 1584 have the chancery's decipherment of the time on the next leaf, and every one has a later fair copy as well. f. 8 deciphered with the key agrees with its translation f. 9 on 571 of 589 compared signs (96.9%), f. 5 with f. 6 on 602 of 624 (96.5%). Nearly every difference is the translator smoothing the cipher's Lombard spelling ( tenire , mazore , se fara ) or a word he dropped. The later copies are in one regular italic hand, headed “Altra simile” where they cover a duplicate; the same hand copied Barbavara's letters in this volume. The f. 29 copy follows the wording of the duplicate f. 31, not of f. 30, so whoever made it deciphered the slips themselves. For ff. 30/31, 36/37 and 64/65 the copies were in view while the slips were deciphered; for ff. 83 and 94 samples were deciphered first and then matched the copies at 99.2% and 98.5%. A correction. The first version of this page said ff. 23/24, 72 and 102 had no clear text. They do: f. 25 and f. 103 are the decipherments of the time (f. 103 had been taken for a parallel letter), f. 73 is a later copy. A second session working the same slips found them, and found nineteenth-century copies of the 1446 slips ff. 110 and 136 in italien 1597. The readings of ff. 23/24, 72 and 102 had been made without those texts, so they are a fair test of the key alone: they agree with the clear texts on 83–88% of words when spelling variants are counted (64–73% exactly). The misses are mostly verbs read in the wrong tense or person and a few clauses rebuilt wrongly around unread signs ( ve mandaremo for vi mandassemo , intentione for affectione , tenire l'estato for tegnire celato ). The copies of ff. 110 and 136 were made by deciphering the slips, not from the originals. The f. 110 copy writes gi where the cipher has the group read vuy , and leaves a blank, marked “V+”, at both places where the slip has the one name sign the key leaves unlabelled. The cipher and copy part in a few places, and the cipher's value is kept in the text: Panaro where the copy has Tanaro , le cose vostre where it has nostre .

They are given in the cipher's own Italian, with gaps marked [..]. 31 December 1446 (ital. 1583 f. 158) Illustris gener et fili noster carissime. Perché vui sapiate che [..] in le cose nostre dezà, ve[?] aviso che, come le [gente d'arme] nostre furono rote, mandasemo Thomase da [Roma] in Franza come[?] domandare soccorso; el quale, esendo prima[?] andato dal duca de Savoia, non havise [se] non parole. Dapoi, vedendo [..], che l'andase dal Dalfino, et lo trovò benisimo disposito de darne bono et groso [s]occorso. [..] sapevamo che se gli [..] no dificultate alcuna [..] come despecto[?] [..], gli facevemo proferire che, dandone el dicto soccorso, gli daresemo Ast in le mane soe; et così cred[i]to[?] che 'l dicto Thomase concludeva a nostro nome in quela forma. Ulterius ve avisamo come li Francesi cercano [..] havere [..], et siamo quasi certi che, stando le cose come le stano, [..] gli capitarà in le mane. [..]ve confortamo et pregamo che ne vogliati avisare del parere vostro circa che è dicto. Data Cusaghi die ultimo Decembris. Filipus Maria Anglus Dux Mediolani et cetera, Papie Anglerieque Comes ac Ianue Dominus. In English. When our men-at-arms were routed we sent Thomase to France to ask for help. He went first to the Duke of Savoy and had nothing but words, then to the Dauphin, whom he found most willing to give good and large help. We had it offered that we would put Asti in the Dauphin's hands, and believe Thomase concluded on that in our name. We ask your opinion. 25 November and 12 December 1446 (ital. 1583 ff. 130, 154) 25 November (88% of signs read): Sforza's brief of 14 November came by Perino da Cotignola; Cosimo de' Medici has always been well disposed, but the men of this world look only to the present; the Duke begs Sforza to come at once, to dispose of the men-at-arms and of the Duke's own person, and to say whether he will stay in the Marche or come to Lombardy. 12 December (80%): Donino has come from Sforza; Pietro da Pusterla and Antonio da Trezzo are to go to him secretly; the Duke awaits answers from the Pope and King Alfonso, begs Sforza to conclude at once and in secret, and wants letters to pass secretly through Cotignola. 1 November 1446 (ital. 1583 f. 110), with its copy f. 136, Milan, 29 November 1446, one of the two 1446 slips with a nineteenth-century copy in italien 1597. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 136, via DECODE R7907. The longest slip, read against its copy: 96.5% of the recto's signs and 69.6% of the cramped verso. After the rout of his army the Duke drops his grudge. Sforza has said many times he would never join him out of necessity; now his kind letter has changed the Duke's mind: “havemo deliberato non esere cosi pertinaci et obstinati come siti vui”. He will never act against Sforza's state, will pay his provision if Venice stops it, and will give him horse and foot at his own cost for any enterprise except against the Church and the King of Aragon. Dealings are to go through men beyond the Panaro, not through the Duke's own servants, who had made each suspect the other. He asks for a quick conclusion. The texts of all nineteen slips, the decipherments and the copies are in the full texts below and in targets/visconti1446/texts/ .

ital. 1584 and the copy volume ital. 1597 were fetched full size from Gallica's IIIF image service (canvas numbers in the table); Gallica's own viewer refuses scripts. ital. 1583 is not digitised (the BnF record gives only a microfilm), so its slips were taken from the DECODE images, about 1,700 pixels wide and binarized. Two sessions worked the slips in parallel and were merged: f. 110 and f. 136 are the other session's transcriptions, aligned sign by sign with their 1597 copies; ff. 130, 154 and 158 are this session's. A language-model decoder for the sign families the scans merge was tried on f. 136, where the copy fixes every value, and got 56% of the ambiguous signs right, so it was not used. Each slip was deskewed and cut into strips along its own baselines, transcribed sign by sign and deciphered with the key by worker agents, one or two slips each, and checked by the main session. A second pass re-cut bent lines and re-read every doubtful sign. The duplicated letters were deciphered side by side: two encipherments of one text fix each other's homophones. Read shares are measured from the token files: signs given a value over signs that are not nulls.

Translation f110_en.md # BnF ital. 1583 f. 110r-v (DECODE R7902): English translation. Filippo Maria Visconti to Francesco Sforza, 1 November [1446] Translated from `f110_text.md` (the cipher reading). Gaps in the cipher are kept as [...]; words in square brackets are supplied from the context. The recto reads almost in full; the verso is cramped and about a third of its signs are unread, so its sentences are broken. [name] is the name sign left blank in the duke's key. Illustrious son-in-law and our dearest son. Many and many times you have told us that you would never bring yourself to be with us out of necessity, in such a way that we could say we had had [you] out of necessity [...] and not by your own good will. That was never our view: for the stronger and more powerful you had been, being one and the same thing with us, so much the better it would have [...] for our state and for us. And it seems to us that fortune has been very favourable and kind to you and has provided well for this, because no danger that [has] arisen in the past has made you willing to change your mind; and now you can say that in doing so, that is, in coming to be one and the same thing with us, you will do it of your own will and not out of necessity. We assure you that since the rout that befell our troops, we have always persisted in the view that we would rather suffer the Venetians to have our whole state than that you should have even one crumb of it; and in this view we persisted until we received this brief of yours, [the duplicate?] of the one you wrote dated the fourth of this month. Having understood it well, and considering how kindly you have been moved to write to us, so that it does not seem to us you could have done it with more kindness if we were your father or your son or the dearest thing you have in this world, it has made us change our mind entirely; so that we have resolved not to be as stubborn and obstinate as you are, for we do not wish to say at all that we have no need of you. On the contrary, we say that we have as much need and necessity of it as could be said, and we believe we could not have a greater one than we have. So that if you come to our aid [now], we shall be all the more obliged to you for doing it, since we are in the greatest need that could come about in this world. We therefore tell you that we are content to come to a good understanding with you, and we have resolved never to act against you, in your state or in your affairs; and as regards your own particular interests, that is, your person, your company and your state, to do all that you will know how and wish to ask. We say the same of the [name]. In the matter of the Venetians we are also content to do as you wish and as you please, provided that they keep nothing of ours beyond what they held before the rout of our troops. We remind you that we mean to be a good father to you and to have you as a good son, and we wish and intend that from this hour on you may always deceive us in your own way; for whatever you do, we shall always believe you do it for good and to a good end, and in good faith and not in bad. We earnestly urge and beg you that from now on, in all the matters you will have to treat with us, you treat them either through the hands of your own trusted men who are from beyond the Panaro and have no dependence on this side, or through those of our men whom we trust. We remind you that the chief cause of all the quarrels there have been until now between you and us has been our having had your affairs handled through the hands of our men who were suspect to us, and who have been the cause of making us suspicious of you as well. We further tell you that if, because of this understanding of yours with us or for any other cause whatever, the Venetians should take away from you the pay they give you, we are content [to give] you the same pay that the [name] give you, so that you may maintain your state [and your men].
